en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Vajra said:
In the beginning, the Blessed One declared to me that victory would belong to Bharata.
Having heard which, O Brahmin, I know myself to be free from all taint.
O Bhārgava, the essence of this narrative is pleasant to hear and heart-pleasing.
And various stories were told by you, O sinless one, in connection with that.
And they are flavorful, O knower of dharma, and they cause the destruction of all sins.
O Brahman, those [women] whose minds were captivated by me through my attachment... (3)
Those stories have been introduced and those very same ones have been abandoned; tell them to me once again.
O Blessed One, knower of all phenomena, whose stainless vision perceives the ultimate reality directly!
But those stories which were previously introduced in the course of other narratives.
Having become separated by a very great distance from Rāma, who was self-realized.
I wish to hear those very [teachings] from you, O scion of Bhrigu's lineage.
Having reached the world of Varuṇa, Rāma, the scion of Bhṛgu’s lineage, [remained there].
O Lord of the gods of gods, what more indeed did the learned Pracetās ask?
Explain all of this to me, for I have a great doubt regarding it.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard that reckoning of time as spoken by Rāma to Pracetas, [he was amazed].
Thereafter, he questioned the god Varuṇa concerning the duties of kings.
Being questioned by the son of Jamadagni, the Lord of Waters spoke to Rāma.
O noble one, hear from me the duties of kings as expounded by Puṣkara, my son.
He has heard the duties of kings from the thousand-eyed god.
O best of the twice-born, he understands the duties of kings exactly as they are.
Having spoken thus, he then summoned Rāma and likewise his son.
He said, "O son, tell me the duties of this descendant of Bhṛgu."
In whatever matter doubt may arise for this high-souled one, [he shall ask].
Therefore, O dear son, drive that away from me by my word; may it be well with you.
Having been addressed thus, he replied, "So be it," and led the best of the Bhrigus from his house.
There he explained to him the highly exalted duties of kingship.
Questioned by Rāma, the son of Varuṇa declared the duties of the best of kings.
O moon among kings, you have taken these great treasures from the earth for the protection of the entire world.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Rāma’s Journey to the House at Puṣkara," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Seated comfortably in the abode of Puṣkara, that best of men—
Rāma, ever devoted to righteousness and having conquered his senses, questioned Puṣkara.
Rāma said:
Tell me, who am asking you, what is the most important duty for a kingdom?
O illustrious one, son of the king of the aquatic hosts, [this was] at the very beginning.
Puṣkara said:
O knower of dharma, the duty of the kingdom is indeed the consecration of the king.
Moreover, the Dasyus overcome a kingdom that is without Indra and lacking in strength. || 3 ||
In kingdoms without a king, the establishment of dharma does not exist.
O Bhārgava, there is no established order of castes and stages of life;
in kingdoms without a king, a maiden is never given in marriage.
That [desire] does not exist for me at all, nor does it exist for anyone else regarding riches. || 5 ||
The principle of self-nature would prevail, and likewise, there would be the destruction of the universe.
In this world, there would be no one at all who carries out the word of a teacher.
The three twice-born castes shall not study the triple Vedic knowledge.
The sacrifice to the gods would not take place, and consequently, there would be drought.
Both the world of men and the world of gods would become objects of doubt.
A terrible epidemic would prevail if the king did not protect his subjects. ||8||
For the sake of protecting the subjects, he was empowered by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
He is born as a king among humans, possessing a body with the nature of a god. || 9 ||
When he is pleased, the grace of the Lord arises.
When he is angry, the anger of these people arises.
O Rāma, a king is born from great accumulations of merit.
O Rāma, the entire world abides by the word of that one alone.
In those regions, the fourfold caste system arises, each remaining established in its own duty.
In those regions, O Indra among kings, where a righteous king reigns. || 12 ||
There shall be no pestilence, nor famine, nor likewise fear of fire or thieves.
And there is no fear of wild beasts for those for whom the king is devoted to dharma. (13)
First one should obtain a king, then a wife, and then wealth.
Under a bad king, where can this people find a wife, and where can they find wealth? (14)
Therefore, with every effort, the lord of men [should act] toward the chief of the realm.
Having been examined by his predecessors, he should be made a righteous man who is true to his promise.
For those on earth whose king is ever devoted to righteousness, there is no fear whatsoever in the world.
Therefore, O lord of men, a king should be diligently disciplined by the principal officers of the realm. ||16||
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Praise of Kings," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning Rāma, within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Puṣkara said:
He was endowed with all the primary and secondary marks of a great man, disciplined, and pleasing to behold.
He was not dilatory, possessed of a righteous soul, having conquered anger and subdued his senses. || 1 ||
Generous, possessing great energy, and one who speaks with a smile.
Handsome, endowed with noble lineage, swift in action, and possessed of great strength. || 2 ||
Devoted to Brahman, free from deceit, firm in devotion, and sweet-spoken.
Free from greed, restrained in speech, profound, and pleasant to behold. || 3 ||
Neither excessively harsh nor devoid of punishment, he moves straight ahead with the spies as his eyes.
When a legal dispute arose between his son and an enemy, he remained impartial.
He has undergone rigorous training in chariot warfare, elephant combat, horsemanship, archery, and physical exercise.
He was devoted to fasting and austerity, a performer of sacrifices, and dear to his teacher.
Dependent upon his ministers and the astrologer, he never retreats in battles.
He was one who knew the proper time, was grateful, and indeed discerned the distinctions between men.
He who constantly honors those worthy of honor, and likewise punishes those deserving of punishment.
He is the one who employs the sixfold policy and is likewise endowed with the [three] powers. || 7 ||
And the lord of the earth should be depicted as adorned with many qualities, both those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned.
Having assembled with the foremost leaders of the realm, he of undaunted spirit acted appropriately for the sake of protecting the kingdom.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Kings," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning the words of Puṣkara addressed to Rāma, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 3 ||
Puṣkara said:
Thus, they would choose a lord of men who is filled with a multitude of such virtues.
Having assembled together, the most eminent men of the realm [should install] a Kṣatriya born of noble lineage. || 1 ||
And chosen by them, the king, having conquered his senses, should undertake the vow.
"I shall protect all of you who abide in righteousness; there is no doubt in this."
Having undertaken the vow, one who desires a kingdom should choose an excellent Brāhmaṇa.
The king [performed] this for one year for the happiness of this entire world.
Possessing all the marks of excellence, disciplined, and pleasing to behold.
He was handsome, endowed with a graceful appearance, and always possessed of a majestic mien.
To one who speaks of the dangers, who is steadfast, constant in Dharma, and has conquered the senses;
One who is free from physical defects, not having extra limbs, and who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. || 5 ||
One who knows the reality of the sixty-four limbs and is skilled in the processes of reasoning and refutation.
He is the knower of the past, the present, and the future, and he is especially skilled in the science of calculation.
Just as a night is without its moon, or a crown from which its gem has fallen.
Likewise, O best of kings, astronomy is deficient without mathematics.
One who is orthodox, full of faith, and well-disposed toward the lord of the earth.
Having gone to the astrologer, the king, restrained and pure, should choose [a day]. || 8 ||
O lord of men, by means of which the king who was consecrated has indeed perished.
O best of kings, a wise man should not choose such a person for a year-long sacrifice.
The king [should not appoint] one who is deficient in limb, nor one who is talkative, nor one who lacks presence of mind.
One who is poorly dressed, filthy, shaven-headed, an atheist, and of sinful resolve. || 10 ||
One should always choose a bridegroom who possesses good qualities, even if he has a divided livelihood.
But having chosen them, they should be addressed by the king himself.
Just as the gods have Agni as their mouth, so do subjects have the king as their mouth.
Just as the mantras have Agni as their mouth, so do the royal astrologers.
You are my mother and my father, as well as my guide and my teacher.
Fate and human effort must always be understood by you. || 13 ||
O knower of dharma, may prosperity be yours; for the kingdom is indeed common to us both.
O best of beings, that auspicious god must be brought by you yourself for my sake.
I must achieve my goal through human effort, and likewise, I must engage in battle.
If he should consider that to be a great virtue of the king. || 15 ||
Or rather, he who quickly [discerns] the virtues and faults of men through his wisdom;
In the conflict between the stroke of fate and human effort, wisdom [prevails]. || 16 ||
But the wise one did not consume the Vāḍava fire at that time, with his very permission.
The king should then appoint the minister and the domestic priest, as previously designated.
And that best of kings should choose as his queen the one thus designated.
Then, that knower of the divine should prepare the requisites for his consecration.
One should provide an elephant and a horse for the examination of that king.
And the auspicious throne, the parasol, and the yak-tail fan as well. || 19 ||
Likewise, the sword-jewel, the bow, and various other precious gems.
O lord of men, all those who were [ministers] of the deceased king—|| 20 ||
Therefore, those [omens] should not be taken into account by the king, according to that astrologer.
If another [king] is not available, it may be performed by a ruler for a year at his pleasure.
One should not perform those actions which, as I have stated elsewhere, are intended for one who possesses superior qualities.
There, neither the elephants were well-maintained, nor the warriors, nor the king’s mother, nor his father, nor any kinsman.
In this matter, even a learned astrologer who knows the dharma may become negligent, whereby his prediction fails here in this world.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Annual Observances," within the narrative of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||4||
Rāma said:
What kind of priest and what kind of minister should be appointed by a king?
And likewise, who was the eldest queen? Tell me that as I ask you. || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
One who is free from physical defects, endowed with auspicious marks, well-disposed, and speaks kindly.
One who is learned in the Atharvaveda and proficient in the Yajurveda.
The king [appointed] a Brāhmaṇa learned in the two Vedas as his domestic priest (purohita), who was an Atharvan.
One should choose a Sudarśana who knows the ritual procedure for the five kalpas. ||3||
The Nakṣatrakalpa, the Vaitāna, and thirdly, the Saṃhitā-vidhi.
The fourth is the Kalpa of the Aṅgirases, while the fifth is the Śānti-kalpa. ||4||
Having obtained a preceptor who is knowledgeable in the ritual procedures of the five kalpas, the king—
With all portents of calamity stilled within himself, he enjoys the earth for a long time. ||5||
And he should always perform that daily duty for the king at all times.
Likewise, one devoted to the words of the astrologers performs rites for specific occasions as well as those for desired ends. ||6||
However, the king must not be abandoned by the astrologer or the domestic priest.
But one who has fallen [from his status] must be abandoned; there is no need for deliberation on this point. ||7||
In the same way, O Rāma, those two who have fallen must not be abandoned by the king.
O Indra among kings, by the abandonment of those two, one should predict the loss of the kingdom. || 8 ||
And in the next world, there is undoubtedly a miserable rebirth for a long time.
However, a domestic priest who acts in contradiction to the almanac (or the science of time) should be dismissed by the king.
The domestic priest is otherwise [to the king] than his mother or his father.
One should ward off his undesirable calamity born from the affliction of fate.
Where can atonement for that [sin] be found by the king, O Brāhmaṇa?
As long as the king has not [appointed] two learned men, namely the astrologer and the domestic priest...
If their means of livelihood are cut off, the king's family shall perish for three generations.
Therefore, one should always avoid cutting the skin of those two, for that leads to hell.
And a division of immovable property between those two must especially be made.
O knower of dharma, [appoint] the astrologer and the domestic priest in accordance with their respective qualifications.
The king should always regard the priest, who is like his own self, as a moon in the lineage of Bhṛgu.
Just as a king ought to have his own kinsmen, so too should he have a wise man as his royal priest. || 14 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Family Priest," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
Likewise, the minister of the king should likewise be endowed with all auspicious marks.
He was a Brāhmaṇa who knew the true essence of the Vedas, humble, and pleasant to behold. || 1 ||
He is liberal, highly energetic, devoted to his master, and speaks kindly.
He understands in every respect the political science (nīti) proclaimed by Bṛhaspati and Uśanas.
Out of passion or hatred, kings do not speak according to what ought to be done.
He for whom no fear arises from public censure or for the sake of the king. || 3 ||
Likewise, he who is patient with afflictions, self-conquered, and has mastered his senses.
He was one whose counsel was secret, skillful, wise, and beloved by his devoted followers.
He knew the truth regarding gestures and physical expressions, and was skilled in the processes of reasoning and refutation.
He was heroic and learned, yet neither arrogant nor envious.
Skilled in the movement of his spies, he was resolute in his vows and possessed of self-mastery.
He was a knower of the true principles of the sixfold policy and likewise skilled in the means [of statecraft].
The speaker is the ordainer of actions; he never allows duties to be neglected.
He was impartial toward the king’s servants and likewise fond of virtue.
He knew the proper time, he knew the right occasion, he was grateful, and he was beloved by the people.
And he is the observer of actions both performed and unperformed. || 8 ||
She was appointed to the Arhats as was appropriate for each individual man.
O best of the Bhṛgus, these matters should be carried out behind the king's back during times of conflict.
O King, having performed [this], the relative gravity or lightness of actions has been explained.
He knows the distinction between enemy and friend, and understands the true nature of the basis for conflict.
O descendant of Bhrigu's lineage, he should perform all the king's duties.
One should act only after things have been understood by the ruler of the earth, not when they are unknown.
O Bhārgava, having performed these tasks while remaining unknown to the lord of men.
Before long, that minister will also come to harbor hatred toward you. ||12||
O Lord of the Earth, he who performs various duties...
There is never any breach of his [treaty] with the king at any time.
Such shall be the minister of that king who delights in his word and possesses these qualities.
The kingdom shall be stable, wealth shall be abundant, and the lineage shall be illustrious even throughout the three worlds. || 14 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Ministers," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
The king’s chief queen should be one who is honored for possessing all the auspicious marks.
She was disciplined, devoted to her guru, and free from envy and anger. || 1 ||
Devoted to the king's pleasure and welfare, she was elegantly dressed and spoke pleasantly.
She knows both those who have been supported and those who have not, and she looks after those who have been supported.
And she set the laborers who had not yet been hired to work for wages.
And she who is always free from passion and hatred toward her co-wives. (3)
She attended to all of them with food, seating, and drink.
She who behaves toward the sons of co-wives just as she does toward her own son; || 4 ||
She always honors the ministers, the year-long officials, and the councilors.
She was devoted to Brahman, endowed with compassion, and sympathetic toward all living beings.
They are also known throughout the provinces as being grateful for what has been done and ungrateful for what has not been done by the king.
She took delight in the wives of other kings, filled with joy. ||6||
She is always the one who dispatches messengers and others at the gates of kings.
And through that means, she especially knows the affairs of the lords of men.
Endowed with such a multitude of virtues, she was blameless in the company of the lord of men.
She should be consecrated in the kingdom by the king who is established in his realm.
Thus, whenever such a lady of great majesty became the wife of that moon among kings, [the following occurred].
The kingdom of that king, along with its inhabitants, shall attain prosperity; there is no doubt about this. ||9||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Chief Queen," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Rāma said: [This applies] to men as well as women, along with elephants and horses.
And likewise of the yak-tail fans, the umbrellas, and the auspicious throne. || 1 ||
Of jewels, bows, and swords as well, O son of a god.
I wish to hear its definition; explain it to me as I ask.
Puṣkara said:
First, indeed, I shall proclaim the characteristics of men.
Listen to that as I speak it, O enhancer of the Bhṛgu lineage!
He who possesses one additional [digit] and two white [digits], and likewise pervades with three;
O Bhārgava, he has three folds on his belly, is bent at three points, and knows the three periods of time.
A man would be well-characterized and likewise expansive in three respects.
Likewise, there is the Caturlekha, and similarly the Catuḥsama. || 5 ||
He has four cubits, four fangs, and likewise four black [features].
He has four fragrances, four short [limbs], and likewise five subtle [features].
O best of the Bhṛgus, he is five parts long and likewise six parts high.
Seven are the attachments, eight are the pillars, and nine are the stains of the stations.
He has the ten marks of a lotus and the circumference of a great banyan tree.
The pair of fourteen equal [syllables] and that which is called sixteen is praised. || 8 ||
Rāma said:
Those qualities of the Puruṣa beginning with "one plus one" (two) which were described by you—
I wish to hear those [details] exactly as they are, O son of Varuṇa.
Puṣkara said:
Every person is attached to dharma, artha, and kāma.
But he who is especially distinguished in the Dharma should be known as one who exceeds by one.
The eyes were without pupils, and likewise the teeth were white.
O Rāma, he who possesses thirty-two [teeth] is proclaimed as "Double-White" (Dviśukla). || 11 ||
That embodied being whose chest, navel, and thighs are deep [is fortunate].
O knower of dharma, he is proclaimed to be the best of men, profound in three ways.
Freedom from envy, compassion, and patience—these three are proclaimed as one [virtue]. || 12 ||
Contact with auspicious customs and purity—these are another triad.
Effortlessness, lack of miserliness, and sovereignty—these three groups consist of three each.
He is celebrated as having three protrusions: by means of his two arms and his scrotum.
And by their direction, region, birth, and creation, as well as by their splendor, fame, and fortune.
O best of the Bhṛgus, he who pervades by means of three [qualities] is remembered as Vyāpin.
That embodied being whose abdomen has three deep folds [is one who has attained perfection]. || 15 ||
O best of the Bhṛgus, he is called the supreme among men who possesses three folds on his belly.
He likewise bowed down before the deities, the twice-born, and his teachers.
O best of the Bhārgavas, he is always declared to be the Puruṣa Trivinata.
He knows the proper distribution of time for the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
He who knows the Dharma and practices it is called a knower of the three times.
That embodied being whose forehead and face are broad and expansive [attains prosperity]. || 18 ||
O best of the Bhrigus, that Vipula was declared to be a man among the three [classes].
The two hands and likewise the two feet are adorned with banners, parasols, and other such ornaments. || 19 ||
That human being is designated as "four-lined" (caturlekha) by means of his lines.
The fingers, the chest, the back, and the hips of which are likewise equal. ||20||
O best of the Bhṛgus, that Puruṣa is declared to be fourfold.
It is ninety-six finger-breadths in height and four cubits in measurement.
O knower of dharma, that [length] is proclaimed to be four cubits by means of measurement.
His four fangs, resembling the moon, protrude from his teeth. || 22 ||
He who knows something of that [Dharma] is proclaimed as Caturdaṃṣṭra, the knower of Dharma.
The pupils of the eyes, the eyebrows, the beard, and likewise the hair are black. || 23 ||
He who possesses these four black [qualities] here is called the best of men.
In the nose, the mouth, the sweat, and the armpits, O best of men. (24)
But that which has a fragrant scent is proclaimed to possess the fourfold fragrance.
His two arms, knees, thighs, and cheeks—these four are indeed equal. || 289 ||
O best of the Bhṛgus, it is declared that for a man, [the lifespan] is fourfold.
Indeed, his fragrance was equal to that of lotuses situated between the mouth and the blood.
O best of the Bhrigus, he was called "Caturgandha" by the twice-born.
Likewise, the male organ and the neck of the embodied being are short, as are the shanks. (27)
O tiger among the Bhārgavas, that [meter] in which there are four short syllables is proclaimed [as the Jagatī].
The joints of the fingers, as well as the nails, hair, teeth, and skin;
O Rāma, that which possesses those subtle elements is called the fivefold subtle body (pañcasūkṣma). || 28 ||
The chin, the eyes, the forehead, the nose, and the space between the breasts.
O Rāma, the wise know him whose [limbs] are long as "the five-longed one. || 29 ||
The chest, the armpits, the nails, the nose, the mouth, and the nape of the neck.
He who possesses six elevations here is called "Six-Elevated."
Skin, hair, body hair, teeth, sight, speech, and likewise nails;
The learned declare him to be "unctuous" (snigdha) here on earth who possesses these seven unctuous qualities. || 31 ||
O Rāma, both your shanks are like the shafts of a chariot, and likewise both your arms are like the shafts of a chariot.
And likewise the two thigh-bones and the backbone, O Bhārgava. (32)
He whose nasal bridge is even is proclaimed as one with eight auspicious marks (aṣṭavaṃśa).
The eyes, the two nostrils, the ears, the penis, the anus, and likewise the mouth; || 33 ||
He whose nine apertures are stainless is indeed "nine-pure" (navāmala).
The tongue, lips, palate, the corners of the eyes, the nails of the hands and feet, and the breasts—these are [the marks]. || 34 ||
He whose penis, tip, and chest—these ten parts of his embodied form—are as radiant as lotuses;
The hands, feet, face, neck, ears, heart, and head. || 35 ||
The forehead, the belly, and the back—these ten are large and are honored.
From the space between the tips of the middle fingers of his outstretched arms here.
He whose height is equal to his circumference is "well-proportioned like a banyan tree" (nyagrodhaparimaṇḍala).
That best of kings, honored with all auspicious marks, was thus described.
The feet, the ankles, the buttocks, the sides, the testicles, the eyes, and the jaws.
The ears, lips, thighs, shanks, hands, arms, as well as the eyebrows. || 38 ||
He for whom these fourteen pairs are indeed equal [is a knower].
That best of kings is said to have fourteen equal pairs [of limbs]. || 39 ||
The fourteen branches of knowledge that have been mentioned here,
And that best of men, O Rāma, beholds with his two eyes. || 40 ||
O best of the Bhṛgus, he who is rightly called "Sixteen-Eyed" in the world has been described.
The body is coarse, with prominent veins, and likewise devoid of flesh.
Everything foul-smelling and impure is praised as being the opposite [of what it appears]. || 41 ||
His gaze is serene and his speech is sweet; his gait is as majestic as that of a rutting elephant.
And from each single pore, hairs arise; the being has leaped up with a smile that is not excessive. (42)
For the weary, a vehicle; for the hungry, food; for one overcome by thirst, a drink; and for others, protection.
O best of the twice-born, they say that the man in whom these qualities exist at the proper time is a fortunate person, preeminent on this earth.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Men," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
A teacher who is a woman, beautiful in all her limbs, and possessing the gait of an elephant in rut.
She who has heavy, broad hips and eyes like those of an intoxicated pigeon. ||1||
She possessed dark-blue hair, slender limbs, and a voice like that of a cuckoo.
She has a slender waist, hairless limbs, a lustrous complexion, and is captivating. ||2||
Her lotus-like feet touch the entire ground.
The navel is spiraled clockwise, and likewise, the breasts are closely set.
The lower lip is well-defined, and likewise, the gaze is sweet.
The secret [place] is clockwise-rotating and resembles a leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha). ||4||
Her two ankles are hidden, and likewise her two hollows of the hips are concealed.
And for her, from the center of the navel, it should be the size of a thumb. || 5 ||
The calves are not bound by muscles, and likewise the waist is not pendulous.
His belly is pendulous, and his eyes are not squinting. ||6||
The hair on the body is tawny, and the head-hair is likewise coarse.
Nor should she be named after a tree or a river, nor named after a deity or a mountain.
Nor should it be named after a snake, a gandharva, a bhūta, or a preta.
Neither talkative, nor greedy, nor deceitful, nor fond of quarreling. ||8||
She is neither greedy, nor malevolent, nor is she one who carries a broken begging bowl.
She was devoted to the worship of gods, the twice-born, the perfected ones (siddhas), and holy men.
Endowed with virtue and endowed with good qualities, she is neither veiny nor hairy. || 10 ||
With cheeks resembling the flowers of the madhūka tree and with glossy lips.
Her eyebrows were not knit together, and her bud-like toes were not pressed closely against one another. || 11 ||
That woman who is devoted to her husband, who regards her husband as a god, is dear to her husband and possesses a vitality equal to his own.
Though it is without characteristics, it is to be known as endowed with all characteristics.
Her eyebrows and pupils do not touch each other in any way whatsoever.
One should not take her as a wife; she is declared by the wise to be Death itself. ||13||
She whose upper lip is like a lotus stalk and whose cheeks have dimples;
It was exceedingly long, stained with impurities, and likewise possessed a mass of quivering flesh.
This must be especially avoided by a man who desires his own welfare. || 15 ||
In brief, I have thus described to you these charming characteristics of women with shapely hips.
This secret has been told: wherever there is form, there qualities reside.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Women," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
O knower of dharma, those nāgas who are superior in size are highly praised.
They have long hands, deep breaths, and especially possess their own seats. || 1 ||
Those of hidden lineage, honey-eyed, foolish, with foolish lips and heads;
Those who have twenty-eight nails and who exude sweat during the cold season; ||2||
And those whose hands, feet, and tails are likewise long;
The right [side] was elevated, radiant, robust, and resembled a rain-cloud. || 3 ||
And those who, despite extreme pain, are brave and endure the sound [of weapons].
And those whose ears are large, with skin marked by fine spots; 4.
O highly fortunate one, those who are thus well-established in the seven are praised.
On whose gums the marks of the svastika are visible. ||5||
The Śṛṅgāravāla fan, as well as the Vardhamāna and the Aṅkuśa;

Puṣkara said:
O Rāma, descendant of Bhṛgu, these mantras which have been proclaimed by me to you in this [work].
The chanting of their names is auspicious and destroys all sins. ||1||
The man who, having risen at dawn, should perform the recitation of these [names],...
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall attain the heavenly world. ||2||
One shall not go to the animal realm, nor to hell, nor to the mixed states of existence.
There is neither suffering nor fear, no death, and he does not become deluded. || 3 ||
And whatever self-restrained person should offer salutation to these,
No evil remains upon him, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.
Having performed the libation for these, one who has bathed and possesses a restrained mind—
Even one joined with great sins is liberated, just as a snake is freed from its skin. || 5 ||
By the gift of these flowers, one attains great prosperity.
And by offering the arghya to these, a person becomes worthy of worship.
By the gift of lamps to these, they shine in heaven like the moon.
Having offered oblations to these, one obtains abundant desires.
And by offering the food offering and the sacrificial oblation, one obtains unsurpassed enjoyments.
O Bhārgava, having dedicated these [offerings] to the brahmins, one should provide them with a meal.
Having gratified them with sacrificial fees, one shall attain the third heaven for a long time.
Likewise, on the day of the consecration of kings, and similarly during the flower-bath (puṣpasnāna).
Likewise, at the anniversary of the year, all [the deceased] should be honored by one who desires their welfare.
And those holy fords and rivers that have been mentioned in brief. || 10 ||
By their mere passage, even those people who are sinners are purified.
For them, bathing, austerity, ancestral rites, and ritual acts likewise yield great fruit.
Giving is said to yield great fruit, and the sight [of the recipient] destroys evil.
O best of the Bhārgavas, there is no doubt in my mind regarding this glorification.
Furthermore, O chief of the Bhṛgus, O lord of men, men who have bathed in these sacred fords go immediately [to their goal].
Therefore, O Rāma, one should go with effort to the sacred fords and to all the holy rivers.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Sacred Fords," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Rāma said:
"What indeed should be the most important duty for a king who has just been consecrated?"
Tell me all of this, since you know everything.
Puṣkara said:
O lotus-eyed one, with his head still moist from the consecration, the king—
One must choose excellent companions; upon them the kingdom is established. || 2 ||
Even that which is a very small deed is difficult for one person to accomplish alone.
How indeed can a great kingdom be attained by a man who is without a companion? || 3 ||
Therefore, the king himself should choose companions who are of noble birth.
[He saw] heroes of unsurpassed lineage, endowed with strength and possessed of sacred learning.
Endowed with physical beauty, virtuous qualities, and nobility, and possessed of patience.
Those who are patient with afflictions, possessed of great energy, knowers of the Dharma, and sweet-spoken.
Those who offer beneficial advice, who are wise, devoted to their master, and seekers of glory.
One should employ such companions as these in auspicious deeds.
Likewise, having personally recognized those who are devoid of virtues, the king [should act accordingly].
O Bhārgava, one should engage them only in such duties as are appropriate for them.
They were of noble birth, endowed with virtuous conduct, and experts in the science of archery.
They were skilled in the training of elephants and the training of horses, and they spoke with gentle words.
In the knowledge of omens, augury, wealth, medicine, and medical treatment;
In the knowledge of other persons, they are determined by means of the sixfold qualities. || 9 ||
Grateful for their deeds, heroic, likewise enduring of hardships, and upright.
He was an expert in the rules for forming battle arrays and knew the distinction between what is worthless and what is essential.
The commander-in-chief of kings should be made either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya.
He was tall, handsome, skillful, pleasant-spoken, and not arrogant. || 11 ||
And for all of them, the seizing of the mind is prescribed as the preliminary attendant rite.
One who speaks as he has been told may be a rogue, yet skilled in the local dialects.
He is learned in the scriptures, patient with afflictions, eloquent, and skilled in speaking according to place and time.
Having understood the place and the time, whatever may be beneficial for the ruler of the earth [should be done]. || 13 ||
Even one who speaks of it at the proper time shall become a messenger and a king.
They were tall, well-proportioned, heroic, firm in devotion, and undisturbed.
The king, however, should appoint guards who are capable of enduring hardship and are well-disposed.
They were incorruptible, compassionate, and firmly devoted to the king.
A woman who carries betel leaf also comes to possess those same qualities.
He was a knower of the principles of the sixfold policy and was proficient in the languages of various regions.
The king should appoint as minister of peace and war one who is expert in political strategy.
He knows income and expenditure, he understands the world, and he is skilled in the production of regions. || 17 ||
One who recognizes what has been done and what remains to be done for his servants should be known as a skillful protector.
Handsome, youthful, heroic, firm in devotion, and worthy of his lineage. || 18 ||
One who is brave, capable of enduring afflictions, and a wielder of the sword is proclaimed [to be a Kshatriya].
He was a hero, highly disciplined, and skilled in the management of elephants, horses, and chariots. || 19 ||
He who is always capable of enduring hardships should be the treasury-keeper of the king.
He was an expert in the knowledge of omens and portents, as well as in the training of horses. ||20||
He was a knower of the essential principles of the science of horses and an expert in the specific characteristics of different terrains.
He was a knower of strengths and weaknesses, a firm-sighted charioteer, and a master of his craft.
One who is both brave and learned is proclaimed to be a true charioteer.
He should be incorruptible, pure, skillful, and devoted to the words of physicians. || 22 ||
A superintendent of the kitchen who is knowledgeable in the prescriptions of the culinary science is highly praised.
They were experts in the rules of the culinary science, invincible, and born of noble lineage. || 23 ||
All the people in the kitchen should have their hair and nails kept short.
He is impartial toward both enemy and friend, and is proficient in the treatises on Dharma.
The chief of the Brahmins, being of noble birth, shall be the presiding officer of justice.
Likewise, eminent twice-born men of that kind should be appointed there as members of the assembly. ||25||
They were proficient in the scripts of all countries and were experts in all the śāstras.
O Rāma, scribes have indeed been appointed over all administrative departments. ||26||
Provided with heads, well-filled, containing water-channels, and level.
He who writes out the syllables is considered the best of scribes. || 27 ||
Skilled in the speech of expedient means and proficient in all treatises.
O best of the Bhrigus, a scribe should be one who can express many meanings with few words. (28)
Those who know the true nature of other persons, who are tall of stature and free from greed.
Men should be appointed as summoners of people in the court of justice. || 29 ||
The king's doorkeepers should be made of such a kind.
He is a knower of the distinctions among metals such as iron and cloth, as well as precious gems.
A knower of the pith within trivial things, he is always incorruptible and pure.
One who is skillful and vigilant is proclaimed as a treasury officer. || 31 ||
In all the gates of income, men should be appointed who are equal to the chief treasurer.
These should be carried out by the ruler of the earth in all departments of expenditure. || 32 ||
He who has reached the further shore in the eight branches of medical science.
He should be an irremovable physician, righteous in soul, and of noble birth. || 33 ||
He should be known as the master of life, and his word must be followed by the king.
Out of affection for Rāma, one should always act as ordinary people would act. || 34 ||
He was knowledgeable in the rules for training elephants and skilled in the characteristics of wild species.

Endowed with these very qualities, he is especially self-dependent.

He was knowledgeable in the rules for training horses and had mastered their medical treatment.

He is unassailable, heroic, wise, and of noble birth.

He was knowledgeable in the rules of architecture, possessed a steady hand, and had overcome all fatigue.
He is proclaimed to be far-sighted, heroic, and a master craftsman. || 39 ||
Whether released from a machine, released from the hand, not released, or held while being released.
Likewise, he is desired to be an instructor in weaponry and skilled in hand-to-hand combat.
There were fifty women and likewise seventy men.
The king should employ those who attend upon the women's quarters in all his affairs. || 41 ||
The elders, who know the truth of birth, are constantly on their guard.
He should be in the king's armory, skillful and diligent in his duties. || 42 ||
The deeds of kings are immeasurable, O descendant of Bhṛgu’s lineage.
Having understood actions to be superior, inferior, and middling, O King. (43)
One should employ superior, inferior, and middling persons accordingly.
A king shall not meet with destruction through error regarding his duties. || 44 ||
Devotion, learning, heroism, strength, and noble lineage [are required] in an appointed official.
Having understood this, the king must provide a means of livelihood for his men.
In the cognition of another person, [these] are based solely on the reality itself.
Marked by the characteristics of a sovereign and knowing the Dharma, the king should remain dependent upon them. ||46||
And his own servants were likewise well-nourished and constantly honored.
A king who desires to conquer the earth should appoint assistants. ||47||
And then the king should employ them well-supported in their duties according to their worth.
Those who are most righteous in matters of dharma and heroic in the business of battle.
Those who are skillful in performing their duties and likewise pure in all respects.
One should employ eunuchs among women, and the fierce in cruel tasks.
In matters of dharma, artha, kāma, and fear, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
The king should treat those who have been tested by means of secret trials according to their merit.
Having passed [the time], he should appoint forest-rangers for the elephant preserve according to their merit.
One should cause an investigation into their origin to be conducted regarding those things that are not perceptible. || 51 ||
O Bhārgava, such rites as these should be performed with diligent effort.
In every respect, the depletion of the king's sharp instruments [of punishment] is not desired. || 52 ||
O best of the Bhṛgus, those actions which are difficult for kings to accomplish are [accomplished] by means of evil spells.
Being virtuous, they do not commit those [sins]; therefore, the king should support them.
The destruction of sharp weapons is not desired for the lords of the earth.
In whatever action one possesses particular skill, || 54 ||
Having examined him for that task, the king should appoint him to it.
One should employ hereditary servants in all tasks. || 55 ||
For they are, in brief, engaged therein in duties other than those pertaining to inheritance.
The king, having examined his own appointed men regarding their duties as heirs, [should act].

The state of a deity is attained through devotion, and the Great State is reached through practice.
When worshipped, they bestow upon men the desires they long for.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, even by taking refuge in a single deity, a king [attains his goal].
One should undoubtedly perform the worship of all these deities. ||8||
One should never, under any circumstances, deprive the deities of their prior endowment.
One should neither destroy that which was already established, nor should one destroy anything new in that same manner.
The one who cuts it down goes to hell, along with his ancestors and forefathers.
Even the smallest amount of property belonging to the gods must not be taken by one who possesses discernment.
For even from a very small [cause], a terrible fruit may arise in another birth.
Sixty thousand years and six hundred years. || 11 ||
By misappropriating the property of the gods, one falls into hell.
O Bhārgava, there are gentle deities here, and there are also fierce ones.
O gentle one, they display anger toward men on account of the loss of their kingdom and other such misfortunes.
In this world, the deities do not at all harbor cruel anger. || 13 ||
By seizing their wealth, the king falls into hell.
Together with his ancestors and grandfathers, he indeed obtains the very fruit previously described.
The misappropriation of divine property shall never go in vain.
Having deprived those who steal the property of the gods of all their voices, [he cast them into hell]. || 15 ||
O best of the twice-born, having branded them, he should banish them from his own kingdom.
The Traividyas, Vaṇijas, Vaiśyas, Liṅgins, and Devapālakas. || 16 ||
Likewise, those bound by that [relationship] should not engage in mutual quarreling.

And these, O highly fortunate one, must be performed by one who desires the world of the gods.

For so long as he remains here, he shines with glory throughout his successive births.

By bestowing assistance, one attains unsurpassed prosperity. || 27 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Greatness of the Worship of the Gods," in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Puṣkara said:

They can make a non-divine being divine, and they can make a divine being non-divine.

For one who bestows food, that many sacrifices are proclaimed.

Because the confluence of all sacred fords resides in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Brāhmaṇas," in the dialogue between Puṣkara and Rāma within the Māgha-saṃvāda of the second section (*dvi-khaṇḍa*) of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Puṣkara said:

The sisters who curse those houses in which they have not been properly honored.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Virtuous Woman," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Rāma said:
O God, I desire to hear the duties of virtuous women in their entirety.
For virtuous women are proclaimed here as the support of the worlds.
Puṣkara said:
This alone, O Rāma, is the supreme cause of righteousness for women.
For they are indeed always dependent upon others in all their affairs. || 2 ||
In childhood, she should remain under the authority of her father; in youth, under that of her husband.
When her husband has died, a woman does not deserve independence from her sons.
In this world, one should not desire separation from oneself's father, husband, or son.

One should serve him while he is alive, but one must not transgress against him when he has passed away.
For their sake, auspicious rites, blessings, and sacrifices are performed.
In marriages, the giving away [of the bride] is performed by the master.
The husband is the performer of the mantra-consecration, whether [the act] occurs outside the fertile period or during the prescribed season.
Women bestow constant happiness both in this world and in the next.
Whether he be immoral, or one who acts out of lust, or even one devoid of virtues.
A husband must always be served by a virtuous wife as if he were a god.
For women, there is no separate sacrifice, nor a vow, nor even a fast.

That supreme Dharma which women whose husbands are living desire. ||13||
Many thousands of utterly simple celibates.

O Bhārgava, that virtuous woman who, upon the death of her husband, takes refuge in her son—

For he, too, should always support her with food and clothing. (45)
When the opposing side has been completely eradicated, the father’s lineage becomes the master of the woman.

Or if that devoted wife takes her deceased husband with her;
O tiger among the twice-born, he should enter the blazing fire.
There are three and a half crores of hairs on a human being.
For that many hundreds of years, he is honored in the heavenly world.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole.
Thus, taking her husband with her, she goes along with him;
[this is the fate] of women who, distressed by the wound of separation, have gone forth to study virtuous conduct. || 49 ||
For when their beloved has died, there is indeed no duty for them other than entering the fire.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Duties of Women," in the account of Puṣkara related to Rāma, within the second section of the Viṣṇudharmottara. 34.
Rāma said:
Proclaim who among women is most worthy of worship in this world, O Goddess.
Their [the goddesses'] time, their ritual procedure, and likewise the fruit resulting from their worship. || 1 ||

Women should always perform the worship of Śrī within the home.
With flowers, water-offerings, garlands, food-oblations, incense, lamps, and unguents. || 2 ||
The sweeping of the house, O Rāma, as well as its plastering.
The offering of flowers and the whiteness of plastered walls as well. || 3 ||

And whatever bathing, anointing, and discernment of fragrance and color there may be. || 4 ||

On that day, she who eats only at night, avoiding oil; || 6 ||
Then, wherever she is reborn, she becomes free from sorrow.
And on all the eighth lunar days as well, O Bhārgava, if he is unable [to fast].

With white garlands and ointments, and with fragrant incense. || 10 ||

And having worshipped that goddess, O Bhārgava, one should eat at night.
If one is ever unable to perform the entire fifteenth day [of the vow], || 12 ||

From the worship of the deity Chandodeva, one obtains a son devoid of virtues.

Likewise, one should indeed worship the deity of the site (vāstudevatā) with devotion using perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Likewise, having reached the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform worship.
O highly fortunate one, by worshipping her, the ruin of one's home does not occur.
Likewise, having reached the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
One should cut a spreading clump of dūrvā grass so that it points toward the northern direction.
Having brought him home, one should worship him with perfumes, garlands, and ointments. || 19 ||
Likewise, O Rāma, one should avoid incense and lamps [when using] fruits and roots.
Likewise, nothing that has been cooked by fire should ever be offered in any way.
And likewise, O Rāma, it should be eaten without having been cooked by fire.
Having worshipped the Goddess of Youthful Beauty, who resides upon a blade of dūrvā grass, according to the prescribed rite.
One attains stable youth wherever one is reborn.
But that woman who observes a fast during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārtika, || 22 ||
On the twelfth day, one should worship Viṣṇu, and immediately thereafter, a cow together with her calf.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food. || 23 ||
All dairy products offered as food-oblations (naivedya) must be avoided with great effort.
O knower of dharma, it should be enjoyed, but it must certainly not be milked, O Arjuna.
By performing this very rite, one obtains cattle; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
If he bestows that cow upon a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite, ||25||
Having reached the heavenly world, one does not return from there.
And likewise, in the month of Kārttika, worship should be performed on the day of the Kṛttikā constellation.
It should be performed with fragrant jars, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
And with various kinds of food, excellent rice-dishes, boiled grains, and likewise with parpaṭas. ||27||
O knower of dharma, [honour them] according to your ability with garments that delight by their deep dyeing.
With jaggery, honey, sugar, and salt.
As well as with ginger, sugarcane, and fruits produced in their proper season.
And with all kinds of various foods, as well as diverse types of perfumes. ||29||
Likewise, the Kṛttikās should be worshipped with pleasing beverages.
O Rāma, together with the moon, one enjoys good fortune through that [rite]. ||30||
And a woman [endowed] with beauty and charm, as well as a preeminent intellect in the Dharma.
And, O knower of dharma, wherever she is born, she shall never suffer widowhood.
Having prepared a *tulā* (weight) of salt, it was dyed with a powerful coloring agent.
Then, with that very garment, she [covered] her white-complexioned body, which was adorned with ornaments.
Having prepared a ball of food smeared with turmeric, one should offer it to the Kṛttikās.
And likewise, when the moon has risen, one should cause that Brāhmaṇa to receive it.
By this rite, a woman attains great good fortune.
Likewise, a man who is pure indeed attains great good fortune.
Having performed their worship on the first day of the Kṛttikā constellation, she who, after honoring the Brāhmaṇas, consumes food consisting primarily of cow-products; ||| 34 ||
For seven successive births, he shall possess good fortune as well as beauty.
But in heaven, that auspicious woman attains enjoyments together with her husband. || 36 ||
Having reached the fifteenth day, O Rāma, as well as the full moon of the month of Kārttika.
O Rāma, one should paint the month of Kārttika and the full moon day of Kārttikī upon the wall of the house.
Outside the house, near the entrance, [one should decorate] with pigments of various colors.
And one should depict the household utensils and those two [deities] on both sides according to one's ability. || 38 ||
Where there are stools, swords, seats, and so forth, as well as carts, mortars, and the like.
Then that pure woman, devoted to various forms of worship, should honor those two. || 39 ||
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
One should especially worship with sugarcane or products derived from sugarcane. || 40 ||
Having performed the worship of those two, as well as the fish together with the sand;
One should place the oyster-pearl into milk and give that to a twice-born man.
And thereafter, one should eat at night, avoiding sesame oil.
By worshipping these two, O Rāma, one shall not suffer the ruin of one's home. ||42||
O illustrious one, a woman devoted to her husband attains a long life.
And likewise in the month of Kārtika, she always dwells together with the Moon.
O twice-born one, on the day of Rohiṇī, the worship of Rohiṇī must be performed according to the prescribed rite.
With all the signs of a non-widow, and with abundant salt. || 44 ||
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
Likewise, O Bhārgava, with a garment dyed with saffron and with power.
By performing this, an excellent woman attains supreme good fortune.
And whatever woman is devoted to her husband on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, || 46 ||
And, observing a fast, she should worship Kāmadeva without weariness.
His wife likewise [adorned] her husband with the application of silken garments and colors.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
With jaggery, honey, sugar, and ginger. ||48||
With salt, with other flavors, with fragrances, and with various grains, each separately.
And with various kinds of foods, as well as with garments moistened with saffron. ||49||
Filled with fragrant water and adorned with the tender shoots of trees.
O Bhārgava, with a full jar, auspicious, and with a garland around his neck.
One should give whatever is sour to Kāmadeva.
And thereafter, everything that is to be eaten must be free from sourness. || 51 ||
She who performs the ritual worship of Kāma attains all her desires.
But if, O Rāma, he is unable to do so for the entire thirteenth day, || 52 ||
By [performing this] during the bright fortnight of Caitra, one undoubtedly obtains the fruit of all [these rites].
Therefore, with every effort, [one should observe it] on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra. || 53 ||
Worship of Kāma should be performed, for she bestows all desires.
Having worshipped Kāmadeva, one should perform the worship of oneself.
Likewise, with saffron marks, garments, perfumes, garlands, and ornaments.
Afterwards, the woman, having adorned herself, should honor her husband.
With a cloth marked by saffron, and with captivating perfumes and garlands.
A man, too, by worshipping Kāmadeva, will undoubtedly [attain his desire]. || 56 ||
One attains all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Likewise, on the fourth lunar days of the bright fortnight, the worship of Gaurī should always be performed. || 57 ||
Having bathed and observed a fast, they [waited] for the rising of the sun.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food. || 58 ||
With jaggery, with sugar, with honey, and with ginger.
And with all the signs of a non-widow, and with abundant salt. || 59 ||
She should be worshipped with all one's power, especially on the two fourth lunar days.
Or in the month of Āṣāḍha, or even in the month of Māgha, O twice-born one.
In the center of all four sacrificial pits dwells she who serves the rays of the sun.
Likewise, she should dwell [in that manner] on the third lunar day of the month of Āṣāḍha while observing a fast.
O Bhārgava, there is nothing in this world that is difficult for her to obtain.
Having fasted in the month of Māgha as well, she was at the end of the night [covered] with masses of frost.
By whom all her limbs were made white, and she occupied her bed.
And thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath with cool water.
She too, O Rāma, obtains whatever desires she wishes for in her mind.
She was always devoted to her husband, yet fickle, fortunate, and endowed with beauty. || 64 ||
She becomes a lover of the Dharma and devoted to the worship of Gaurī.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, a pomegranate flower; in Madhu (Caitra), one produced from cotton. || 65 ||
Having offered everything to the Noble Lady (Āryā), one enjoys great good fortune.
And likewise, Śakrāṇī should be worshipped in the month of Bhādrapada. || 66 ||
For women, she indeed grants all desires through the ritual procedure dedicated to Gaurī.
On the fourth day of the month of Proṣṭhapada, O best of the twice-born.
Having performed the worship of Śakrāṇī, one is glorified in the vault of heaven.
O Rāma, among all forms of worship and hospitality for guests, the honoring of Brāhmaṇas is paramount.
Whatever food offering (naivedya) ought to be prepared, that should be given to the fortunate women.
Likewise, one who gazes upon the Gaurī-lamp without having first worshipped Gaurī [commits an offense]. || 69 ||
One incurs great misfortune; his sight is avoided.
O twice-born one, whatever woman desires to worship Gaurī on that day, [attains her goal].
She too should perform her bath with warm water, and she shall enjoy good fortune.
Having worshipped Gaurī according to the prescribed rite, wherever one is born, [one attains excellence].
And she also becomes endowed with beauty, charm, and good fortune.
O Rāma, she shall likewise always remain a non-widow and remain devoted to her husband.
These are proclaimed as the most worshipful among women; they are declared to be deities.
But hereafter, she who would abandon the path of virtuous women, || 73 ||
O best of the twice-born, [a sacrifice] that is violent in nature, not prescribed by rule, or impure—
But she who performs the propitiation of deities for a long time falls into hell.
Furthermore, it is detrimental to longevity and increases the influence of malevolent planets and spirits.
But that woman who is violent by nature yet devoted to the worship of the deity, [is as follows]. (75)
O best of the Bhṛgus, she who is devoted to malevolent magic should be married by her husband.
O Rāma, even for women who are prone to unchastity, violence is indeed to be avoided. (76)
O Rāma, the female nature is auspicious, characterized by gentleness, mildness, and compassion.
"O best of the twice-born, O Rāma, is she a merciless Rākṣasī or a Piśācī? (77)
Or else, having renounced everything, she should be intent upon the worship of her husband.
O bull among men, one should perform the worship of Keśava and Śrī.
By that alone one obtains everything whatsoever that one seeks.
Everything performed without the husband's permission would be entirely fruitless. (79)
O Rāma, nevertheless, the worship of Keśava is fruitful for women as well.
Govinda is the supporter of all beings; for a woman, there is no other.
Therefore, without the permission of her husband, worship is not prescribed from that [point]. || 80 ||
For Nārāyaṇa is indeed the most worthy of worship in the world; Nārāyaṇa is omnipresent and the primordial source.
A woman intent on the worship of Nārāyaṇa attains her desires; there is no doubt in this matter. || 81 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Female Deities," within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra concerning Rāma, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 35 ||
Puṣkara said:
Even Dharmarāja does not practice perversion with women.
O knower of dharma, those women devoted to their husbands are always worthy of worship even by him.
In this regard, I shall relate to you a story that destroys all sins.
Just as her husband, who was ensnared by the noose of death, was liberated by his wife. ||2||
In ancient times, there was a king named Aśvapati in Śākala among the Madras.
Being childless and suffering, he [worshipped] that [tree] which grants all desires for the sake of a son.
He caused the Lakṣahoma sacrifice for Sāvitrī to be performed by the most excellent of the twice-born.
O twice-born one, Sāvitrī was daily offered as an oblation with white mustard seeds.
On the fourth lunar day, when ten days have passed from the beginning of the month, [one should perform the rite] with a hundredfold [offerings].
But at the proper time, he revealed his own body to the lord of men.
Sāvitrī said:
"O King, you have been my constant devotee; you shall obtain an auspicious daughter."
And by her grace, you shall obtain beautiful sons given by me.
Puṣkara said: O Bhārgava, having spoken thus to the king who was bowing down, she—
The goddess vanished from sight, O Rāma, like a flickering flash in the sky.
That king has a wife named Mālavyā, who is devoted to her husband.
In due time, she gave birth to a daughter who was like Sāvitrī herself in beauty.
Then, by means of the Sāvitrī oblation offered, one who resembles her in form was bestowed.
"This must surely be Sāvitrī herself," the king said to the twice-born ones.
When she had reached youth in due time, her father gave her to Satyavat.
Then Nārada spoke to the king of blazing splendor.
This prince's life span will be exhausted within a year.
O lord of men, a daughter is given away only once after due consideration.
Nevertheless, he gave his auspicious daughter to the son of Dyumatsena.
And Sāvitrī, having obtained as her husband that delight of kings, [remained devoted]. || 12 ||
With his heart tormented by the words of Nārada, he remained there.
In the forest, she performed the highest service toward her husband and father-in-law.
The lord of men, deprived of his kingdom along with his wife, was also deprived of his sight.
Having then obtained that princess as his daughter-in-law, he was filled with joy.
"O twice-born one, when Satyavān was destined to die on the fourth day,"
Then that daughter-in-law was given leave by her father-in-law, the king.
O knower of dharma, when that day arrived, he observed a three-night fast.
Satyavān went to the forest for food consisting of beautiful flowers and fruits.
She was permitted by her father-in-law, who feared the refusal of her request.
Sāvitrī also went quickly with her husband to the great forest.
With a grieving heart, she concealed that fear.
In the forest, she questioned her husband, as well as the trees and the deer.
He comforted the princess, who was exhausted in the forest and possessed eyes like lotus petals.
Then, by observing the deer, birds, and trees in the forest, that hero among men [proceeded]. || 19 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Entry into the Forest," within the Legend of Sāvitrī, in the Legend of Puṣkara, addressed to Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Satyavān said:
In this forest, there is a charming mango tree crowded with bees.
Behold the ears, nose, and mouth, which increase pleasure in the springtime. (1)
Having seen this beautiful verse about a flower in the forest, she became enamored.
O long-eyed one, my mind seems to laugh at you with envy.
Look at this beautiful woodland grove to the right with your right eye.
It was filled with blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees, which, due to their radiant luster, made it appear as if it were ablaze. || 3 ||
The breeze, fragrant with the scent of sweet-smelling flowers and emerging from the forest groves,
dispels our fatigue through its southern course.
O lady with eyes as wide as blue lotuses, even by means of the well-flowered karṇikāra trees.
This enchanting row of trees shines as if made of gold.
The forest grounds where the paths were blocked by networks of *atimukta* creepers.
Behold, O lady of beautiful limbs, adorned with a profusion of flowers!
O woman of excellent complexion, under the pretext of the humming of bees intoxicated by honey.
Kāma seems to fashion a bow-staff with the intent to slay the traveler.
Her beautiful face was like a full-blown campaka flower, and she warbled like a male cuckoo.
This forest region, possessing a beautiful tilaka tree, shines like you.
The cuckoo, dusted yellow by the pollen of flower-clusters, perches upon the tip of a mango tree.
He becomes manifest through his words, just as one of noble birth is revealed by his actions.
With his limbs smeared with the pollen of flowers, he followed his beloved through the forest.
The humming, amorous bee goes from flower to flower. || 10 ||
The flower-cluster of the mango tree, severed by the tip of the beak of a beautiful bird.
Even when the flowers are abundant, the young male cuckoo relishes [only] the tree.
A crow, with its beak filled with meat, [sat] upon the tip of a tree where a female had recently given birth.
He causes his mother crow to nourish her young, who is covered by his wings.
Having reached a low-lying spot on the ground, the young man was accompanied by his beloved.
Even though he was full of desire, the kapiñjala bird did not even take food at will.
But the kalaviṅka bird, standing upon a branch with its mate, sang out with its warbling notes.
O large-eyed one, it repeatedly causes lovers to feel longing. ||14||
This parrot, together with his beloved, has perched upon a small branch.
Bending the branch with its weight, it makes it appear as if laden with fruit. || 15 ||
Satiated by the taste of the flesh of wild elephants, he fell asleep.
The young lion lies down, his face covered by the feet of his beloved.
Behold a pair of tigers dwelling together in a mountain cave.
By the light of the radiance of their eyes, the cave appears as if it were pierced through. || 17 ||
This leopard licks his beloved again and again with the tip of his tongue.
And being licked by its luster, it attains great joy.
With his head resting in her lap, his mind was carried away by sleep.
The female monkey delights her beloved precisely by means of rescuing living beings. || 19 ||
Falling to the ground, the female cat displayed her belly to her beloved.
She pricks him with her nails and teeth, yet she does not cause him pain in that way. || 20 ||
Both Śaśaka and Śaśikā are fast asleep; these two are now afflicted.
When his limbs and feet were withdrawn and [the breath] became manifest through the ears. || 21 ||
An elephant, slow with rut, had bathed in a lake abounding with lotuses.
O slender-limbed one, the female elephant honors you with fragments of lotus stalks.
The beloved [earth] was dug up by the ploughshares, following the path of her lover.
She makes a mouthful of musta grass in the forest of Varāhī-potaka.
In the forest, there was a buffalo with firm joints and a body moist with mud.
He follows his beloved as she runs, with his four limbs bound together. ||24||
Behold, O lady of lovely limbs, the deer in the forest that resembles your sidelong glance.
But me, seeing him together with my wife, filled with curiosity. || 25 ||
Behold, Rohiṇī scratches her face with her hind leg.
The husband, his heart softened by affection, scratches [her] with the very tip of the point of his horn. || 26 ||
Behold the white-tailed yak, with its bushy tail like a pomegranate, as it moves along.
The lustful yak sits nearby, and he gazes at me with pride. || 27 ||
"Look, the gavaya is settled in the sunlight together with his mate."
Chewing cud in his mouth and bearing a crow upon his hump. || 28 ||
Behold the goat with its two forefeet placed upon its wife.
Upon the vast trunk of a jujube tree, with the desire to consume its foliage. || 29 ||
A swan wandering with its mate in a perfectly pure lake.
Behold this splendor, which resembles the perfectly white orb of the moon.
This ruddy goose, together with his mate, stands in the midst of a cluster of lotuses.
O beautiful one, he makes her lovely like a lotus pond in full bloom.
O fair-browed one, I have gathered the fruit, while you have gathered the flowers.
No fuel has been prepared at all; I shall prepare it now.
You have taken refuge in the shade of a tree on the bank of this lake.
Wait but a moment and rest, O beautiful lady.
Sāvitrī said:
"I shall do exactly this: you must [remain] out of my sight."
"O beloved, you must not go far; I am afraid in this dense forest. (34)
Puṣkara said:
As he was felling the wood, a pain arose in his head.
Afflicted by pain, he approached his wife and spoke these words. || 35 ||
Satyavān said:
From this exertion of mine, a pain has arisen in my head.
And I seem to enter into darkness, nor do I know anything at all. || 36 ||
Placing his head upon your lap, his eyes overcome by sleep, he lay there.
Puṣkara said:
Placing his head upon her lap, he fell asleep, deprived of consciousness. || 37 ||
Then that illustrious princess, devoted to her husband, [spoke].
He beheld Dharmarāja himself having arrived at that place. 38.
The Lord, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, wearing yellow garments.
His limbs were entwined by lightning-vines, like a rain-bearing cloud.
He was resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and with two earrings.
With his chest adorned by the weight of necklaces and likewise decorated with armlets.
And thus it is pursued by Time together with Death.
Having reached that place, he then [departed] from the body of Satyavat.
The Person, the size of a thumb, bound by fetters and brought under control.
Having drawn [his bow], he then proceeded swiftly toward the southern direction.
Sāvitrī too, of beautiful form, having abandoned him whose life had departed, [departed].
She followed the King of Dharma as he went, remaining unwearied.
Yama said to her, "Go back, O blameless one, by the way you came."
Devote yourself to performing the funeral rites for your husband. 44.
Having gone to another world, he cannot be followed by you.
Because you are devoted to your husband, you perceive this for even a moment.
O blessed lady, through service to his guru, Satyavat likewise attained greatness.
"I myself shall lead him away by means of the merit he has accumulated. (46)
This alone is to be done by a discerning person.
Service to one's mother, father, and teacher, O lady of excellent complexion. (47)
And these three elders were always [honored] by Satyavān in the forest.
O auspicious one, by honoring those who are worthy of honor, heaven is attained for a long time through that merit.
Through austerity, through celibacy, and likewise through service to the sacred fire.
Men go to heaven by means of service to their teacher as well.
The teacher, the father, the mother, and the elder brother—these are indeed [to be honored]. || 50 ||
They must not be treated with contempt even by one who is distressed, especially by a Brahmin.
The teacher is the embodiment of Brahman; the father is the embodiment of Prajāpati.
The mother is the very embodiment of the earth, and the brother is indeed the embodiment of one's own self.
The suffering that parents endure during the birth of human beings— || 52 ||
No atonement can be made for that, even in hundreds of years.
One should always do what is pleasing to those two and to the teacher at all times. || 53 ||
When these three alone are satisfied, austerity and truth are fully accomplished.
Service to these three is said to be the highest austerity.
Without being authorized by them, one should not practice another dharma.
For those very three worlds are indeed those three stages of life (āśramas). || 55 ||
These very three Vedas are said to be those same three fires.
The father is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire. || 56 ||
The preceptor is indeed the Āhavanīya fire; the triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, the householder conquers the three worlds.
For he, with a divine body, rejoices like a god in heaven.
One devoted to his mother attains this world; one devoted to his father, however, the middle world. || 58 ||
Indeed, by serving the guru in this manner, one attains the world of Brahmā.
All dharmas are honored by him by whom these three are honored.
But for one who disregards these, all ritual actions are fruitless.
As long as those three live, one should not perform any other [duty].
One should offer one's body to them through mind, speech, and action.
For it is within these three that a person's duty is fully accomplished. || 61 ||
This is the supreme Dharma directly perceived; any other is called a secondary dharma (upadharma).
Your husband is devoted to the worship of his guru, and you are a virtuous woman faithful to your husband.
Turn back, O knower of dharma; you are now suffering from exhaustion.
Sāvitrī said:
For the husband is the deity of women; the husband alone is their ultimate refuge.
A husband, the lord of one's life, wealth, and master, is to be followed by a virtuous wife.
For a father gives in limited measure, a brother gives in limited measure, and a son gives in limited measure. (64)
For who would not honor a husband who is a giver of the immeasurable?
"Wherever my husband is led, or wherever he goes of his own accord. (65)
O best of gods, I too shall go there according to my ability.
When I was about to follow my husband as he departed, taking me with him, || 66 ||
O Lord, I shall certainly not be able [to live] then; I will give up my life.
And who was that high-minded woman, defiled by the syllables of widowhood? (67)
One who is worthy of adornment may live even for a single moment without being adorned.
Yama said:
"O devoted wife, O highly fortunate one, O auspicious lady, I am well-pleased with you."
Choose a boon, do not delay, except for the life of Satyavat.
Sāvitrī said:
I desire the kingdom, along with my sight, for one whose eyes have been destroyed.
O knower of dharma, [this was done] for my high-souled father-in-law who has been deprived of his kingdom. || 69 ||
Yama said:
O auspicious lady, turn back with your desire fulfilled; all that you have spoken shall come to pass.
"There would be obstruction for me and exhaustion for you on that path; therefore, I speak thus to you."
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna of the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. ||37||
Sāvitrī said:
Whence comes fatigue, whence comes suffering, when one is in the company of the virtuous?
Therefore, O best of gods, I have no weariness in your presence, for you are among the virtuous.
Whether for the virtuous or even for the wicked, the good alone are the supreme refuge.
They do not belong to the non-existent, nor to the existent; they are neither non-existent, nor do they belong to the self. (2)
Fear does not arise from poison, fire, serpents, or weapons to such an extent.
Just as it arises from wicked enemies of the world who act without cause. || 3 ||
The virtuous, even at the cost of sacrificing their own lives, act for the sake of others.
Likewise, even those who are wicked are intent upon causing suffering to others. ||4||
This world abandons its very life-breaths like a blade of grass for the sake of that [wealth].
Attached to the support of others, they likewise [neglect] the world beyond, O virtuous one.
In each and every collection of scriptures, in the past, Brahmā, the teacher of the world, [spoke thus].
For the sake of suppressing the wicked, kings have themselves performed [these acts]. || 6 ||
The king should investigate through spies and should always weed out rogues.
And he shall effect the suppression of the wicked; he is indeed the supreme conqueror of the world.
For the purpose of protecting the grain, one should sweep while clearing away the dust from the side.
Just as one causes grain to increase, so should subjects be caused to prosper. || 8 ||
By the punishment of the wicked and by the protection of the virtuous, a king [attains his purpose].
Only this much must be done by a king who desires heaven. || 9 ||
For there is no other royal duty in the worlds, O Lord of the Earth, than this.
Precisely through the suppression of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous. || 10 ||
As the king, you are their ruler; you are the punisher of those who are wicked.
Therefore, O God, you appear to me as superior even to all the gods.
The world is sustained by the virtuous, and you, O Best of the Virtuous, are likewise its sustainer.
Therefore, O Lord, no fatigue arises in me as I approach you.
Yama said:
I am pleased with you, O large-eyed one, by these words consistent with the Dharma.
"Choose a boon, O Satyavat, without delay, even at the cost of your life."
Sāvitrī said:
O Lord, I desire a hundred brothers who are my uterine siblings.
May my childless father attain joy through the acquisition of a son.
Yama said:
"O blessed lady, turn back with your desire fulfilled; all that you have spoken shall come to pass."
Now, therefore, I tell you this: otherwise there would be obstruction for me and exhaustion for you. ||15||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Second Attainment of Boons," in the Sāvitrī-upākhyāna of the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Sāvitrī said:
For women, dharma is indeed their deity, and the husband alone is their ultimate refuge.
A husband, the lord of one's life and wealth, is to be followed by a virtuous wife.
O best of gods, in the acquisition of dharma, whence can there be weariness? Whence can there be exhaustion?
This very root of your feet is the supreme cause of dharma.
A wise man should always strive to acquire merit.
This gain is superior to all gains, O Lord, because it is distinguished above them all. || 3 ||
Dharma, artha, and kāma—this threefold aggregate is the fruit for one who lives.
For one devoid of Dharma, both desire and wealth are like the sons of a barren woman. || 4 ||
From dharma comes wealth, as well as pleasure; from dharma likewise comes both worlds.
Dharma alone follows him wherever he goes.
For everything else indeed goes to destruction along with the body.
