One should designate courtesy and perseverance as the qualities of sattva. || 18 ||
He is clever, irascible, timid, talkative, and fond of quarreling.
In his dreams, he will see himself traveling through the sky and will become a man of great wind-like vigor. || 19 ||
Prematurely gray-haired, wrathful, possessed of great wisdom, and fond of battle.
And in dreams, a man with an excess of bile will see glowing objects.
Steady-minded, steady in his enthusiasm, and endowed with a firm physical bearing.
A person who perceives water and white light in a dream will have an abundance of phlegm. || 21 ||
The rasa, moreover, is nourishing to the body and likewise vitalizing to the blood.
Likewise, its application to the flesh provides fat; it is also a provider of unctuousness.
The bone is said to be the support, while the marrow is the filling.
It produces the semen that causes conception and likewise increases virility. || 23 ||
Tejas always bestows vital breath; therein the individual soul (jīva) is established.
It is more essential than even semen, undrunk, and like the very heart.
I shall describe to you the six principal limbs; listen.
Two arms, two thighs, the head, and the belly. || 25 ||
And learn from me the six layers of skin that are described in this body.
For externally, O Rāma, the lower skin is that which carries the blood. || 26 ||
Another, the fourth, is Vilāsakāriṇī, who causes leprosy.
The fifth is considered the seat of abscesses (vidradhi), and the sixth is known as the life-sustainer (prāṇadharā). || 27 ||
The Kalās are traditionally said to reside in the body; I shall describe their characteristics.
O Rāma, there is one muscle-bearing vessel where the arteries are situated. || 28 ||
The second, however, is the blood-bearing vessel, which is considered to have its seat in the liver and spleen.
The third is Medodharā, which is that which rests upon both the subtle and the gross.
The fourth, however, is considered to have marrow as its basis, and likewise that which is dominated by phlegm.
And another is the bearer of feces, as it resides in the receptacle of digested food (the colon).
The sixth, named Pittadhara, is situated within the digestive fire.
The seventh should likewise be known as Śukrāśayā and Śukadharā. || 31 ||
In this context, the five sense organs are hearing, the vital breath, and the two eyes.
Likewise, the skin and the tongue are indeed supported by the great elements.
Likewise, there are five objects of the senses; hear their names from me.
Sound is said to belong to the ear, and odor, which is earthly, to the nose. || 33 ||
Form is to be known by the eye, and likewise, touch is to be known by the skin.
And the taste of the tongue—these indeed have the great elements as their substratum. (34)
There are five organs of action here; hear their names from me.
The anus, the generative organ, the hands, the feet, and the tongue as the fifth among these. || 35 ||
Their meanings are likewise five; I shall explain them hereafter.
And likewise, Ānanda, [there is] emission, as well as grasping and movement. || 36 ||
These are the ten sense-faculties; the mind is indeed their leader.
In this [body], there are five organs of action and five organs of cognition. || 37 ||
And here, there are the five sense objects and the five great elements.
The four [objects] are said to be superior to the senses, O descendant of Bhṛgu. (38)
Mind, intellect, as well as the self and the unmanifest, O mighty-armed one.
The sense faculties have those [objects] as their support, and they [the objects] are superior to the sense faculties. (39)
Know these principles to be twenty-four in number.
O fortunate one, for those whose unity is the twenty-fifth principle, the Puruṣa.
He is both conjoined with them and yet disjoined from them, just as fish are in relation to both water and themselves.
The mind is always the creator of doubt, while the intellect is the discerning faculty. (41)
O Rāma, the self (ātman) is known as the living being (jīva), which is the experiencer of pleasure and pain.
The Unmanifest is here mixed with rajas, sattva, and tamas. || 42 ||
But the other Puruṣa is to be known as he who is all-pervading and great.
He who exists beyond the number twenty-four is eternal and stands apart.
The principles are threefold, and likewise, they are unified within the Puruṣa.
And there are no principles whatsoever that exist apart from the Puruṣa. 44.
O Rāma, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), the twenty-fifth principle, are fruitless.
The wise one should understand that his modification is the remaining group of principles (tattvas). || 45 ||
He has hands and feet everywhere; he has eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
That person is to be known as supreme, possessing all powers in every respect. ||46||
There is neither beginning, nor middle, nor end, for the two—pervasion and possibility—are one.
He whom the sages know, he who knows him—he is the knower of the Veda.
He who knows the Supreme Person goes to the highest abode.
And listen now, O Bhārgava, to this very consciousness which has been introduced. 48.
Seven receptacles are known to exist in the body; hear about them as well, O Bhārgava.
One is the receptacle for blood, and another likewise for phlegm. || 49 ||
The receptacles for undigested food and bile are two others, and the receptacle for digested food is another.
And two others that have air alone as their substrate; thus, seven substrates are proclaimed.
O Rāma, the womb of women is located between the receptacle of bile and the receptacle of digested food.
He among them would be the eighth, in whom that embryo remains.
During the fertile period, the womb is always open like a lotus.
Then, in the womb, it receives the semen conjoined with blood. || 52 ||
Except at that time, the womb of women remains closed like a bud.
Therefore, O Sage, the semen deposited in the womb does not enter the uterus.
Moreover, even during the fertile season, if the womb is obstructed by wind, bile, or phlegm, [conception does not occur].
For the sake of her purification, it would not at all arise for her. || 54 ||
The kidneys, the spleen with its flowers, the heart, the thoracic cavity, the limbs, and the liver are the solid organs.
And, O illustrious one, rice grains were bound within your belly.
From the essence of the rasa as it is being digested, [the bodily constituents] of embodied beings arise.
O Knower of Dharma, from the spleen and liver [the Kārṣṇa was born], and from the froth of the blood, the Pukkasa. || 56 ||
And from the dregs of blood, that which is known as the *daṇḍaka* likewise arises.
It is taught that fat arises from the refined essence of blood, and its origin is also held to be from the kidneys. || 57 ||
And from the refinement of blood and flesh, the intestines of embodied beings come into being.
One should prescribe those [mantras] numbering thirty-six for women.
Those who know the Vedas declare that women likewise possess three voids.
It is taught that Time arises from the conjunction with the blood-wind.
From the refined essence of phlegm (kapha), the heart arises, resembling a lotus.
That hollow opening is downward-facing, wherein the living soul is situated.
All entities, being permeated by consciousness, are established therein.
On its left side is the spleen, and likewise on the right side is the liver.
And likewise, the kloman is proclaimed to be on the right side of the lotus.
Those channels in this body which carry phlegm and blood, however—62.
But for those beings who follow after the elements, there arises the manifestation of the sense faculties.
The white circle of the eyes arises from phlegm (kapha), while that which is [yellowish] arises from bile (pitta). || 63 ||
And the black circle likewise becomes the Mātṛkā due to the wind.
The entire heart-maṇḍala should be known as originating from the mother and father. || 64 ||
One is the circle of eyelashes, while the second is the circle of the eyelids.
The third is said to be white, and the fourth is the black mandala.
The fifth is the circle of vision; the eye shall consist of five circles.
Others, however, [place] two parts in the eyes, as well as the outer corners and the pupils. (66)
O twice-born one, it was by these two that the eye was caused to assume the shape of a fish.
That which is said to be near the nose is designated by the name apāṅga.
Likewise, the *kanīnikā* is said to be near the two cheeks.
The tongue is produced from flesh, blood, and phlegm; [the uvula] is produced from fat, blood, phlegm, and flesh. (68)
And likewise, the two testicles are to be known as belonging to all embodied beings.
Learn from me these ten extensions of the vital breath (prāṇa). 69.
The head, the heart, the navel, the throat, and the attachment of the tongue.
O Bhārgava, the blood, the semen, the rectum, the bladder, as well as the two ankles [are likewise produced].
Sixteen tendons (kaṇḍarā) are said to exist in the bodies of embodied beings.
Two are located in the hands, and likewise two are located in the feet, each separately.
Four [channels] are to be known as running along the back, and exactly the same number in the neck.
There are exactly sixteen waters here; their division is now described.
From the flesh, sinews, vessels, and bones, however, four [types of worms] arise separately.
The wrist-bands were fastened to the ankles, one to the other.
And the "stakes" (śaṅkus) are recorded here as being located in the hands and likewise in the feet.
And likewise, [the locations] in the neck and the penis have been described by the wise. || 74 ||
And likewise, within this body, four muscular cords (māṃsarajju) are to be known.
Two [veins] each are proclaimed there, situated on both sides of the spinal column. || 75 ||
And yet, these [senses] are likewise as many, and they are the causes of bondage for them.
Likewise, the seven *sīvanyas* and five [channels] are situated upon the head.
One is located in the penis, and another is likewise situated in the tongue.
In this [body], there are three hundred and sixty bones. ||77||
Including the subtle ones, there are sixty-four teeth and twenty nails.
And the longitudinal bones of the hands and feet; these constitute their four locations. || 78 ||
There are likewise forty bones in the two shanks, and exactly that many as well.
There are two each produced from the knees, the cheeks, the lips, the palms, and the shoulders. (79)
One should likewise indicate eight [lines] on the area of the eyes and on the surface of the hips, and so forth.
There is one bone in the pubic region, and likewise forty-five in the back.
There are fifteen bones in the neck, one in the collarbone (jatrū), and likewise one in the jaw (hanu).
The root of the eyebrows, the two [eyebrows], the forehead, the eyes, the cheeks, and likewise the bones of the nose; 81.
Together with the Sarjukās and Āsthālakas, there are seventy-two Arbudas.
There are two temples, four skull-bones, and likewise the head. || 82 ||
The chest consists of seventeen bones; such is the summary of the bones of a human being.
And likewise, there are exactly two hundred and one joints here.
And there are sixty-eight branches, and sixty minus one.
And eighty [years] are said to be the intermediate period, O descendant of Bhṛgu. (84)
And there are not hundreds of sinews here; rather, they are considered to be two hundred and thirty.
But those within the two intermediate regions are indeed said to be seventy, moving upwards. || 85 ||
And these six types have been described by the wise among the various branches [of the Veda].
There are five hundred and forty peśīs here, as well as those that move upwards. || 86 ||
There are four hundred [verses] here, and likewise [four hundred] in the branches, according to the learned.
Likewise, sixty peśīs are said by the wise to exist within the two internal channels. ||87||
And for women, it should be known that the maximum [life span] is thirty-four years.
O Rāma, ten are to be known on the breasts, and likewise ten on the vulva.
Likewise, four [veins] in the uterus should be known by those who contemplate the embryo.
Thirty million, and likewise another ten million. || 89 ||
Fifty-six thousand vessels have indeed been described.
They carry the essence through the body, just as small irrigation channels carry water to a field.
Likewise, all such things as oil massages, as well as fomentations, ointments, and so forth.
Know, O mighty-armed one, that there are likewise seventy-two crores of hairs.
Of marrow, of fat, and likewise of muscle-fat, O twice-born one.
And likewise of urine, bile, phlegm, and feces. || 92 ||
Furthermore, the number of handfuls for blood and for lymph are traditionally recorded in successive order.
All [the fingers] are said to be increased by half and half more than the previous añjali-measure. ||93||
And there was half an añjali of Śukra, as well as half an añjali of Ojas.
Likewise, four [stages] for women during their menstrual period have been described by the wise. ||94||
This is declared by those who contemplate the body to be the measure of the element of samādhi.
The bodies of embodied beings are always indeed distinct from one another.
Through their differentiation, they are divided according to the nature of their impurities and defects. || 95 ||
This body is a mass of impurities and defects, a receptacle for the elements, bound by the power of karma.
He for whom there is liberation here in this world is blessed, for Viṣṇu is indeed the supreme cause of liberation. ||96||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Subject of the Body," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 115 ||
Puṣkara said:
When the lifespan and the karma of men have been exhausted and death has arrived.
The heat, provoked within the body and impelled by a violent wind, [causes distress]. || 1 ||
Having then obstructed the body, it indeed holds back all the humors.
It indeed pierces the seats of the vital breaths as well as the vital points (marmas). || 2 ||
The wind, provoked by coldness, then seeks out an opening.
Likewise, there are two eyes, two ears, and two nostrils. ||3||
Above, however, there are seven apertures, and likewise the face is a group of seven.
By these [veins], the vital breath generally departs for those of virtuous deeds. || 4 ||
Below, the anus and the generative organ are declared to be the two apertures.
Then, by means of those two openings, those who have performed unwholesome deeds die. || 5 ||
O Bhārgava, having pierced the crown of the heads of yogins, the individual soul departs.
Or else, O Rāma, they may do so according to their own will, as the yogins desire.
But when the time of death has arrived, remaining established within the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
When knowledge is shrouded by darkness and the vital points are obstructed.
That living soul, seated upon the navel, is moved by Mātariśvan.
That living being, however, being impelled by those past actions, [wanders].
O twice-born one, he gradually causes that eightfold vital sustenance to cease.
He abandons this body, and from that point, there is only exhalation.
Whether passing away, being born, or entering into wombs.
The perfected ones (siddhas) behold such a living being in this manner with their divine eye.
But when the time for the abandonment of the body arrived, O sinless one, he then—
At that very moment, he assumes a subtle, transportable body (ativāhika-śarīra).
From this body of his, three elements ascend upwards.
Space, wind, and fire, and two below them, O descendant of Bhṛgu. (12)
And likewise, O illustrious one, the waters and the earth.
In this way, a person who has attained the state of the five elements is so designated. || 13 ||
Thus, when the body has reached the state of the five elements, that subtle body (ativāhika) remains.
Likewise, [they were] terrifying, most formidable, and wearing various kinds of disguises.
Then, he was swiftly bound with the noose of Time.
He is led by the agents of Time along the path of Yama, which is exceedingly difficult to traverse.
It was vast, resembling a glowing iron frying pan, and like a great mass of iron fibers.
It consists of terrifying, heated sand that resembles copper-colored leaves.
The surface of the earth is eighty-six thousand yojanas.
But the city of Yama, O Rāma, is known as the terrible Saṃyamanī.
He was led by that very same path to that city.
Being dragged across the surface of the earth by terrible messengers of Yama.
Experiencing suffering there, O giver of honor, he does not die.
That path is said to be exceedingly uneven and terrible to behold.
O Rāma, the great one, assuming universal forms, was covered by Śītā upon the earth.
Abounding with falling snow, it was exceedingly cold and very difficult to cross. ||20||
And likewise, dwelling in a difficult place shrouded in darkness is comparable to dwelling in a womb.
By crows, ravens, and jackals, whose mouths were like the touch of fire; || 21 ||
He was surrounded by flies, gadflies, and mosquitoes, as well as by snakes and scorpions.
Even while being devoured by them, the creature is also devoured by the rākṣasas.
Even after being cut again and again, he does not suddenly lose his life.
He is crushed with terrible mallets and pierced with iron spikes. || 23 ||
He is indeed afflicted by hunger, thirst, and even by terrible [suffering].
Being scorched by that most terrible sand, he is led away. || 24 ||
Being thus tormented, he reaches the abode of Yama.
In ten muhūrtas, he crossed that exceedingly difficult path.
One encounters that which has a terrifying roar and is foul-smelling and fearsome to behold.
At that time, a person perceives it as something very great due to the divine illusion (māyā).
At that time, a result corresponding to his evil deed arises for him there.
For some it lasts for twenty kalpas; for others, its manifestation occurs every hundred [years]. || 27 ||
Furthermore, great terrors arise, born indeed of hunger and thirst.
O knower of dharma, by [the failure to provide] a staff and alms-food, the state of a preta arises. || 28 ||
Then that man dwells in the world of the pretas for one year.
Water-pots, food, and other offerings are given for him by his kinsmen. || 29 ||
O knower of dharma, whatever [is done] day after day, that one enjoys; of this there is no doubt.
But for one to whom this is not given, he is there just as he himself [is].
Furthermore, he himself receives the food and other provisions that were previously given.
But it was not given by himself, nor is there anyone else who gives it. || 31 ||
Yet there is no giver of water, and he alone suffers for it.
But wherever water is offered by his kinsmen, there it arises for him.
There is a river named Śītajalā, abounding with much water.
And whatever śrāddha is performed month after month, that is offered there for him. || 33 ||
By that, one attains supreme satisfaction; there is no doubt in this matter.
But one human month is recorded as a single day in the world of the ancestors.
But in the world of the pretas, a day is reckoned according to human standards.
Therefore, food should be given to the deceased day by day for a year.
Thus being tormented, he reaches the abode of Yama.
Then that evil-souled one beholds the god of terrible appearance.
Then Citragupta, having understood his deeds exactly as they were, [acted accordingly].
The knower of dharma issues a command, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
Then there are the gods known as the Śmaśānikas, who belong to Yama and are terrifying.
Then they protect that man from cold, wind, and heat. || 38 ||
Just as someone here in this prison might be guarded by treacherous men.
O Bhārgava, from the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) offered thereafter, he obtains a body.
This is declared to be the body of enjoyment (bhogadeha) through the sequence itself; of this there is no doubt.
For whomsoever the funeral cakes for the departed ancestors are not offered, there is liberation [from that state]. || 40 ||
For the deities of the cremation grounds, there is no end to their existence, even until the dissolution of the universe.
There, he undergoes terrible torments arising from cold winds and heat. || 41 ||
Then, when the sapindikarana rite has been performed by his kinsmen, the man—
When a full year has passed, he assumes another body.
Thereupon, he goes to hell or to heaven according to his own karma.
Thereafter, he dwells for a period of time in accordance with his past actions. || 43 ||
For one whose sapindikarana has been performed before the completion of a year.
It is declared that even for him, the state of a preta will certainly last for one year.
By those who have sacrificed with various sacrifices, and by whom Keśava has been worshipped;
Those who are slain in battle likewise do not go to the world of the hungry ghosts.
They do not come under the control of those deities who dwell in cremation grounds.
In that same way, they enter the terrible and fearsome realm of the hungry ghosts (pretaloka). || 46 ||
Thus do the sinful, the lowest of men, travel by the southern path.
In the same way, those who plant trees go to the abode of the grove. ||47||
But by a cool path, abounding with fruits and flowers, one travels happily.
And those who give umbrellas travel along the road with ease and comfort. || 48 ||
Those who give shoes mount a vehicle yoked with mules.
Those who give vehicles travel by means of celestial chariots, as do those who provide beds and seats. (49)
Givers of houses go to the celestial abodes, and givers of water go there satisfied.
Satiated with various kinds of food and edibles, the givers of such meals depart. || 50 ||
Those who offer lamps proceed easily along the path by means of light.
Being honored by the servants of Yama, the devotees go to Janārdana.
They have no fear whatsoever, neither in this world nor in the next.
Satisfied with all their desires, those men proceed with speed.
But those devotees of Janārdana, the Lord of the Gods, who rely upon a sattvic intellect—
Their destination, O Rāma, is there where the white men dwell, freed from all sins.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Path of Yama," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, within the second section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. 116.
Rāma said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear who those men are that go to heaven.
O best among the upholders of the Dharma, by what means do they thus go to hell? || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
Those best of the twice-born who abide in the stages of life as they have been described, [attain their respective goals].
Those men who are constantly devoted to their own duty go to heaven.
Those who abide, O protector of the earth, in accordance with the duties of kings.
Kings who act in accordance with the counsel of their domestic chaplain go to heaven. || 3 ||
Those who find happiness in the happiness of their subjects, and who are pained by their suffering.
Those who act as punishers of the wicked should be known as those who go to heaven. ||4||
Those who have been slain for the sake of their master, for the sake of Brahmins, or for the sake of a friend;
And those men who were slain during the seizure of the cows have gone to heaven. || 5 ||
Having abandoned the bodily elements in water, forests, or fire, [one attains liberation].
Or, O knower of dharma, those who die by fasting shall go to heaven.
And those constantly engaged in pilgrimages, exhausted by the journey;
And those who have emaciated themselves through austerity are to be known as those who go to heaven.
They abstained from honey and meat, and they desisted from the drinking of intoxicants.
And even those who engage in sexual desire and intercourse should be known as goers to heaven. || 8 ||
Devoted to their parents, self-controlled, respectful toward their gurus, and pleasant in speech.
And those men who are devoted to truth and uprightness go to heaven. || 9 ||
Those who provide garments and drinks for wedding ceremonies;
Those men who establish gardens and groves go to heaven. || 10 ||
Those who construct tanks and wells, as well as those who give away their daughters in marriage.
Those men who give umbrellas and sandals go to heaven. || 11 ||
Those who provide fuel for the fires, as well as those who give gifts of cows and villages;
And those men who are devoted to the service of cows go to heaven. || 12 ||
They are devoted to helping others and avoid forming attachments to others.
Those men who both worship and are worshipped go to heaven. || 13 ||
Devoted to the study of their own sacred texts, wise, and intent on serving their gurus.
And those lay followers who show respect to the elders should be known as those destined for heaven. ||14||
Likewise, those who provide shelter and those who give sacrificial sessions (satra).
Those men who are devoted to cows, gods, and Brahmins go to heaven. || 15 ||
Those who are listeners of the teachings, and likewise those who perform sacrifices;
And those who are devoted to fasting should be known as destined for heaven. || 16 ||
Those intent on the study of the scriptures experience afflictions here in this world.
And those who are devoted to the welfare of the scriptures should be known as those destined for heaven. ||17||
Those who bestow life upon the distressed, and those who indeed refrain from violence;
And those men who do not cause suffering to living beings go to heaven.
They are givers to the poor and are powerful yet endowed with forbearance.
And those men who, though established in youth, are peaceful, go to heaven. ||19||
Those who are endowed with sons' sons and daughters' sons, as well as those who are long-lived.
Those men who act for the benefit of children go to heaven.
Those who provide for the destitute and those who act as their marriage brokers.
And those men who give the gift of a second visitation go to heaven. ||21||
And those who are worshippers of the planets, as well as those who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha).
And those men who practice sharing [with others] go to heaven. || 22 ||
And of all the deities, and those who are always devoted to their worship.
And those men who are always delighted in giving are destined for heaven. || 23 ||
And having likewise performed an exceedingly difficult task there, they remained unharmed.
O Rāma, even those men who die in due time go to heaven. ||24||
Those who are constantly devoted to Madhusūdana, the lord of gods who is without equal;
Devoid of passion (sattva) and separated from activity (rajas), they go to the celestial realm, honored by the hosts of gods. ||25||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Portion of Heaven," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, within the second section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Puṣkara said:
Those who are perpetrators of great sins, as well as those people who are perpetrators of sins.
Those men who are meat-eaters, as well as those who approach women who should not be approached;
And those who take pleasure in the wives of others, they indeed go to hell. || 1 ||
Those men who transgress against their wives and those who oppress other men [fall].
Those who are censured in assemblies indeed go to hell.
And those who have many wives, yet do not behave toward them with impartiality.
And those who cause the loss of the proper time for conception (ṛtukāla) indeed go to hell.
Those women who conduct themselves rightly toward their husbands, and not out of arrogance;
Likewise, those who are attached to what is unpleasant should be known as destined for hell. ||4||
They disregard their husbands and speak unpleasant words to them.
And they function with independence; they should be known as leading to the downward path. || 5 ||
Those lords of the earth who completely abandon the instruction of the treatises on statecraft,
Those who engage in all such activities indeed go to hell.
But those men who, having abandoned the dharma prescribed for their caste and stage of life, continue to live...
O highly fortunate one, those who follow external scriptures are indeed destined for hell.
Those who officiate at sacrifices for those unworthy to sacrifice, and those who give false testimony;
Likewise, those who are devoted to falsehood are indeed destined for hell.
Those who are attached to worldly affairs and speak with partiality;
And those who possess incorrect vision are indeed destined for hell.
Those men who eat sweet foods while their attendants are looking on [are reborn as flies].
O Knower of Dharma, those who do not share [their wealth] indeed go to hell.
But those who, O highly fortunate one, do not pay their wages, are merely hirelings.
And those whose arms are not designated [for giving] indeed go to hell. ||11||
They are deceivers of laborers and likewise deceivers of those who depend upon them.
And likewise, those who deceive others should be known as destined for hell. || 12 ||
Those who are ungrateful, those who are merciless, and those who seize the property of others.
And those who act deceitfully toward their friends indeed go to hell. || 13 ||
Likewise, those who create obstacles for cows that have set out to drink;
Likewise, those who [act similarly] toward other living beings indeed go to hell. || 14 ||
Those men who create obstacles for one engaged in performing the work of the Dharma.
And those who incite others to evil indeed go to hell. ||15||
Those who abandon their dependents, and those officiating priests who abandon their duties;
Those who [speak ill] of those worthy of sacrifice and of their gurus indeed go to hell. || 16 ||
Those who are generous toward the deities and those who are generous toward the sacrificial fires.
And those who abandon the scriptures indeed go to hell. || 17 ||
O giver of honor, [this applies] to children, guests, Brahmins, and indeed to the gods as well.
And those who always eat before [others] surely go to hell. || 18 ||
And those who approach a woman during her menses, and those who act as servants to women;
And those who approach women of improper birth are indeed destined for hell. || 19 ||
Those pitiless ones who discharge semen outside the womb, as well as into empty space;
And even on the sacred festival days (parvan), O knower of dharma, they indeed go to hell.
O Rāma, those who perform their private Vedic recitation here during times when study is forbidden—
And those who indeed revile their gurus are surely destined for hell. ||21||
And those who revile the deities, the Vedas, and the Brahmins.
And those who [speak ill] of the deeds of the Purāṇas indeed go to hell. || 22 ||
O Rāma, those men who are nihilists and those who are devoid of faith—
And those who are seized by egoism are indeed destined for hell.
Men who are addicted to evil deeds and who abandon virtuous actions.
And those who betray their master or their friend, they indeed go to hell. ||24||
And those who delight in harming kings, brahmins, or even cows.
O knower of dharma, even those who are friends go to hell.
But those who are addicted to slander and who even pierce the vital secrets of others, [are reborn as gadflies].
Likewise, those mortals who are impure are indeed destined for hell.
And those who sell Soma, as well as those who sell seeds;
And those who sell themselves should be known as destined for hell. || 27 ||
O knower of dharma, those in whose house there are young maidens behold the dust [of prosperity].
And those by whom she was given for a bride-price (śulka) are indeed destined for hell. || 28 ||
And those men who propound the doctrine of difference regarding Brahmā, Īśa, and Keśava;
Overcome by darkness on all sides, they indeed go to hell. ||29||
Those who are of noble birth and share the ancestral offerings (sapinda), as well as those who cause the cessation of the offering of the rice-balls (pinda).
And those who lack faith in their ancestors are indeed destined for hell. ||30||
Those men who are devoted to sensual pleasures, as well as those who are intent upon worldly wealth.
And those in the world who are haters of the Dharma, they indeed go to hell. || 31 ||
Those who, by their power, do not behold one who is distressed, afflicted, and dependent.
And those who do not rush to the aid of one in distress are indeed destined for hell. ||32||
And those who, arrogant with pride, treat the lowly with derision.
These people, who go to hell, treat the innocent with contempt. || 33 ||
O Rāma, having caused suffering to a person in any way whatsoever, one goes to hell.
Therefore, O Rāma, a person should strive with effort to avoid causing pain to others. || 34 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Those Going to Hell," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* (The Legend of Puṣkara) addressed to Rāma, within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Rāma said:
And the names of the hells, as well as their various tortures.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear [the fate] of those men who go to hell. || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
Tāmisra, Mandhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, and Raurava.
The Kālasūtra hell and the Mahānaraka hell as well. ||2||
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tapana, and Saṃpratāpana;
And Saṃghāta, Kākola, Kaśmala, and Pūtimṛttika. || 3 ||
The iron stake, Nṛbīma, the churning-stick, Śālmali, and the river.
As well as the Forest of Sword-leaves and likewise the Iron Workshop. || 4 ||
In the netherworlds, O mighty-armed one, there are three times three, according to the order of increase.
In the same manner, there are eight [spheres] for each one, in the cardinal directions as well as in the intermediate directions.
Those hells of terrible appearance should likewise be known as being situated there.
O best of the Bhrigus, these men of evil deeds go to those [hells].
Some [beings] are in a single hell, while others are in many hells, one after another.
O Rāma, these men go on, being tormented again and again.
Those who inflict torments upon hell-beings and upon men.
They are said to be of terrible form, bringing fear by their mere sight.
Those with the faces of a cat, an owl, a jackal, a vulture, a hawk, and a donkey;
Likewise, others [were born] as elephants, horses, camels, boars, and lions.
Of the iguana, the buffalo, the crow, as well as the water-fowl and the crane;
Likewise, [the enmity] between sheep and goats, between moths and [birds], and between snakes and mice. || 10 ||
And likewise for other beings, there are other men with stomachs.
Likewise, others appeared as headless trunks, resembling the forms of *kabandhas*. || 11 ||
They had terrifying faces, were fearsome, and likewise bore various weapons.
They were fierce in speech, invincible, and entwined with serpents and scorpions.
Having cast men into a vat of oil and ignited the fire, [he burned them].
Having thoroughly kindled it, they repeatedly boil certain men within it. || 13 ||
And others in vessels of bell-metal, and still others in copper bowls.
And others [were cooked] in iron vessels, even in molten sparks of fire. ||14||
Others were impaled on stakes, and likewise others were roasted in dry fires.
Having cut these up, they cook them; likewise, having cut others, they cook those as well. || 15 ||
They were striking some with whips, and others likewise against other men.
O illustrious one, they feed those heated by fire iron balls. ||16||
Likewise, others [spit] even dust, or elsewhere something else that has been vomited.
He placed the excrement in one place, the phlegm in another, and likewise the thorns elsewhere.
Except for the sands, O Bhārgava, which resemble fire.
Likewise, in other places, they cause them to drink the Vāruṇī liquor, which has the color of fire.
Except for those in the hells, they cut their limbs into pieces.
Likewise, elsewhere they repeatedly split them apart with saws. || 19 ||
Likewise, elsewhere they torment the denizens of hell by placing them in mechanical devices.
And they beat others who were made of wooden mortars with pestles.
Likewise, those who have entered the cauldron, and others who have risen slightly out of the cauldron.
They strike those who have fallen into great agony with heavy mallets and clubs.
And having flayed the skin elsewhere, they give it to dogs dwelling in hell.
They abandon them, and they are devoured again and again by those with sharp teeth.
In darkness, as well as elsewhere, in places of terrible stench and terrifying danger.
And in those [hells], people are cast into extreme heat that is equal to dwelling in a womb. || 23 ||
By crows, jackals, snakes, scorpions, and even by mice.
And they are devoured by flies, except for those who have received the teaching.
Except for the terrible śālmali tree, which is scorched and possesses sharp thorns.
The lowest of men are made to ascend [the mountain] which is teeming with serpents, insects, and other such creatures. || 25 ||
And elsewhere, one likewise [sees] a terrifying, heated slab of iron.
Yet, by their very command, those [fires] which are so painful to touch embrace them.
Elsewhere, they dwell in uninhabited dwellings, oppressed by fear.
In that regard, O giver of honor, [the marks] were on their noses, eyes, ears, and mouths.
Large, flesh-eating worms enter [the body].
Likewise, other hell-beings are repeatedly cast into the River of Alkali.
And they are cast into another hell characterized by intense cold and darkness.
Others enter the great river that carries blood-red waters. ||29||
And others of terrifying appearance are dragged through the Asipatravana forest.
Other men there are afflicted by thirst and hunger. || 30 ||
Desiring the food and drink of others, they are struck with forged mallets.
Likewise, in other places, non-combatants cause others to drink one another. || 31 ||
O giver of honor, having bound them with thick smoke while facing downwards upon the trees.
Elsewhere, the soldiers perform the flaying of the skin, cutting it into pieces as small as sesame seeds. ||32||
In the same way, the logs of the hell-beings are bound together by their bones.
And with bodies as large as gabled palaces, they were tormented by fear. ||33||
Elsewhere, those with needle-like mouths are driven about, tormented intensely by hunger.
And likewise elsewhere, they are drenched with oil and molasses.
O highly fortunate one, [this was done] by one who was tormented by those who cause intense suffering.
Elsewhere, they were covered in boils, with tongues hanging out and utterly bewildered. ||35||
Cast into the fierce heat, they are devoured by ants.
Elsewhere, they are cut with a thread, starting from the feet and proceeding in sequence. || 36 ||
O tiger among the Bhṛgus, even those who are like mountains become as small as sesame seeds when they are in hell.
And as far as their heads extend, [he struck] there again and again. || 37 ||
And having prepared a frying pan with flour, others likewise cook [the food] intensely.
And in iron vessels, or elsewhere, with sharp iron spikes. || 38 ||
O mighty-armed one, they are restrained by terrible tortures while being scorched in those heated places.
Likewise, elsewhere they are crushed after being pinned down upon stone slabs.
Having been placed in pits with earth thrown over them, they are beaten violently with pestles.
Likewise, men are cast against pillars and elsewhere by means of arrows.
And they are bound with chains and rolled upon thorns.
They are awakened by fragrance in one place, but again and again by poison in another.
And likewise by hell-beings, appearing in various terrifying forms.
And they are tormented intensely in hell by many kinds of agonies. || 42 ||
And likewise, others devour one another's flesh.
Crying out again and again, "Alas, father! Mother! (43)
Censuring their own actions while being beaten by those soldiers.
And they are tormented by many agonies, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
For some have their hellish torments liberated, while others find the fire to be perfectly cool.
O highly fortunate one, they likewise perceive it as having the most pleasant touch. || 45 ||
Released from the cold hell, he reached a mass of snow that was pleasantly warm.
He considers everything else to be most pleasant to the touch in that same way. || 46 ||
And that lowest of men who is released from the hells and from the weapons—
Other weapons were produced as well, which were equal in their pleasant touch. ||47||
In the human realm there is both pleasure and pain, whereas in the triple heaven there is only pleasure.
In hell, O descendant of Bhṛgu, there is only constant and fierce suffering.
There is thirst there, hunger there, and a pungent, terrifying odor.
Various torments are described there, and the fear therein is exceedingly terrible.
It was foul-smelling, strewn with thorns, and likewise crowded with corpses.
But that hell is indeed terrifying and full of suffering, abounding with hair and bones. || 50 ||
It was crowded with crows and flesh-eating beasts making great cries of distress.
It is teeming with worms, insects, and moths, and likewise abounds in pus and blood.
Bound together by mutual afflictions, they act as mutual draggers.
It was a terrible mutual striking, as well as a mutual causing of fear.
Thus, those wicked ones have come together in these hells.
Indeed, many men who have committed evil deeds are sent away.
O best of the Bhṛgus, this continues until their sins have reached exhaustion.
For that long they are not liberated from that hell of terrifying appearance. || 54 ||
The hells are exceedingly terrifying and most dreadful, strewn with hosts of fearsome serpents.
O foremost of the Bhārgava lineage, those who bear devotion for the Supreme Person do not go [to such states].
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Torments of Hell," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* addressed to Rāma, within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Rāma said:
O Knower of Dharma, by what action do men become inhabitants of hell?
Tell me, which various wombs do animals enter? (1)
Puṣkara said:
Worms in the midst of impurity are people who have committed great sins.
They appear in many ways upon the earth, and likewise upon stones.
One gradually attains the state of grass, clusters, creepers, shrubs, and trees.
And subsequently, the deer are always tormented by the fear of hunters. || 3 ||
For those who seize the property of Brahmins are indeed harmful and always follow fierce conduct.
In a forest of terrible form, they are born as Brahmarākṣasas.
Delighting in the wives of others, those fools [suffer] upon the earth thus scorched.
For they are born as lizards and immediately thereafter as piśācas.
In a forest of terrifying appearance, within the hollow of a withered tree.
For black snakes are indeed born from that; of this there is no doubt.
Those wicked ones who provide false testimony become worms in impure matter for a long time.
Having done so, they become serpents, and immediately after that, they become piśācas.
Those wicked people who betray their gurus and friends, and those individuals who betray their own masters;
Likewise, those who harm brahmins or their disciples, the ungrateful, and the atheists; || 8 ||
He was a renouncer of wealth toward his kinsmen, and a renouncer [of fear] toward those seeking refuge.
Those who misappropriate deposits and those who purchase young girls; || 9 ||
In impurity there are worms, snakes, deer, and likewise predatory beasts.
Then they are born as wicked jackals, accompanied by a terrible pack.
Those who steal the property of others become sinful elephants, horses, and donkeys.
Likewise, they are born as oxen and camels; of this there is no doubt. || 11 ||
But for him whose property has been taken by them, it shall be restored according to his fortune.
According to the nature of their own faults, those who are wealthy are born [with such traits]. || 12 ||
Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or sun, men are born as elephants.
Likewise, having eaten at an *āmaśrāddha*, they are born into the wombs of vultures.
O Rāma, having likewise accepted gifts from the unworthy, the monkeys [fell].
Likewise, having thus shattered their hopes, even the most base jackals [were satisfied]. || 14 ||
But one who is a slanderer and of wicked conduct is born as a hunter named Vāgurin.
"O highly fortunate one, for a long time, again and again"—thus is the sacred tradition. ||15||
O Rāma, as many embodied beings as a meat-eater consumes his own flesh, so many does he devour.
One attains the womb of that many [beings] again and again; of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
And they, O Rāma, must undoubtedly eat his flesh.
As many living beings as were struck down by him outside the sacrificial altar.
O best of the Bhrigus, one must go through as many wombs as there are [for those sins].
And he must be slain in womb after womb; of this there is no doubt. || 18 ||
One who eats what has been vomited, one bound by the fetters of virtue, one who eats pus, and one who eats blood.
Castes that have fallen from their own duties are born into the wombs of hungry ghosts. ||19||
By stealing grain one becomes a rat; by stealing bell-metal, a swan; and by stealing water, a water-fowl.
A bee [steals] honey, a crow [steals] milk, a dog [steals] juice, and a mongoose [steals] ghee.
As flesh he becomes a vulture, as fat a cormorant, and as oil a bird that dwells in oily waters.
The Cīrīvāka bird [sees] salt, and the Balākā bird [sees] curd. || 21 ||
A partridge, having stolen silk, and a frog, having stolen linen;
Cotton, woven cloth, a curlew, a cow, a monitor lizard, a bag, and molasses.
The muskrat [enjoys] auspicious fragrances, and likewise the peacock [enjoys] leafy vegetables.
Likewise, flies [defile] cooked food, while a porcupine defiles uncooked food. || 23 ||
By stealing fire, one becomes a frog; and a thief who steals household goods becomes a [frog].
By stealing red garments, one is born as a jīvajīvaka bird.
A wolf [sees] a deer or an elephant; a tiger, a horse; but a monkey, fruit and flowers.
By abducting a woman one becomes a yakṣa; by stealing a vehicle, a camel; and by stealing livestock, a goat.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property whatsoever, a man...
Having consumed an oblation that has not been offered in sacrifice, one inevitably goes to the state of an animal. || 26 ||
Having understood that suffering among animals is supreme, a person should always avoid evil deeds.
And devotion to Madhusūdana should be practiced; by that, he abandons all suffering. || 27 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Animal Births," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, within the second section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Rāma said:
They go to the hells and so forth, then to the state of animals, and thereafter to the human state itself.
O son of Varuṇa, tell me their signs in human form.
Puṣkara said: "There are gems, pearls, corals, and various kinds of jewels."
O Rāma, by stealing [gold], a man is born among those who work in gold.
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property whatsoever, a man—
O tiger among the Bhṛgus, he incurs the state of being a burden-bearer in human existence. || 3 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, even after having caused any living being whatsoever to be killed, [one is not defiled].
O knower of dharma, having eaten meat, one becomes afflicted by disease in this world.
A thief of gold has deformed nails; a drinker of liquor has black teeth.
The killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; he who violates the teacher’s bed shall have scabies.
A slanderer shall have a putrid nose, and a backbiter a putrid mouth.
A thief of grain shall become limb-deficient; one who steals mixed grain shall be deformed.
One who steals food shall be diseased, and one who steals speech shall be mute.
A stealer of clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo, and a stealer of horses becomes lame.
O Rāma, he was bald-headed, envious, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas.
O twice-born one, in that same way, he again falls into the state of nihilism.
One who steals a lamp becomes blind, and likewise, one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed.
The killer of a cow becomes blind, as do the bell-ringer and the oil-presser.
One who steals the wealth of others becomes poor, and likewise, one who sets fire to dwellings becomes insane.
He who is hostile toward his guru is born as one afflicted with epilepsy.
O highly fortunate one, even a man who eats only sweets may become afflicted with a wind-tumor (vātagulma).
One who eats the flesh of birds, one who eats from a sacrificial pit, one who suffers from chronic disease, and one who inflicts pain [are excluded]. || 11 ||
In this world, one becomes a deer-hunter by selling that which is not for sale.
One who has intercourse with a woman during her courses shall suffer from elephantiasis, and one who reviles others shall become a fool. ||12||
I have indeed described the principal wombs of animals and their respective characteristics.
It is not possible for me to describe in their entirety all the torments that await those who are the lowest of men.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Marks of Hell," in the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*. 121.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard this, O best of the Yadus, Rāma, who brings delight to his father, [acted accordingly].
He fell motionless upon the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
O illustrious one, while he was unconscious, those women with full and elevated breasts [attended to him].
The celestial women sprinkled him with sandalwood-scented, cool waters.
And by the command of Varuṇa, others [fanned him] with beautiful palm-leaf fans.
They fanned Rāma, the most fortunate one and the best among the upholders of dharma. || 3 ||
In a moment, Bhārgava regained consciousness, though his mind remained distraught.
Then the son of Varuṇa, the slayer of enemy heroes, comforted him;
having been comforted, Rāma then questioned the son of Varuṇa.
The heroic Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, is one who enables the crossing over of difficult passages.
Rāma said:
While living beings are being afflicted here and there by various conditions.
Tell me, O son of Varuṇa, that by which one may cross over difficulties.
Puṣkara said:
In the hermitages as described, those twice-born ones [behave] as prescribed.
Those who abide with self-restrained minds cross over all difficulties.
Those who do not abandon hypocrisy here, and whose conduct is concealed;
They do not grasp at sense objects and they cross over difficult places.
Those who always provide lodging for guests and those who are ever free from malice.
And those who are constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas cross over all difficulties.
And those who, being skilled in the Dharma, maintain the proper conduct toward their mother and father.
Those who avoid sleeping during the day cross over all difficulties.
They abide by righteous conduct with their own wives during the proper seasons.
Those virtuous ones who are devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice cross over all difficulties.
And those heroes in battles who, having abandoned the fear of death, [stand firm].
Those who desire victory through righteousness cross over all difficulties.
Those who do not commit evil deeds through action, mind, or speech.
Those who have laid down the rod of punishment toward living beings cross over all difficulties.
Their actions are free from deceit, and their words are truthful and pleasant.
Those whose wealth is for the sake of righteousness cross over all difficulties.
Those who practice austerity while remaining celibate from their youth;
Those who have bathed after completing their studies, the Vedas, and their vows, cross over all difficulties. || 15 ||
Those of whom no one is afraid, and who do not fear anyone.
Those for whom the world is as dear as themselves cross over all difficulties.
The virtuous, the best among men, do not burn with envy at the prosperity of others.
And those who have turned away from the taste for worldly pleasures cross over all difficulties.
They pay homage to all the gods and listen to all the teachings of the Dharma.
Those men who have faith cross over all difficulties. ||18||
Those kings who, though enveloped by passion, do not lead people away from their wealth through greed;
Those who guard their sense objects cross over all difficulties. ||19||
Those who do not wish to be honored, yet honor other men;
Those who honor those worthy of honor cross over all difficulties.
And those who, desiring offspring, perform acts of faith on every lunar day;
With a perfectly pure mind, they cross over all difficulties.
Those who do not give way to anger at all, and who pacify those afflicted by anger;
They do not become angry with their servants, and they overcome all difficulties.
Those men who here constantly abstain from honey and meat, [attain the highest state].
And those who abstain from liquor from birth onwards cross over all difficulties. ||23||
For those whose eating is for the sake of sustenance and whose sexual union is for the sake of progeny.
Those who employ speech for the sake of truthful utterance cross over all difficulties. ||24||
Likewise, those who construct tanks and groves, as well as others who plant trees;
And those who are the makers of wells cross over difficult places. || 25 ||
Those who give mouthfuls of grass to cows and those who scratch the bodies of cows;
And those who possess devotion to cows cross over all difficulties. || 26 ||
They always honor the Brahmins, as well as the virtuous and their gurus.
And those practitioners of austerity, O knower of dharma, cross over all difficulties.
Those who are devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī and those who are intent upon pilgrimages to sacred fords;
And those who rely upon this one ford cross over all difficulties. || 28 ||
And those who have taken refuge in the one God with their whole being, O Bhārgava.
Those who know the Dharma and are disciplined cross over all difficulties. || 29 ||
Those men who eat only in the evening and in the morning, and drink water [at those times], [attain purity].
O Rāma, those who observe the fast constantly cross over all difficulties.
They were constantly devoted to fasting and always dedicated to their religious observances.
And those whose minds are constantly restrained cross over all difficulties.
And those who recite and cause others to hear this "Crossing Over Difficulties," [attain liberation].
And they say to the Brahmins: "They cross over even the most difficult obstacles."
The Lord is the source and the place of dissolution for all beings and for the worlds.
Those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa indeed cross over all difficulties. || 33 ||
O Rāma, for devotees of Keśava, there is no fear anywhere.
Likewise, O Bhārgava, listen to this verse sung by Yama: || 34 ||
[The protection against] that which arises from kings, thieves, serpents, fire, evil dreams, ill omens, death, and enemies;
Indeed, there is no fear for those among men who are devotees of Madhuripu, the sole lord of the world.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Crossing Difficulties," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, within the second section of the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*. 122.
Rāma said:
Explain further by what action human beings [attain this].
They swiftly cross over all difficulties, O best among the upholders of all dharmas.
Puṣkara said:
Those men who perform difficult deeds quickly cross over all hardships.
In that same way, they indeed obtain all desires wished for by the mind.
Rāma said: "I wish to hear the names of the kṛcchra penances as well as their prescribed rules."
Tell me thus, O knower of dharma, for you know things exactly as they are.
Puṣkara said:
O Rāma, these duties are to be performed by the three social classes with great effort.
In these hardships, no entitlement for a Śūdra is prescribed. || 4 ||
O Bhārgava, at the outset, however, shaving of the head must be performed in every kṛcchra penance.
One should perform the ritual bath three times daily and worship Keśava constantly.
There is also the fire sacrifice with purificatory mantras, as well as the recitation at the conclusion.
And likewise, one should avoid conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts. || 6 ||
This should be performed without distinction in all instances of the kṛcchra penances.
And the heroic posture (vīrāsana) should be assumed, whether out of desire or not. ||7||
When combined with the vīrāsana posture, the kṛcchra penance becomes manifold in its merit.
That which is devoid of the vīrāsana posture is proclaimed to be lacking in ritual procedure. || 8 ||
Rāma said: O observer of noble vows, I desire to hear from you about the vīrāsana posture.
Since the Kṛcchra penance performed together with the Vīrāsana posture possesses manifold virtues. || 9 ||
Puṣkara said:
Having risen, he should remain standing during the day, and likewise seated at night.
This is declared to be the vīrāsana posture, which destroys even the greatest sins.
With curdled milk (āmikṣā), however, he [remains] for two months, and likewise with milk for a fortnight.
Likewise, one should fast for eight nights with curd, and then for three nights with clarified butter.
Or, fasting for three nights, one should perform the tālaka-vrata.
It pacifies all sins and likewise grants all desires. || 12 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, kindle the fire for your own sake.
Then one should offer oblations into the fire and give food to someone.
While the mantra "Brahmā deva" was being recited, the wise one [performed the rite].
"One should indeed bind darbha grass for the sake of protection; such is our sacred tradition. (14)
That which has been infused, that which is being infused, and likewise that which has been placed in a vessel.
O Rāma, with this mantra, a person should consecrate [the water] three times.
"You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are joined with honey."
It is remembered by the sages as the purifier that washes away all sins. || 16 ||
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is indeed the waters of immortality.
May all my evil, whatever misdeed I have committed, be purified. || 17 ||
An evil dream or an ill-considered thought, and whatever action has been committed through speech or deed—[may all that be purified].
O barley grains, destroy misfortune and likewise purify everything for me.
That which has been licked by a dog or a pig, and that which has been defiled by leavings;
May these barley grains purify all my failure to serve my mother and my teacher.
The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, and likewise that of Vaiśyas—
May the barley grains purify for me all the food of a thief and the food from a recent funeral rite.
The conduct of fools, unrighteousness, and that which is performed under the guise of royal duty.
Stealing gold, being an *avrātīna*, and officiating at a sacrifice for one who should not be sacrificed for; 21.
May the barley grains purify for me all slander against the brahmins.
Having placed this mantra upon the vessel, one should then recite it aloud.

"O gods born of mind, yoked by mind, highly skillful, sons of Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; to them, Svāhā! O knower of dharma, one who is self-restrained should always offer this oblation into oneself.
One should not eat to excess, for this is the vow of barley-gruel.
For one seeking intelligence, it is for three nights; for one who has committed a great sin, it is for six nights.
O subduer of enemies, it is declared that for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), [the penance lasts] seven nights.
For those who have committed the great sins (mahāpātaka), it is prescribed that the period be doubled for six nights.
Within twenty-one nights, one obtains the desired objects of desire. || 25 ||
Within one month, one undoubtedly attains liberation from all sins.
Having performed this very same rite with barley grains that have been offered as fodder for cows. || 26 ||
O knower of Dharma, he certainly obtains a fruit ten times greater than that.
Within a month, he directly perceives the thirty deities, the Vedas, and the sciences.
O Bhārgava, one who is capable of both bestowing boons and pronouncing curses becomes such [a person].
From the commencement of the bright fortnight, a man should begin this every day. || 28 ||
Indeed, one should eat the rice-balls mixed with sandalwood paste, increasing the number by one each day.
One should decrease [the morsels] one by one during the dark fortnight, starting from the first day (pratipad) in due order.
O highly fortunate one, one should not eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) at the time of the moon's disappearance.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Puruṣasūkta," within the Puṣkara-narrative addressed to Rāma, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa. || 129 ||
