Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Anomalies of the Water," in the account of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 139 ||
Garga said:
Women give birth at the proper time, and likewise, offspring are born after the lapse of time.
And those who give birth to deformed offspring, as well as those who give birth to twins. || 1 ||
They were non-human, hideous, and likewise afflicted by calamity.
They may be born with missing limbs or with extra limbs, or even as females. || 2 ||
Beasts, birds, and likewise reptiles as well.
One should predict the destruction of that region as well as of the family. || 3 ||
The king should banish them from his own kingdom; thereafter, the best of the twice-born are to be honored and cherished.
Furthermore, one should satisfy the Brahmins with whatever they desire; thereby, the evil attains pacification.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Abnormality in Childbirth," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, concerning the legend of Puṣkara as told to Rāma.
Garga said:
If a mare, an elephant-cow, or a cow gives birth to twins;
Whether it be born deformed or even disfigured, he shall indeed die within six months.
And those who engage in sexual intercourse with those of improper wombs are destroyers of their instruction.
Except for the occurrence of dawn, there is no sexual intercourse among men before they have reached puberty.
Snakes, mice, cats, fish, and dogs are to be avoided.
They should be known as creators of famine and eaters of the flesh of their own kind.
The terrible, untimely intoxication of four-footed beasts and winged birds.
And this milk of a cow [should be avoided], especially that of a dog, just like the milk of any other species. || 4 ||
If non-human beings speak like human beings, they are indeed living creatures.
Or if they give birth to deformed offspring, one should predict the arrival of a foreign army.
Abandonment, expulsion, and giving—these are the duties for one who understands them.
One should gratify the Brahmins here and cause the recitation of prayers and the performance of fire-oblations to be carried out.
Indeed, worship of the dwellers of heaven should be performed with mṛdaṅga drums, kettledrums, and songs.
Likewise, the sacrificial rite should be performed according to the prescribed rules, and food should be given in great abundance to the twice-born.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Pacification of Portents," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, concerning the legend of Puṣkara as told to Rāma.
Garga said:
If unyoked vehicles do not move, and likewise yoked ones do not move, [then what need is there for them?]
When these are urged upon him, great suffering will befall him. || 1 ||
Musical instruments being played do not sound, yet those not struck sound forth.
The immovable indeed move, and likewise, the movable do not move.
In the sky there were sounds of musical instruments and the voices of Gandharvas moving through the air.
If wood, such as a product of the *dārvī* tree, should act upon an axe; || 3 ||
If there is contact with the tail of a cow, but he should cause a woman to fall [into water], [he must perform penance].
One should predict terrible fear of weapons resulting from celestial eclipses. || 4 ||
O twice-born one, having performed the worship of Vāyu with parched grain flour (saktu), one should recite the mantras prescribed for that purpose.
One should offer abundant *paramānna* (milk-rice) here; at the end of the circumambulation, may there be peace for him. ||5||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Transformation of Household Utensils," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, in the narrative of Puṣkara concerning Rāma.
Garga said:
When wild beasts and birds enter the village from the forest, [it is a sign of impending danger].
Village-dwellers go to the forest, and those born in the water go to dry land.
Those born on land enter the water, or they cry out fearfully and without dread.
Jackals howling at the palace gate and at the city gate portend misfortune.
Whether they are night-wanderers by day, or day-wanderers by night.
Villagers may abandon their village, or one should point out its emptiness. || 3 ||
Blazing, they cry out at the twilights and form circles.
Wherever one cries out discordantly in the spring, one should declare that this same result follows there as well.
If a cock should crow at dusk, or even a cuckoo should sing during the winter;
If at sunrise a dog faces the sun, there will be danger from the king.
If a pigeon enters the house, or a flesh-eating bird alights upon the head;
If it be honey from bees, one should declare the death of the householder.
In the gate-houses of the walls, at the archways, marketplaces, and streets.
If a carnivorous bird should alight upon the banner, the umbrella, the weapon, or other such objects, [it portends misfortune].
Or if an anthill arises, or if honey is seen;
That region goes to ruin, or else the king dies. ||8||
Upon seeing numerous mice and locusts, fear of hunger arises.
Pieces of wood, charcoal, bones, horns, and the like were defeated by the dogs and monkeys.
Having departed from the village toward the cremation ground, they brought about the destruction of the village chief.
Whether the crows have but a single egg, or even if they have no eggs at all.
And establishing [the teaching] among those who are lowly is considered to cause the destruction of the doctrine.
And those skilled in battle moved in a circle, keeping their right sides turned away from the enemy.
If crows are known to steal grain, they should be understood as portending famine.
Overpowering the people, fearless, and skilled in the ways of battle. || 12 ||
If a crow is seen to be intent on mating and white in color, [it portends misfortune].
Either the king dies there, or that country perishes. || 13 ||
Where an owl hoots or where one falls, such is the state of that house.
The death of the householder, as well as the loss of wealth, is to be known [as occurring]. || 14 ||
In the event of abnormalities among wild animals and birds, one should perform fire offerings accompanied by ritual fees.
And the verse beginning with "devāḥ kapota" should be recited by the five twice-born men.
And cows should be given to the twice-born according to the prescribed rule, together with gold and pairs of garments as upper coverings.
When this has been done, whatever evil was indicated by wild animals or birds comes to an end.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Portents of Animals and Birds," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* addressed to Rāma, within the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Garga said:
Of palaces, archways, watchtowers, gates, ramparts, and houses.
However, the falling of firm objects without a cause portends the death of the king.
Or where the quarters of the sky are completely filled with dust or smoke.
The sun, moon, and stars become discolored, portending an increase in fear.
Where Rākṣasas are seen, and where Brāhmaṇas act contrary to the Dharma.
The seasons have been inverted, and one unworthy of worship is being worshipped by people. (3)
The constellations are separated; that is a sign of great danger.
And the rising of comets, eclipses, and the perforation of the moon and the sun. || 4 ||
Wherever there is an abnormality of the planets or the constellations, one should predict fear in that very place.
Women quarrel with one another, and children kill other children.
Devoid of moral conduct and right behavior, they are fond of liquor, meat, and falsehood.
Likewise, there are twice-born ones who consist mostly of stone and have fallen from the path of the three Vedas.
In whatever region they are born, one should know that there will be a calamity there.
They are not always honored with the customary offerings of sacrificial posts and oblations.
And where there occurs an interruption of appropriate ritual actions;
Where the fire does not blaze even while the propitiatory offerings are being poured. || 8 ||
But the flesh-eating ants likewise go forth from the four directions.
Full jars leak, and the sacrificial oblation is spoiled.
And where auspicious words are not heard on all sides.
Then, sneezing and running about, they laughed and wept.
And they do not abide among the gods nor properly among the Brahmins.
The vital points (marmans) and their defects are being described, as well as the various musical instruments being played.
Where people betray their gurus and friends, and are devoted to honoring their enemies.
Where a person shows contempt for Brahmins, well-wishers, and ministers. ||12||
Where atheism arises during rites for peace, auspiciousness, and fire-offerings.
Either the king dies there, or that country perishes. ||13||
Understand from me the omens that have appeared when the king's destruction has arrived.
He first hates the brahmins and comes into conflict with the brahmins. ||14||
He is censured by the brahmins, and he even seeks to slay the brahmins.
He does not recall them in his duties, and when entreated, he is overcome. || 15 ||
He takes delight in them and is merciless toward them, and he does not rejoice in their praise.
But out of greed, he likewise imposes a new tax upon the people.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship Śakra together with his consort upon these [images].
And likewise, the foods, the rites for the gods, and the bracelets must be prepared. ||17||
Cows should be given to the best of the twice-born, as well as land, gold, and garments.
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed and the worship of the gods; when this is done, sin attains pacification. ||18||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Pacification of Portents," within the account of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Rāma said:
What indeed is the most important duty of a king? Tell that to me, who am asking you.
How should the system of government be protected by a wise king? ||1||
Puṣkara said:
And by a king endowed with the proper disposition toward the seven-limbed kingdom.
O best of the Bhṛgus, this alone is the duty to be performed by a king regarding the administration of the state.
Conciliation, bribery, siege, treasury, and likewise force;
An ally and the territory—this is said to be the sevenfold kingdom. || 3 ||
And he should banish those who create obstacles for the seven-limbed kingdom.
The king should cause those who act for his harm to be executed immediately, without hesitation.
And the prosperity of the seven-limbed kingdom must be secured within a well-governed realm.
And in all mandalas, they are to be drawn forth by the lord of the earth.
Rāma said:
Explain the strategic encirclements according to the rule for one who desires victory.
Depending upon which [of these], kings should deliberate on peace and war.
Puṣkara said:
In this context, one's own maṇḍala itself constitutes the first maṇḍala.
However, those who are enemies of that mandala should be recognized as being on all sides.
Now listen to the method of calculation regarding the person to be addressed in that case as well.
An enemy is traditionally defined as one who must be attacked; even in that case, one should wait for the right moment.
One who is devoted to that [purpose] should be known as a well-wisher (suhṛt), a friend (mitra), and likewise a friend-enemy (mitraripu).
This has been explained previously; now listen to me regarding what follows as well.
Beyond that is the rear-enemy (pārṣṇigrāha), and beyond that is said to be the ally of the rear-enemy (ākranda).
But an *āsāra* different from that is called an *ākrandāsāra*.
O twice-born one, [this applies] to one who desires victory, whether he is equipped with weapons or likewise devoid of them.
One who is capable of both punishment and favor is proclaimed to be impartial. || 11 ||
He who is capable of both punishing and favoring all beings.
That powerful lord of the earth is said to be indifferent.
O Rāma, this much alone has been told to you regarding the Twelve Kings.
Even in this matter, O bull among men, it is not possible to state a definitive certainty.
There is no such thing as an enemy by birth, nor does a friend exist by birth.
Friends and likewise enemies arise through the application of one's own capability. || 14 ||
Three kinds of enemies are declared: those born of the same lineage, those situated nearby, and those who are artificial.
Among these, each preceding one is considered more difficult to treat than the one following it. ||15||
Even that enemy who is immediate is considered by me to be artificial.
The king who attacks the enemy's ally shall become the rear-enemy (pārṣṇigrāha). || 16 ||
And he should likewise pacify his own rear-enemy by means of strategic expedients.
The ancients do not recommend the destruction of an enemy by means of a friend. || 17 ||
For even a friend becomes an enemy due to being situated immediately adjacent as a neighbor.
One who desires to conquer an enemy should uproot him himself, provided that he is capable of doing so.
Because his majesty has increased through that, no fear arises for him from a friend.
O Rāma, one who desires to conquer cannot otherwise be capable of winning the earth.
Therefore, a king must increase his majesty by whatever means possible.
In such a way that the world would not be alarmed by him, and he would become someone worthy of trust.
Desiring victory, one who conquers through righteousness should likewise bring the world under his control.
People tremble before one who achieves victory through unrighteousness.
Even having obtained the entire earth, one does not enjoy it for long.
Through righteousness, sacrifice prospers here; through righteousness, there is likewise prosperity in the world beyond.
Having conquered his enemies and enjoyed the earth obtained through righteousness for a long time, he proceeds to the celestial realm.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Circle of Kingdoms," within the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* concerning Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Rāma said:
Likewise, conciliation and sowing dissension have been proclaimed, as well as bribery and punishment.
The staff has been described for one's own country; tell me now concerning a foreign land. || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
The ancients have declared that punishment in a foreign land is of two kinds.
Understand that it is both manifest and unmanifest, O best of the twice-born. ||2||
Plundering, the destruction of villages, and likewise the destruction of crops.
And likewise, the slaughter of enemies by means of the fourfold army. || 3 ||
The staff is said to be light, while the direct illumination is fire.
Lack of light, poison, fire, and assassination by hidden men—these are the dangers. || 4 ||
The spoiling of fodder and the like, and the spoiling of waters.
And various auspicious medicinal preparations (rasakriyā), such as those for causing emesis and so forth. || 5 ||
These and other such actions should be performed by the ruler of the earth when faced with an enemy army.
And even for the powerful, O best of the twice-born, there is corruption within their own kingdom.
These four are declared to be the principal means for kings on this earth.
Beyond this, O Rāma, I shall tell you of the remaining three weapons which have not yet been mentioned by me.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Administration of Punishment," in the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Puṣkara said:
The king might think, "By this [act], he will engage me in war."
It would result in a continuous succession of misfortune, and it would be so through the act of making peace. || 1 ||
In this case, conciliation is a source of shame, and giving results in depletion.
If there is punishment for causing division, then one should take refuge in that side. || 2 ||
One who is struck down by contempt there should be made an enemy by the king.
O knower of dharma, equanimity alone is prescribed therein for the sake of the highest good.
But where an objective can be accomplished through equanimity, there is no need for exertion or agitation; that is equanimity.
The task may be accomplished by means of a Brahmin’s form, even if it be a cause for shame, or else through a treaty.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Indifference," within the account of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Puṣkara said:
Kings should cause alarm in their enemies by means of false portents.
In this place, there dwells a bird whose camp is the enemy's army.
O twice-born one, having made that large meteor the tail of that massive [serpent], he—
Having released it from there, one should then display the falling of a meteor upon the shore. || 2 ||
Having ascertained with effort through the intellect this very essence herein.
Likewise, other portents should be observed by kings.
Likewise, one should cause agitation among the enemies by means of two kinds of deceptive stratagems.
And for one year he shall not eat; they shall also declare the destruction of his enemy.
Desiring to conquer the sovereignty of the earth, he should cause agitation among his enemies.
But the favors of the deities toward him are indeed to be celebrated.
Likewise, one who desires victory should recount his gains from dreams.
And likewise, it is certain that there will be the experience of bad dreams by others as well. || 6 ||
Our friend’s army has arrived; strike fearlessly!
When battle has arrived, one should say: "The enemies have been routed by me. || 7 ||
There were shouts of "kṣveḍa" and cries of "kilakila," as well as the words, "My enemy has been slain!"
Strengthened by the command of the gods, the king equipped himself for battle. ||8||
O best of the twice-born, such kinds of illusions should be employed by kings who are elated against their enemies.
An enemy struck by illusion can then be easily and forcefully slain by one of undaunted spirit.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Adornments," in the account of Puṣkara related to Rāma, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
The king should display a fourfold army by means of the net of illusion.
He should show him the inhabitants of the three heavens who have arrived for the sake of companionship.
And a rain of blood should be displayed toward the enemies' auspicious banner.
One should display the severed heads of enemies upon the tips of the victory standards.
O Rāma, for one who desires to establish peace, an act that would be like a great Indra’s net must not be performed by one of undiminished virtue.
I shall declare that to you from the Upaniṣads, as well as other yogas that bring victory.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Illusions," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
Peace and war, as well as the state of deficiency, have been described by the wise.
Relying upon which, others likewise have proclaimed the sixfold policy (ṣāḍguṇya). ||1||
Peace, as well as subjugation, marching, and halting;
The sixfold policy is proclaimed as consisting of duplicity and seeking refuge. || 2 ||
A treaty is traditionally defined as a formal agreement, whereas hostility is declared to be war.
For one desiring victory, marching against the territory of the enemy is prescribed as the course of action. || 3 ||
Even during conflict, remaining in one's own country is called "sitting" (āsana).
The measure of half one's strength is said to be the state of double-dealing (dvaidhībhāva). || 4 ||
Whether toward a neutral or a middling king, seeking refuge is considered "seeking refuge" (saṃśraya).
Peace should be sought with an equal, and by one who is weak, peace should be sought with one who is stronger. || 5 ||
A king himself should engage in conflict with one who is weaker than he, but not with one who is more powerful.
Even there, one should not rely on his rear guard, for it is more powerful.
When an enemy is seated, he is capable of interrupting one's ritual action.
One who is powerful but whose rear is unprotected should resort to a dual policy. || 7 ||
But that by which a king considers himself as being restrained by one who is powerful—
Therefore, he must resort to that which is the lowest among virtues. ||8||
Their vehicle is proclaimed to involve great loss, expense, and exertion.
O Rāma, one should then take recourse to that which brings about abundant gain. || 9 ||
But when one is deprived of all power, then one should seek refuge.
And having understood this, the king [should apply] virtues according to the time, the place, and likewise their distribution.
One should take refuge with the foremost of the Bhārgava lineage; this much is the duty of the king that has been stated. || 11 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sixfold Policy," in the account of Puṣkara related to Rāma, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 150 ||
Rāma said:
"O lotus-eyed one, tell me of the perpetual duty of kings."
And whatever task belongs to the lords of men, as it is performed year after year; || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
When two muhūrtas remain of the night, the king should abandon sleep.
With the sounds of flutes, lutes, mṛdaṅga drums, and kettledrums. || 2 ||
And with the sounds of bards as well as those reciting auspicious verses.
Then, at night, the protector of the earth should observe secret agents.
Those who are not recognized by anyone in the world as belonging to him.
Thereafter, the hearing of the income and expenditure should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having relieved himself, the king should proceed to the bath-house.
Having been given an oil massage at dusk, he was then cleansed according to the ritual procedure.
Thereafter, one should perform the bath, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
With various auspicious waters purified by mantras and medicinal herbs.
Having performed the twilight devotions, being self-restrained, having completed his recitation, and being composed in mind.
Then, having entered the fire-sanctuary, he should look upon the fires together with the family priest.
Then, having properly offered the oblations, he should perform the worship of Vāsudeva.
In that situation, the domestic priest should perform rites for the pacification of bad dreams. ||8||
And the king himself, when the fire has been established, should offer the purifying oblation (pavitra) into the flame.
Then he should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with water offerings according to the prescribed rule.
One should give a cow with its calf and gold to a twice-born man,
having honored him according to one's ability with wealth, and having constantly received the blessings bestowed by the twice-born;
then, anointed with unguents, wearing garlands, well-dressed, and adorned.
And one should behold one's face in a mirror and in clarified butter mixed with gold.
If the clarified butter (ājya) should be clear and fragrant, there will be victory;
but if it emits a foul odor while being offered or if it falls [from the ladle], there will be danger. 12.
If the king should see a distorted face, he would meet with death.
And when one sees it shining brightly, then there shall be auspiciousness for him. ||13||
Then the king should hear that which has issued from the mouth of the astrologer.
On whatever day, lunar date, or asterism [this is performed], it destroys all inauspiciousness. ||14||
And one should follow the advice of physicians; thereby, health will increase.
Having performed the ritual touching of auspicious objects, the king should then behold his teachers. ||15||
After receiving blessings from his teachers, the king should then proceed in every direction.
There he should see the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the ministers and counselors, stationed there.
And, O highly fortunate one, understand the subjects from the wardens of the gate.
There, one should listen to the Itihāsas with some degree of alertness.
Thereafter, he should carry out the decision on the cases of those seeking justice according to his best judgment. ||18||
Thereafter, having become impartial toward both enemy and friend, he should oversee legal proceedings.
Having then left the assembly hall, he should hold counsel together with his ministers.
Wherever anyone might hear this mantra of his, it would not be possible by any means.
One should perform it with a single person; one should not perform it with many.
Nor should the king [be served] by fools, nor by those without names, nor likewise by the unrighteous.
One should empower the mantra by means of which the kingdom does not run away.
But it is said that confusion regarding mantras is the very root of destruction for kings.
A mantra, when incorrectly applied, becomes a cause of destruction, like a non-mantra.
Success is said to come for rulers of the earth when the mantra is well-determined.
No one at all knows the actions being performed by him.
That king, the lord of the earth, recognizes only those deeds that have already been performed.
Furthermore, counsel was deliberated separately by the ministers, and then again collectively.
Having carefully deliberated for oneself, one should thereafter take refuge in that which is virtuous.
The king, conceited in his own wisdom, took no pleasure in the words of his ministers. || 25 ||
It quickly goes to destruction, like a pond whose water has been drained.
The concealment of one's outward appearance is considered the supreme protection of a king’s counsel. || 26 ||
Through facial expressions and gestures, wise and learned people discern a secret counsel.
He was devoted to the words of the astrologers, physicians, and ministers.
The king attains prosperity and remains long-established in fame.
The wise ones maintain that he is thus addicted to hunting. ||28||
O Bhārgava, pride in women and in dice is likewise in vain, as is being superior [in such matters].
For that lord of men was devoted to the solicitation of taxes and to violence. || 29 ||
Likewise, in the case of backbiting and even in a powerful conflict.
And they restrain him when he is intent upon other harmful things as well. || 2.151.30 ||
Having performed the mantra-ritual, the lord of the earth should then engage in physical exercise.
Likewise, [he was skilled] in chariots, elephants, and horses, as well as in the sword and the bow. || 31 ||
And furthermore, in other weapons and in hand-to-hand combat.
Having bathed after anointing himself with unguents applied by his feet, he should behold Viṣṇu, who has been well-worshipped. ||32||
One should behold the sacrificial fire into which offerings have been made, and one should behold the Brahmins who have been well-honored.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, they were honored by their masters with sacrificial fees.
Then, anointed with perfumes, wearing fragrant garlands, and adorned with beautiful ornaments, he appeared resplendent.
Wearing fine garments, one should partake of food and listen to songs at that time. ||34||
It was tested by fire and likewise by the signs of beasts and birds.
It had previously been examined by others and consecrated with the *jāṅgulī* mantra. ||35||
And the king wore poison-destroying gems as well as medicinal herbs.
Having eaten and taken betel, he performed a special circumambulation.
Then, lying on his left side upon his bed, he should contemplate the scriptures.
And he went toward the storehouses, the armories, and the foremost of the mounts.
Having seen the warriors and followed them, the evening twilight then set in.
And having deliberated upon the tasks to be done, he then dispatched his spies.
Having entered the inner apartments, he ate light and wholesome food. || 38 ||
One should indulge in sleep, which has been rendered secure by prior protection, accompanied by the sounds of flutes, lutes, and drums.
For this eternal ordinance, which brings glory to kings, has been declared to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Daily Routine," in the account of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 151 ||
Puṣkara said:
The king, however, should perform [this rite] every month on his own birth-star.
That action which is the cleansing of birth has already been described by me previously.
Then, O lord of men, the king should perform the flower-bath every month.
At the time of the sun's transit, one should worship the Sun and likewise the young Moon.
The king should worship the planet as it has emerged from the solar disc.
Likewise, upon the rising of Agastya, worship should be performed by the lords of men.
One should worship Madhusūdana while he is asleep for four months.
During the month of Proṣṭhapada, one should protect and worship Śatakratu.
And on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, one should worship Bhadrakālī.
When the sun has reached the Svāti constellation, one should likewise perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
After one year, he should perform a koṭihoma sacrifice using only clarified butter.
In the book of the regnal year, one should perform that worship of Rudra.
Now, O Rāma, these duties of a king which I have declared to you are constant.
Having performed these according to the prescribed rules, O lord of men, he shall rule the entire earth for a long time.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Annual [Observances]," in the account of Puṣkara related to Rāma, within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Rāma said:
For how can the worship of Keśava be performed for four months?
O best of gods, tell that to me who am asking, as it pertains to a king. || 1 ||
Puṣkara said:
O descendant of Bhrgu's lineage, a king must always be diligent.
At the end of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the king should take up his residence in that place.
Invincible to foreign kingdoms, it abounded in fodder and fuel.
Likewise, [a place] endowed with water, free from mud, and affected by the rainy season. ||3||

If its left side moves, that indicates long-term success for him.
The right limb as well as the left arm [indicate] fear.
But he who causes an obstacle to a journey, having come before one's face for the sake of joy; || 52 ||
O Bhārgava, the thief who obstructs the path strikes at the path itself.
The sinful one has a mouth like a firebrand and bones, and likewise a mouth like a rope and a reed.
A person is fortunate if their mouth is covered by shoes, and likewise if it is filled with meat.
Furthermore, one should avoid inauspicious objects as well as an inauspicious location.
One who goes at the very front, disregarding value, shall have no fear once he has set out.
In that same manner, through such a form, he goes to a beautiful region and likewise proceeds by stages. || 55 ||
And likewise, auspicious articles should belong to him for the sake of accomplishing his purpose.
And in this same way, O Rāma, those such as jackals and others are to be understood. || 56 ||
It should be known that this portends danger for the master and groundless fear for the cattle.
At night, it leads to the danger of thieves; likewise, a distorted form leads to death. || 97 ||
If a bull should bellow at night, it portends well-being for one's master.
A bull that has been released bestows victory upon the king. ||58||
They ate what was not fit to be eaten, and likewise, the cows ate the Nyāsa-ambakas.
Having abandoned affection for their calves, he is considered a destroyer of the cows. || 59 ||
Having been trampled by his feet, the beings became miserable due to that transformation.
And cows whose tails are entangled with one another are considered to be bringers of fear.
With their limbs moist and their hair standing on end, they thus enter the house.
Alternatively, those with earth clinging to their horns should be known to bring prosperity to their owner. || 61 ||
A wise person should state all of this regarding the chief queen and the other women as well.
In the eyes, nostrils, mouth, shoulders, seat, and head; || 62 ||
The blazing of horses is auspicious; elsewhere, it is praised.
The flaming of all the limbs is not desired, nor is the arising of smoke.
The emergence of sparks and likewise eating one's own excrement in feces.
Likewise, the mounting of another horse equipped with a saddle. || 64 ||
Sitting in water is not desired, nor is rolling about on the ground.
Whether from its own nature or without an external cause, it is like a wave upon a tree of calamity.
Furthermore, an aversion toward fodder and water is also said to arise quite suddenly.
A horse purchased from crows, pigeons, or mynah birds [is inauspicious]. || 66 ||
Then it portends the death of either oneself or one's master.
Afflicted by suffering, devoted to meditation, with tearful eyes, he was terrifying to behold. || 67 ||
This creature, though terrifying, even licks his own foot with its tongue.
Or if it falls without a specific sign, then it will lead to prosperity among men. || 68 ||
And likewise, scratching the earth with his left foot.
Or if it is on its own left side, or during the day, it does not bestow auspiciousness. || 69 ||
Trembling, they neigh and weep again and again.
Discharging excrement and urine, they experience great terror.
Rising and sitting during the twilight hours with dejected minds.
Their limbs were relaxed, their eyes filled with tears, and they were dejected; neighing, they inspired terror. || 71 ||
But when, while neighing, flames or moonlight should issue from its mouth;
Then it certainly announces victory for the master. || 72 ||
Scattering the earth with his right foot, Jayavardhana advanced.
And at night, O best of men, he should sleep on his right side.
One should ascend a new [vehicle] or go home in the opposite direction.
Likewise, touching his left foot indicates an obstacle to the journey.
When it moves forward in regular order, it is preceded by a preparatory tremor.
Likewise, he strokes his right side and his face with the upper part [of the hand]. ||75||
But in battle, the horse was urged on by a favorable wind.
If it neighs while moving toward the enemy, then it shall bring victory. || 76 ||
If an elephant engages in sexual intercourse while walking through a village, it will bring ruin upon the country.
The female elephant gave birth and became intoxicated for the sake of the king's rest. || 77 ||
If a tooth breaks in an auspicious place or on a tree, it increases fear.
O Rāma, especially during cruel times or at inauspicious planetary conjunctions,
one should hold a mouthful of water on the right side of the face.
Having grasped the hand with his own hand, [he should do so] either of a Naga or of another person. || 79 ||
Or raising his trunk high, or else his right tusk.

Otherwise, that which is perverted is proclaimed to be impure.
If he does not grant her an ascent [to his bed], she may go back home against his will. ||81||
Or a rutting elephant might abandon its pride if it were to become a source of harm.
The elephant, seized by a crocodile, emerged from the watery depths along with its captor.

The falling of weapons, goads, and banners from the elephant to the ground. || 83 ||
And whatever [fault] may arise from the throwing of clods of earth, wood, or dried cow-dung;
This escort is for the sake of victory; a counter-escort is not recommended. || 84 ||
When an elephant, though being restrained, advances toward its enemy, it is like a hero.
And then, apprehensive, he [beheld] that light with its pupils dormant.
But he who touches desirable foods as well as an elephant-woman (hastinī) [is likewise affected].
Rāma is provoked by the echo of the loudly ringing bells.
When the girth is being fastened, if it even cries out loudly;
And the elephant becomes joyful, following along on the journey. || 87 ||
In that same manner, he steps upon his left foot with his right foot.
And likewise, if he rubs his right tooth with his hand, [it portends the same]. (88)
Then it wraps around the ears and likewise makes them stiff.
It leads to victory for the king, even while producing a spray of water droplets. || 89 ||
One should wrap the left foot with the left [hand] and the right [foot] with the right.
And even while treading upon his foot, though stumbling and falling, [he did not falter].
And when he does not raise his hand from the surface of the earth.
And he was one who detested morsels of food along with his mother-in-law; he was wretched and increased the fear [of others]. || 91 ||
Exhaling with great effort, whether calmly or even with agitation.
It is declared to be terrifying, as well as moving in a contrary direction. || 92 ||
The destroyer of milk-yielding trees and shrubs brings about victory.
Likewise, O Rāma, he has wide-open eyes and has attained his station.
When a bull, a horse, or even an elephant advances against the enemy army, [it is a favorable omen].
From that, O descendant of Bhṛgu, defeat is to be known as its characteristic. 94.
And by beholding Khaṇḍamegha, he brought about the destruction of his army.
And likewise, she sat facing him, though the planets and stars were unfavorable. || 95 ||
During a journey or even in battle, there is danger from the falling of an umbrella or similar objects.
The wretchedness of those who are fierce should likewise be understood by the protector of the earth. ||96||
Men, horses, and elephants were delighted, and the smokeless fire blazed forth.
Furthermore, when the planets are in their direct course (anuloma), these should be understood as the characteristics of victory. 97.
The blazing of weapons and their emergence even from their scabbards.
At the time of battle, however, the signs of victory are to be discerned. ||98||
Crows engage in combat, and carnivorous beasts form circles.
When a secondary army appears above the main army, it should be recognized as a sign of danger. || 99 ||
An itch on the right hand and an auspicious shadow are favorable signs.
O tiger among men, at that moment, her splendor brought about victory.
O best of the twice-born, one situated within the divisions of an army becomes a source of fear, or else becomes a carnivorous beast or even a fly.
The hundred-petaled lotus, the blue jay, the peacock, the swan, and the pheasant bring auspiciousness. || 101 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Omens," within the account of Puṣkara concerning Rāma, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Puṣkara said:
O Bhārgava, in an auspicious location for the questioner, that which is to be known becomes auspicious.
Or if it is inauspicious, O Rāma, hear from me as I speak of that which is inauspicious. || 1 ||
In cremation grounds, slaughterhouses, dwellings, prisons, and houses;
In the mud and difficult terrains of the streets, and in empty dwellings; || 2 ||
In places overgrown with thorny trees, where walls and houses have crumbled to ruin.
One should declare it inauspicious if [the sound] comes from anthills, mice, snakes, or insects. || 3 ||
Especially regarding flowers that have been touched by or smeared with meat.
One should recognize the characteristics of victory in knowledge in places endowed with excellent trees. || 4 ||
Upon the banks of rivers and lakes that were covered with lush grass.
One who possesses discernment should utter auspicious words in various dwellings.
Anointed with oil, being lamented, and likewise having disheveled hair.
One should know that it is inauspicious for them when they approach one who is standing on the ground.
They were clothed in joyful white garments and were likewise of serene mind.
O twice-born ones, one should know that for those who approach an astrologer, there will be auspiciousness.
And many [demons] were there with staffs in their hands, likewise clad in saffron-colored robes.
Likewise, those with ointment on their heads, the shaven-headed, the fallen, eunuchs, and women. ||8||
Some held chains and ropes in their hands, while others carried moist fruits in their palms.
But those who ask [such questions] should be recognized as bringing all manner of fear upon men. ||9||
Clad in white garments and adorned with flowers, they likewise held fruits in their hands.
Those with jewels in their hands are to be known as auspicious, as well as those who utter words of blessing. ||2.165.10||
One should observe all the times for one who makes inquiries in the forenoon.
They are censured at the two twilights, in the afternoon, and at night. ||11||
Then, having established oneself in a peaceful direction, one should declare the success for those who inquire.
To the north, to the northeast, and especially to the east. || 12 ||
The thumb-nails, feet, thighs, ankles, scrotum, chest, and breasts;
The cheeks, the horns, the eyes, the ears, the teeth, the lips, the arms, and the head. || 13 ||
The neck, the back, the bladder, the chest, the armpits, and the joints of the thighs are heavy.
Thus, for one who touches or asks about auspicious things, such as those with names beginning with "puṇya" (merit), [there is no fault]. || 14 ||
The outer edge of the ear, the two eyebrows, the nose, the tip of the tongue, the neck, and the nape of the neck.
The navel, the hips, the buttocks, the shanks, the calves, and also the toes; || 15 ||
The lines resting on the hands and feet, and the whorls at all the joints;
One should point out "pārṣṇi" and so forth as names of women. || 16 ||
The head, the forehead, the chin, the mouth, the back, the belly, and the sacrum.
The belly, the head of the bladder, the penis, and likewise the two knees. || 17 ||
Likewise, [one should place] the heart on the ear-base, the eye-socket, and the side.
Those expert in the science of bodily marks (aṅgavidyā) should recognize these as neuter.
A [piece of wood] bearing a masculine name, firm, smooth, unsplit, and unpierced.
When one touches the ground with a limb that is level, composed, and free from pain; || 19 ||
One should predict the accomplishment of whatever purpose one may inquire about.
Even by an enemy [planet], when it rises; likewise, when that ascendant (lagna) rises for the querent. ||2.165.20||
If the rising sign is an enemy sign to the querent, or if the lords of those [enemy signs] have risen, [it portends misfortune].
But defeat must be declared when the eighth house from one's own ascendant is the rising sign. || 21 ||
O highly fortunate one, one should likewise understand the inauspiciousness regarding one's own zodiac sign.
O Rāma, likewise, when one's own ascendant rises, or when the ascendant of an enemy sign rises. || 22 ||
Whether from the ascendant or from the [natal] sign, when the third, sixth, or tenth house is the rising sign;
Or even when there is the rising of the eleventh house, or the rising of their own lords. || 23 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, it should be understood that the fulfillment of all goals belongs to the questioner.
Either in the ascendant, or in the fourth house, or in the seventh, or even in the tenth. || 24 ||
In the fifth or even the ninth house, the benefic planets are considered auspicious.
Malefics are auspicious in the third, sixth, and tenth houses, while benefics are auspicious in the eleventh house. ||25||
O descendant of the Bhrigu lineage, they should be known as the accomplishers of all goals for the questioner.
The benefics are to be known as possessing superior strength, while the malefics are likewise of inferior strength. || 26 ||
Likewise, a strong ascendant at the time of inquiry bestows auspicious results.
Thus, at the time of the inquiry, the king, having understood the auspicious [omens], [acted accordingly].
O Rāma, this journey should be known as auspicious; it is never otherwise.
And having understood the Jātaka at that most auspicious time of the ten-fold period, he [acted].
When the strength of the eightfold group (aṣṭavarga) is pure, the time for a journey is praised. || 28 ||
O best of the twice-born, for one's own welfare, one should always perform auspicious journeys and give gifts to another deity when one's own deity is inauspicious.
When given during the auspicious ripening periods of the planets and so forth, it shall truly accomplish its purpose as prescribed. || 29 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Application of the Science of Limbs," within the account of Puṣkara, addressed to Śrī Paraśurāma, in the dialogue between Mātaṅga and Vajra, in the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 165 ||
The illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, questioned Puṣkara, the son of Varuṇa.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the science of astrology."
The son of Varuṇa said to him:

In ancient times, Bhrigu addressed the venerable Lord Brahmā, who was seated in the midst of a host of celestial sages and who possesses the extraordinary power of protecting and withdrawing the entire world.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the course of the luminaries.
The blessed Grandfather spoke to him.

When you were born from my heart at the beginning of the Kalpa, I then spoke to you the twenty-four hundred thousand verses known as the Jyotirayana; that very same [teaching], O Mahādeva, I shall now speak in its most condensed form for you who have emerged, piercing through the flame by the curse of Varuṇa at this sacrifice, having been born in another life.
Upon hearing all that has been told regarding their previous births, their knowledge of astrology will manifest.

Then the Blessed One, the thousand-rayed, the stainless one with stainless beams, who is for the sake of security like a flame-tipped crest, is visible like the moon for the propitiation of the planets; he is as the moon is seen when positioned in the northern mid-sky at the conjunction of the planets.
And according to the circumstances, even the lunar mansions and so forth are praised when they meet with the stars and other celestial bodies.

Now, on whichever lunar mansion Mars attains its rising, from that point he forms the mouth called *Pūṣṇomukha* across the seventh, eighth, and ninth mansions, by which Brahmins who maintain sacred fires and those who live by fire are afflicted.
In the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth, he forms the one called *Aśvamukha*, which causes a great mortality.
In the thirteenth and fourteenth, he forms the one named *Vyāla*, which increases the power of serpents and predatory beasts.
The blood-faced [aspect] in the fifteenth and sixteenth [tithis] indicates war;
the sword-faced [aspect] in the seventeenth and eighteenth [tithis] causes the prevalence of thieves.
Now, when Mercury (Budha) moves through Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Rohiṇī, he traverses his ordinary course, which produces abundance.

When he is in Āśleṣā, Ārdrā, and Maghā, his course is mixed, yielding mixed results. Furthermore, in Punarvasu, Puṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī, it is a brief mixed course that yields mixed results. In Revatī, Aśvinī, Puṣya, Jyeṣṭhā, and Kṛttikā, his course is called "Fierce" (Tīkṣṇā), which causes conflict; yet, due to its conjunction with the triad beginning with Mūla, it bestows beauty, fame, and other blessings. In Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Citrā, his course is "Terrible" (Ghorā), yielding terrible results.
The planet Jupiter, moving through the zodiacal signs for thirteen months, becomes auspicious; otherwise, it yields painful results.

Now, regarding the movements of Venus at its rising and setting: the first four asterisms beginning with Yamya (Bharaṇī) constitute the first mandala, which produces abundance of food; the next four beginning with Raudra (Ārdrā) bring fear to the twice-born; the five asterisms beginning with Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā) produce disease; and the six asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā cause excessive rain.
In whatever country, substance, person, or lunar mansion the planet Saturn moves, great afflictions arise there.
In whichever direction the crest of Ketu appears blazing, toward that region the king should launch an expedition.
An eclipse—whether white, red, yellow, or black—causes suffering to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras respectively.
Agastya, when flickering and rough, is invoked for the purpose of paralyzing the crest of the peacock.

When the Seven Sages are of such a nature, and when even the three worlds are thus afflicted, the boy Kārttikeya rises together with the Kṛttikās in the northeastern direction; in such a time, there is affliction for children.
Jupiter, Mercury, and Saturn are stationary planets (*paura*);
Mars and Venus are moving planets (*yāyin*);
and the Moon and the Sun are intermediate planets (*madhyama*).
In that case, there is the setting of the planets together with the Sun;
conjunction with the Moon; and mutual combat.
One situated on the northern path, possessing excellent luster, becomes victorious.

When the *yāyī-graha* (the planet destined to march) is victorious and straightforward, the king should launch an attack against his enemies; otherwise, while the city-dwellers remain powerful, there would be the destruction of the marching forces.
When a lunar mansion is afflicted like [the constellation] Agastya, there will be suffering for that region, its resources, and the people born therein.
Or, the king should march toward whichever direction the earthquake moves.
If it falls with a loud crash and is long, there will be the death of a king.
In whichever direction the meteor goes, in that direction the king should march.
A meteor that emerges from the sun or moon during the day, which is upward-pointing, excessively thick, accompanied by sparks, and moves upwards, portends the death of the king.
If a halo is multicolored, there will be suffering for the subjects; if the halo is fragmented, the king should march toward that direction.
A most terrifying atmospheric crash portends the death of the king;
the king should march toward whichever direction it comes from.
A city of the Gandharvas appearing from the east portends great danger;
a white rainbow at night when the sky is cloudless portends great danger;
and a mock sun (pratisūrya) to the north or south of the sun, produced by the wind, [portends the same].
Stationed on both sides for great rain, and above for the death of the king.
Likewise, [a fire] below leads to the destruction of the people;
in both cases, it brings great fear from all sides and causes affliction to the three worlds.
The king should march toward whichever direction is ablaze with the fire of the quarters (digdāha).
If the indicator of the shadow is excessively bright, one should know that the king will die.

Alternatively, in the case of the *dhruva*, *dāruṇa*, *ugra*, *kṣipra*, *cara*, and *sādhāraṇa* [classes of constellations], any action performed according to its own specific duty—such as the rites beginning with the *dhruva*—attains success. However, during the *vyatīpāta*, *viṣṭi*, and *vaidhṛti* yogas, or when the asterisms are eclipsed (*astamita*), nothing at all succeeds. Likewise, it is the same regarding asterisms that are "sunned" (*arka*), "fiery" (*anala*), "smoky" (*rāhu-dhūmita*), "blazing" (*jvalita*), "burnt" (*dagdha*), or "pierced" (*viddha*), as well as those afflicted by various portents (*utpāta*). One should know that the birth-asterism (*janmanakṣatra*) is the one in which a person was born; the tenth from that asterism is the [second] birth-asterism, and the nineteenth from that is the [third] birth-asterism.
The second [asterism] from every birth asterism brings about prosperity;
the third brings about calamity;
the fourth brings security.
The fifth is the enemy;
the sixth is the practitioner;
the seventh is the one who brings death.
The eighth is friendliness;
the ninth is supreme friendliness.
In that regard, one should perform all rites for achieving prosperity, protection, and security during the periods of Maitra and Atimaitra,
as well as in the tenth lunar mansion.
Just as in ritual acts, [a deed] performed without regard for the lunar mansion or a "void" (riktā) lunar day is [ineffective].
O child, when the Sun is in Taurus, one attains success without a doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Branches of the Science of Astrology," within the account of Puṣkara told to Rāma, in the second section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Mahāpurāṇa.
Puṣkara said:
Then Bhrigu made a request to the Blessed Brahmā: "O Blessed One, I wish to know the wheel of the lunar mansions.
The Blessed One said to him:
"Child, the wheel of the zodiac consists of twelve signs."
Thirty parts constitute a sign (rāśi);
sixty liptās constitute a part (bhāga);
sixty viliptās constitute a liptā; and sixty further viliptās constitute a [higher unit].
Sixty *nāḍikās* constitute a day and night;
sixty *vināḍikās* constitute a *nāḍikā*. In that context, the breath (*prāṇa*) which occurs during a [single] *nāḍikā* is a *liptā* in the field (*kṣetra*).
Therefore, in as much time as it takes for a breath—characterized by ten long syllables—in that same amount of time one *kalā* of the stellar wheel (*bhacakra*) rises.

The entire stellar wheel [is traversed] in sixty *nāḍikās*. Therein, at the very beginning, the sign (Aries) is red in color, the head of Time, located in the eastern direction, belonging to the day, with its door facing east, four-footed, strong at night, moving, rising from behind, cruel, uneven, masculine, and the *nīca* (depressed sign) of Saturn. It is twenty degrees lower than the Tathāgata [sign].
The exaltation of the Sun is [the sign] Aries; its tenth part is the very high exaltation, which is the field of Mars. Its trine is likewise [the field of Mars].

The bull is white in color; it is wild in the face of Time (Kāla), domestic by day and night, and belongs to the southern gate. It has four feet, is strong and stable at night, and rises from the back. It is even, gentle, a female sign, the domain of Venus, and a trine of the Moon; furthermore, in its third part, it is in its state of extreme exaltation (*atyucca*).

The Gemini man holds a mace, while the woman holds a lute; they are green in color. They are the arms of Time (Kāla), belonging to the village, with two feet, and are situated at the western gate. In the eastern direction, they are strong during the day, possess a dual nature, and rise in the head. The male sign is cruel, uneven, and is the domain of Mercury. Thus it is said.

Capricorn is strong, a movable sign, rising from the back, a quadruped, a masculine sign, even, a female sign, the domain of the Moon, and the debilitation sign of Mars; its twenty-eighth degree is the point of extreme debilitation for Mars, while the fifth degree of Sagittarius is the point of extreme exaltation for Jupiter.

The Lion is lion-shaped, pale in color, the belly of Time, and a forest-dweller; it has its entrance in the east and four legs. In the southern direction, at night, it is strong, stable, and rises with its head;
it is cruel, uneven, and masculine. Its domain is that of the Sun, and its triangle is thus described.

The sign of Virgo is a young maiden standing on a boat, holding a lamp, and of variegated color; it is the waist of Time (Kāla). It is rustic, has its door facing south, is strong in the eastern direction, fixed, rising from the head, even, and gentle. It is a feminine sign, the debilitation point of Venus, located in the twenty-seventh degree; it is the extreme debilitation of Venus and the exaltation of Mercury, located in the fifteenth degree, which is the domain of Mercury and its trine.

Tulā is a merchant man; he is found in the market-street of the scales-seller, black in color, situated in the bladder of Time, rustic, with his door facing west, twice as strong in the eastern direction, a wanderer, rising with the head, cruel, and of an odd-numbered sign. Venus is its domicile; the Sun is its sign of debilitation, being at its extreme debilitation in the tenth degree of that very sign. Saturn is its sign of exaltation, being high up; it is at its extreme exaltation in the twentieth degree of that same sign, while Mars is its sign of extreme debilitation. Thus it is.

The one named Dhanvī is an archer, a man with the hindquarters of a horse, tawny in color, the thighs of Time (Kāla), rustic, and facing the eastern door; his first half has two feet and the second half has four feet. His first half is strong during the day in the eastern direction, while his second half is strong at night in the southern direction. He is of dual nature, rises in the back [of the zodiac], is cruel, masculine, uneven, the field of Jupiter (Jīva), and its trine is likewise.

The animal named Makara has the front half of a crocodile and the rear half of a deer; with its front half it is a forest-dweller and with its second half an aquatic creature. Kavera’s knees belong to Time (Kāla); with the front half it is a four-footed animal and with the rear half an insect. It is the guardian of the southern gate: with its front half it moves as a strong being in the southern direction at night, and with its rear half it moves in the western direction during twilight. It is the depression of Jupiter, and in its very western part it is the extreme depression. It is the exaltation of Mars, and in its twenty-eighth part it is the extreme exaltation.
This is the domain of Saturn.

The personage named Kumbha carries an empty pitcher on his shoulder; he is tawny, two-footed, rustic, and belongs to Time (Kāla). He is associated with the western door and is strong during the day. Rising in the head, he is stable, cruel, masculine, and uneven. This is the domain of Śanaiścara, and its trine is likewise.

The sign named Mīna consists of two fish facing each other with their tails and mouths joined; it is the color of a fish, has black feet, and is a worm-like creature. It rises in the north at twilight in the western direction. It is powerful, has its back and tail elevated, possesses a short nature, is gentle, even, and a female sign. It is the fall (nīca) of Mercury, and in its fifteenth degree it is the extreme fall (atinīca). It is the exaltation (ucca) of Venus, and in its twenty-seventh degree it is the extreme exaltation (atyucca). It is the field (kṣetra) of Jupiter.

Half of every sign is a *horā*. Among them, in odd signs, the first half belongs to Saturn (*saurī*) and the second to the Moon (*cāndrī*); in even signs, the first half belongs to the Moon and the second to Saturn. In all signs, there are three decans (*dreṣkāṇa*). These are the lords of the first, fifth, and ninth signs [of each sign]. For signs with doors facing east, the divisions begin with Aries; for those facing south, they begin with Capricorn; for those facing west, they begin with Libra; and for those facing north, they begin with Cancer. The ninth-parts (*navāṃśaka*) that begin each sign are the "excellent divisions" (*vargottama*). The final degrees of Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces are the *gaṇḍāntas*.
In each sign, there are twelve degrees for each of the two [planets].

For Mars, there are five thirty-degree divisions; then five for Saturn; then eight for Jupiter; and seven for Mercury. In an odd sign, there are eight for Venus; but in an even sign, there are eight for Venus, then seven for Mercury, then eight for Jupiter, five for Saturn, and five for Mars.

Thus, a planet occupying the sixth house (the *ṣaṭpadārtha*) becomes powerful when it is conjoined with or aspected by its own lord, Jupiter, Mercury, or Venus; if it is free from and unaspected by the others, it shall be weak. Furthermore, a planet situated in the seventh house aspects the sign with its full aspect.
The quarters situated in the fourth and eighth houses are to be understood as being seen by a full aspect; those in the fifth and ninth by a half-aspect;
and those in the third and tenth by a quarter-aspect. However, one situated in the first, second, eighth, or twelfth house does not see [the others].
Therein, the house situated in the middle is the ascendant (lagna), the rising point (udaya), the ascendant-cusp (vilagna-kendra), and the trine (trikoṇa).

The first house is called the body; the second, grain and family; the third, prosperity, warriors, brothers, and the name *duścikya*; the fourth, the house of friends, *hibuka*, happiness, vehicles, and the names *kendrapālaka*; the fifth, sons, *trikoṇa*, and intellect; the sixth, the names *upacaya* and *ari*; the seventh, wife, *jāmitra*, the path of setting (*astamārga*), decline, and the name *dyūna*; the eighth, the names *chidra* and *āyu*; and the ninth, the names *dharma*, *trikoṇa*, *tritrikoṇa*, and *chidra*.

The tenth house is designated by the terms *karma*, *kendrā*, *ākāśa*, *meṣūraṇa*, *upacaya*, and *apanaya*; the eleventh house by the terms *upacaya*, *āya*, *lābha*, and *dravya*; and the twelfth house by the terms *riṣpha*, *dyūna*, and *savyaya*.
The second from all those known as *kendras* is the *paṇaphara*; the second from every *paṇaphara* is the *āpoklima*.

The second house from the sign occupied by the Sun is *veśi*, and the twelfth is *bosi*; both are *ubhayacarī* (moving in both). From the Moon, the second is *sunaphā* and the twelfth is *anaphā*. In both cases, the ascendant is also included; these are designated as *durudharā* when associated with their respective lords. Here, the thousand-rayed Sun is not too high [in the sky], has the proportions of a *nyagrodha* tree, is of bilious temperament (*paittika*), has bone as his essence (*asthisāra*), is reddish-dark, malefic, a man, a Kṣatriya, the soul of Time (*kālātmā*), a king, facing the east or south, strong during the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). 5.

The Moon has a thousand rays; there he is circular-bodied, handsome, with beautiful eyes, composed of phlegm and wind, having blood as his essence, fair-complexioned, waning when sinful and full when gentle, a feminine planet, a Vaiśya, the pacifier of Time, a king facing the northeast, powerful in the northern direction, at night, during the northern solstice, and in the bright fortnight.

Mars has nine rays; he is short, with tawny eyes, reddish-brown, of bilious temperament, with marrow as his essence, blood-fair in complexion, sinful, a male planet, of Kṣatriya caste, the essence of Time, and a commander of armies. He faces southward; he is strong when retrograde, in the southern direction, during the dark fortnight, and at night.

Budha has eighteen rays, possesses a medium form, and has the nature of the Pramāṇa measure; he is like the inner bark of a bamboo, dark green as durvā grass, gentle, and has the nature of the nyagrodha tree. He is a neuter, a Śūdra, the speech of Time, and the crown prince; he faces north, is powerful at all times in the northern direction, and also during the bright fortnight when the moon is curved.

The Sun is seven-rayed, black, tall, of a windy temperament, sinful, neuter, the suffering servant of Time, and faces the direction of the earth; he is powerful at night in that same direction, during retrograde motion, and in the bright fortnight.

All planets are strong in their own year, their own solstice, their own season, their own month, their own fortnight, their own day, and their own hour; they are also strong when situated in their *vargottama*, in their exaltation, or in their triplicity, as well as when victorious in planetary war and possessing a radiant body. For the Sun, the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter are friends; Mercury is neutral; and Venus and Saturn are enemies.
The Sun and Mercury are the friends of the Moon; the remaining planets are neutral.
For Mars, Jupiter, the Moon, and the Sun are friends; Mercury and Saturn are enemies; and Venus and the Sun are neutral.
For Mercury, the Sun and Venus are friends; the Moon is an enemy; and Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are neutral.
For the soul (Jīva), the Sun, Moon, and Mars are friends; Saturn is neutral; and Mercury and Venus are enemies.
For Venus, Mercury and Saturn are friends; Mars and Jupiter are neutral; and the Sun and Moon are enemies.
Mercury and Venus are the friends of Saturn; Jupiter is neutral; and the Sun, Moon, and Mars are its enemies.
And at that time, planet after planet attains the state of being second and third, while Mars, having become neutral, assumes the state of an enemy.
In that regard, in the first month the embryo becomes a *kalala*, and in the second it becomes a solid mass (*ghana*).

In the third month its limbs form; in the fourth, the bones; in the fifth, the skin; in the sixth, strength; in the seventh, hair; in the eighth, hunger; in the ninth, agitation; and in the tenth, birth. Therein, according to the sequence of months, [the planets] are Venus, Mars, Jupiter, the Sun, the Moon, Saturn, and Mercury.

The lords of the ascendant, the Moon, and the Sun are the [relevant] rulers at the time of conception; whichever among them is afflicted (kaluṣa) causes suffering to the fetus during its own month. Whichever is defeated by another planet or struck by a comet or a meteor brings about a miscarriage during its own month. If the Moon is in the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth house from the natal ascendant, conjoined with malefics and devoid of the aspect or conjunction of benefics, it leads to death. Furthermore, if it is situated between two malefics in the first, fourth, seventh, or eighth house, or even if it is aspected by malefics in the sixth or eighth houses, it likewise results in death.

When the sixth or eighth house is occupied by any one of Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus, and that planet is aspected by a malefic in retrograde motion while not being aspected by a benefic; when the lord of the ascendant is conjoined with a malefic at the end of its sign; when the ninth *navāṃśa* is in any sign during the *saṃdhyā* of a malefic; when the Moon’s *horā* is present; when all four angles (*kendras*) are occupied; when the planets other than Saturn, the Sun, the Moon, Mars, and Rāhu are in the malefics in the first half of the zodiac and the benefics in the latter half; and when there is an ascendant of either Cancer or Scorpio along with the eighth angle—[these conditions lead to death].

When the moon has waned due to evil [planets] situated in the ascendant, the sixth, or the eighth house—namely the Moon, Saturn, the Sun, and Mars—and Jupiter is devoid of strength; or during a lunar eclipse when the Moon is with a malefic and situated in the ascendant while Mars is in the eighth house, one dies along with one's mother. If the Sun is in such a configuration, death occurs by a weapon. One should recognize such fatal signs (ariṣṭas) as occurring within eight years. Now, the degrees, minutes, and seconds of the planet at that specific time should be calculated by multiplying by 150 (half of three hundred and eighty). When reduced by multiples of twelve, the remainder constitutes the years, months, days, and ghaṭikās.

Situated in the twelfth house from the ascendant, a planet takes away everything; in the eleventh, half; in the tenth, one-third; in the ninth, one-fourth; in the eighth, one-fifth; in the seventh, one-sixth. A malefic does this, while a benefic takes half of that amount. When several planets occupy a single sign, only the strongest one [exerts this influence], with the exception of Mars. Situated in an enemy's sign, a planet takes one-third; those who are combust, as well as Venus and Saturn, do not take anything. If a planet is in a *vargottama*, its own sign, or its own decanate (*dreṣkāṇa*), the loss or gain is doubled.

It bestows only one great period (*daśā*). Thus it is determined that the lifespan given by whichever planet [is the ruler] lasts for as long as that time; the periods (*daśās*) are to be known from the ascendant (*lagna*), and the period is like the planet [in strength]. Furthermore, the ascendant bestows other years equal to the number of signs it occupies.

Regarding the order of the periods: first belongs to the strongest among the Ascendant, Sun, and Moon; then, in order of strength, to those situated in the *kaṇṭaka* houses; then to those in the *paṇaphara* houses; and finally to those in the *āpoklima* houses.

In that regard, the ascendant's *daśā* is auspicious for one who is situated in its exaltation, a trine, its own sign, or its *vargottama*; it is inauspicious for the opposite case. According to the influence of the planet ruling the ascendant, [the results] arise from planets occupying the same sign. A planet in the seventh house imparts its qualities to the lord of the ninth and fifth houses, while one in the third [imparts them] to the fourth; one in the fourth [imparts them] to the seventh, and if there are many [such planets], even a single part [of their influence applies]. Furthermore, in the final *daśā*, death occurs according to the influence of the planet in the eighth house: by fire through the Sun, by water through the Moon, by weapons through Mars, and by fever through Mercury.

By [the planet in] the eighth house being devoid of a planet, one dies by the body of that element; [specifically], by *jīva* (Mercury) one dies of disease, by *śukra* (Venus) of thirst, and by *saura* (Saturn) of hunger. If the eighth house is free from planetary conjunction and aspect, one dies by the death predicted by the lord of the *dreṣkāṇa* in the twenty-second [house].

At the time of birth, from the position where the Sun is situated, [the results apply] to the third, sixth, tenth, and eleventh houses; from the position of Mars, to the first, second, fourth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth houses; from Mercury, to the third, fifth, sixth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth houses; from Jupiter, to the fifth, sixth, ninth, and eleventh houses; from Venus, to the sixth, seventh, and twelfth houses; and from Saturn, to the first, second, fourth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh houses.

From the Ascendant (Lagna), [the planets are strong] in the third, fourth, sixth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth houses; from the Moon, in the third, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses; from itself (the Sun), in the first, third, sixth, seventh, tenth, and eleventh houses; from Venus, in the third, fourth, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh houses; from Mars and Saturn, in the third, fifth, sixth, tenth, and eleventh houses; from itself (Mercury), in the first, second, fourth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses; and from Mercury, in the third, fifth, sixth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth houses.

[The planet] is auspicious in the sixth, eighth, eleventh, and twelfth houses from Venus; in the first, fourth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses from Saturn; in the first, third, sixth, tenth, and eleventh houses from the Ascendant; in the fifth, sixth, eighth, ninth, and eleventh houses from Mercury; in the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses from the Moon; in the first, second, fourth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and eleventh houses from Mars; in the first, third, fifth, sixth, ninth, eleventh, and twelfth houses from itself (the Sun);
and it is auspicious in the sixth, eighth, eleventh, and twelfth houses from Jupiter.

Jupiter is strong in the first, third, fourth, fifth, eighth, ninth, and eleventh houses from Venus; in the first, second, fourth, seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, and eleventh houses from Saturn; in the first, second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses from the Ascendant; in the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses from the Sun; in the second, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh houses from the Ninth House (Dharma); and in the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses from Mars. [The same applies] from Mercury.

From the soul (jīva), [the results are obtained] in the first, second, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, tenth, and eleventh houses; from the lord of the house, [they are obtained] in the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, eighth, tenth, and eleventh houses.

From Venus, [the results are obtained] in the 2nd, 5th, 6th, 9th, 10th, and 11th houses; from Saturn, in the 3rd, 5th, 7th, 10th, and 11th houses; from the Ascendant (Lagna), in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 10th, and 11th houses; from Jupiter (Jīva), in the 5th, 8th, 9th, and 11th houses; from oneself (Svāt), in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 5th, 8th, 9th, and 11th houses; from Saturn, in the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th, 9th, and 11th houses; from the Ascendant, in the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 8th, 9th, and 11th houses; and from the Sun (Saura), in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, 7th, 8th, 10th, and 11th houses.

From the Moon, [the planets] in the 2nd, 6th, 1st, and 11th houses; from Mars, in the 3rd, 5th, 6th, 10th, and 11th houses; from Mercury, in the 6th, 9th, 10th, 11th, and 12th houses; from Jupiter, in the 5th, 6th, 11th, and 12th houses; from Venus, in the 6th, 11th, and 12th houses; from the Ascendant, in the 1st, 2nd, 4th, and 10th houses—whichever [houses] have not been stated as auspicious, in all those [houses], every [planet] becomes inauspicious.

The distinction between auspicious and inauspicious results is granted according to the strength of the planetary periods (cāra); the fruit of the planetary periods is unfailing. However, the inauspicious fruit of the Aṣṭavarga is neutralized by propitiatory rites and the like, provided that in this context there is no Anaphā in the Anaphā position, nor is it occupied by a malefic planet.
And for all the centers, emptiness is not praised.
And [the signs] Cancer and the final degree of Pisces likewise.
Likewise, the enemy's domain, the debilitation of the planets, and their censurable positions.
Furthermore, those planets that enter the solar disc are likewise not auspicious.
The lord of the birth sign and the lord of the ascendant are both excellent when endowed with strength.
One should designate that person as unfortunate, whose these two are powerless.
Even a single planet situated in the highest exaltation is likewise regarded as a friend.
It produces the status of a sovereign ruler, which brings about the destruction of the enemy faction.
A planet situated in its own exaltation sign while occupying the ascendant should be known as being exceedingly healthy.
Pride is not praised; likewise, it is declared [to be a fault] at birth.
Indeed, the Moon is to be known as auspicious when it is aspected by the lord of its own field.
O Brahmin, that [action] was likewise praised by his friends and censured by his enemies.
When all four of the Kendras are occupied by planets situated in their exaltation signs.
Then he was designated as the sovereign of the entire earth, having been born.
Or there may be three [sons] for him who holds the earth together with the oceans under his control.
But for one whose two planets are situated in the angles and the Moon is in Cancer, [there is success].
O twice-born one, that king was likewise designated by even a single [verse].
By means of all [these mantras] situated in the highest position, one becomes the sovereign of the three worlds.
Likewise in the field of friends, in one's own [field], and also in those that are the most excellent among the groups.
The placement of planets in their own exaltation or their own trine is commended.
Likewise, the conjunction of four or more planets is censured.
Likewise, kings in royal lineages [arise] through the planets occupying their respective houses starting with the third.
O twice-born one, kings born of other lineages [are also considered] when increased by five.
Especially when they have reached their exaltation in a trine, O best of the twice-born.
Benefic planets in a house cause modifications [or improvements] therein, while malefic planets cause the destruction of that house.
And likewise in the third, the sixth, the tenth, and the eleventh [houses].
And the stationing of malefic planets is proclaimed to be auspicious.
All planets are auspicious in the sixth house; they are not auspicious in the twelfth and eighth houses.
When the Moon is situated in the ascendant, people are foolish, except for those born in the signs of Taurus and Cancer.
When the Sun has reached the ascendant, those known as Jayabalānanās should be understood [to apply].
And those joined with powerful planets are to be known by their lordly appearance and conduct.
Likewise, those who have the Candra and Dyugra yogas, as well as those who are Puṣpa and Viśīla, are to be understood in the same way.
Malefic planets are to be known as having malefic strength, and benefics likewise as having benefic strength.
Planets situated in signs that are upacaya (houses of increase) from the Moon are to be known as endowed with wealth.
Thus has been stated to you this much of the essence, the supreme compendium of horā.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Birth Astrology," within the *Puṣkara-ākhyāna* concerning Rāma, in the second part of the second section of the *Śrī-Viṣṇumahāpurāṇa*.
Puṣkara said:

Then Bhṛgu, having approached the Blessed One—the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, the teacher of all that is moving and unmoving, and possessed of great fame—petitioned him:
"O Blessed One, since the science of astrology is difficult to fathom without calculation, please explain this secondary method."
The Blessed Lord said to him: "Listen, my child, to the science of calculation (gaṇitajñāna).
Time is without beginning or end; it is Prajāpati Viṣṇu. Knowledge of it, according to the motion of the planets, is calculation (gaṇita).

Among these, the passage through a degree of the sun constitutes a solar day-and-night (saurāhorātra), while a lunar day (tithi) is lunar (cāndra). A civil day (sāvana) is measured from sunrise to the next sunrise."
The moon's passage through the constellations constitutes a lunar day (nakṣatra).
For humans, a solar day and night (sāvana) consists of thirty such days;
for them, three solar days make a night, and [thirty] such nights make a day for the moon and the ancestors (pitṛs).
For them, the rising of the sun occurs on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
at midday on the new moon day;
and the setting of the sun on the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
At midnight on the full moon day is the celestial day-and-night (*divyāhorātra*), which is the duration of the sun’s passage through one zodiacal sign (*arkabhagaṇabhoga*).
Among those, at the sun’s entry into Aries (*meṣapraveśa*) it is sunrise; at its entry into Cancer (*karkaṭapraveśa*) it is midday.
The sun sets upon entering Libra; it rises at night upon entering Capricorn.
