When Jupiter is in the middle [sign] starting from Aries, the years beginning with Āśvayuja are those in which one lives.

At the rising of the sun at Laṅkā, at the commencement of the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, at the beginning of a solar day, at the start of Aśvinī, or at the beginning of Kiṃstughna, there is the commencement [of the year], whether during the night or at the time of sunrise;
and likewise the commencement of the *horās* and other divisions.

From Laṅkā to Meru, across the interval between the southern and northern regions, there is a meridian line; to the east and west of that, the commencement of the rising of the sun at the time of *balakāla* (the period of strength) occurs. That circle is the equatorial circle for the time of sunrise at Laṅkā.
Due to the influence of the caradala (ascensional difference), the sunrise daily becomes the equatorial circle for the equinoctial sunrise at one's own location.
This is the horizon circle (*kṣitijamaṇḍala*).

Therein, a solar year is determined by the passage through the zodiacal signs of the sun. Of those years, three multiplied by four constitute one Kali Yuga; twice that is Dvāpara, thrice that is Tretā, and four times that is Kṛta. Four zeros, followed by the numbers eight, three, and seven (4083), form a cycle of four Yugas (Caturyuga).
Seventy-one such Caturyugas constitute a Manvantara.
Fourteen manvantaras constitute a kalpa;
and within the intervals between the manvantaras, the duration equal to a Kṛtayuga is the junction (sandhi).
Thus, a cycle of four yugas constitutes a kalpa.
In one kalpa, there are seven zeros followed by seventy-three (703) revolutions of the fixed stars.
For the moon, there are five zeros followed by thirty-five thousand seven hundred and fifty-two (53,5752).
for Mercury: 8, 9, 8, 9, 9, 3, 9, 7, 1; for Jupiter:
For Venus, the [periods] are 12, 7, 3, 8, 3, 7, and 7;
for Saturn, they are 8, 9, 2, 7, 6, 5, and 9.
The rising periods for the Sun and Rāhu are 8.
For the Moon, the values are eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one;
for Mars and Saturn, they are the sides of a triangle (three, two, and one); for Mercury and Saturn, they are doubled and tripled respectively;
and for Jupiter, they are five, five, two, six, two, twenty-one, six, and three.
For Venus, the ascendants are 12, 7, 2, 9, 3, 8, 3, and 7;
for Saturn, they are 8, 9, 2, 7, 6, 5, and 9;
and for the Sun, they are 12, 9, 0, and 8.
For the Moon, the values are eight, four, seven, and six;
for Mars and Saturn, they are two, three, five, and six; and for Mercury and Saturn, they are two, three, and six.
For Jupiter and Saturn, [the degrees] are five, five, three, and six; for Venus and Saturn, they are three, five, three, and six; for Saturn and the Sun, they are one, four, and four.
For the node of the Moon (Rāhu), the values are 8, 6, 1, 11, 3, and 2;
for the node of Mars, they are 7, 9, 2;
and for the node of Mercury, they are 1, 2, 5, and 2.
The qualities and tastes of the node of Jupiter (Jīva-pāta) are [180]. Those of the node of Saturn (Saura-pāta) are 398.
[Those of the node of Rāhu are] 800, 125, 670, 84, and 1.

Among the seven planets, starting from the east, for whichever planet the number of revolutions in a kalpa—multiplied by eight—is divided by the number of degrees in its revolution, that very planet’s orbital circumference in *yojanas* is obtained.
For that planet which has many revolutions of its circle, its orbit lies above it;

for that which has few, its orbit is below. The square root of one-tenth of the square of the orbit is the radius (*karṇa*); the planet’s position is at half of that radius. The square root of ten times the square of the radius is the orbit.
Thus is the calculation of the circumference and diameter for all revolutions.

And where the unity of all the planets is observed, that is the orbit of the khara-sindu-yama (1400). From its *yojanas* and *taliptas*, the *liptā-yojanas* of whichever planet’s orbit is divided by the middle khara-sindu-yajña (4200) are obtained. Indeed, the orbits are equal to the *yojanas* from the beginning of the Kalpa.
Immediately after which, the sun dispels the darkness, appearing like a mass of light equal in measure to the orb of the moon.
The Vedas and non-Vedas [make] sixteen for the Moon;
fifteen for Mars;
sixty for Mercury.
Thirty-six for Jupiter;
thirty for Venus; thirty for Saturn.
The moon has twelve visible and invisible parts;
Mars has seventeen;
Mercury has thirteen.
Eleven for Jupiter,
nine for Venus,
and fifteen for Saturn.
Fourteen parts minus one-third belong to the Sun;
thirty-one parts and thirty-six *liptās* belong to the Moon;
and seventy [parts] belong to Mars.
Eight Rāmas belong to Mercury;
seven Rāmas belong to Jupiter;
eleven belong to Venus.
The [paridhi] of Saturn is thirty. Thus are the paridhis of Mars.
And the swift paridhis, multiplied by the [number of] houses, are forty for Mercury.
The portions for Jupiter are eight times those of Yama, Agni, and the Moon;
for Venus, they are the Vasus, Arthas, and Pakṣas.
Twenty-five [days] belong to the solar [year]. By means of a halo, the motion of the planets above and below is to be known.
The first sine [jyā] is ninety-six parts of sixty thousand.

Thus, having first divided the first chord-difference by its own first sine-value and subtracted the quotient from that first chord-difference, the second chord-difference added to the sum of the first and second chord-differences becomes the second sine.
Then, having subtracted the quotient obtained by dividing the first sine by itself from the second chord-difference, the third chord-difference is obtained.
Subsequently, the sum of the second and first sines becomes the third sine.
Then, having subtracted the fourth sine-difference from the first sine, [one obtains the second].
Having thus added [the result] to the third sine, one obtains the fourth sine.
Having divided that by the first sine and subtracted the quotient from the interval between the fourth and fifth sines, one obtains the interval between the fifth and sixth sines.
Then, having added that to the fourth sine, one obtains the sixth sine.
Then, having subtracted the first sine-derived difference from the fifth [sine], and having added the sixth sine-difference to the fifth sine, one obtains the seventh sine.
Then, having subtracted the first sine-derived difference from the seventh sine-difference, one obtains the eighth;
having added that to the seventh sine, one obtains the ninth sine.
Then, having subtracted from the tenth sine-difference the quotient obtained by dividing the first sine-difference into the tenth sine-difference, one obtains the ninth sine-difference.
Having added that to the ninth sine, the tenth sine is obtained.
From that, the quotient obtained by dividing into the first sine-difference [is the eighth sine-difference].
Having subtracted the twelfth chord-interval from the eleventh chord-interval,
and having added that result to the eleventh chord, the twelfth chord is obtained.
Then, having subtracted the quotient obtained by dividing the first chord into the twelfth chord-interval from the twelfth chord-interval, the thirteenth chord-interval is obtained.
Having added that [value] to the thirteenth sine, one obtains the fourteenth sine.
Then, having subtracted the result obtained from the first sine from the interval of the fourteenth sine, one obtains the fifteenth sine-interval.
Then, having added that to the fourteenth sine, one obtains the fifteenth sine.
Then, having subtracted the first chord-result from the fifteenth interval between chords, one obtains the sixteenth interval between chords;
that, having been subtracted from the fifteenth sine, becomes the sixteenth sine.
Then, having subtracted the first chord-result from the sixteenth interval between chords, one obtains the seventeenth interval between chords.
Having added that to the sixteenth sine, the seventeenth sine is obtained;
then, subtracting the result obtained from the first sine from the interval between the seventeenth sine, the eighteenth sine interval is found.
Having added those seventeen to the chord of life, the eighteenth chord is obtained;
then,
having subtracted the nineteenth chord-interval from the eighteenth chord-interval, [the result is the twentieth].
Then, having added the nineteenth sine to the eighteenth sine, one obtains the twentieth sine.
Next, having subtracted the value obtained from the first sine from the interval between the nineteenth and twentieth sines,
that result is added to the nineteenth sine to obtain the twentieth sine.
Then, having subtracted the value obtained by the first chord from the twenty-first interval between chords, and having added that to the twentieth chord,
one obtains the twenty-first chord.
Then, having subtracted the value obtained by the first chord from the twenty-second interval between chords, [one obtains the twenty-second chord].
Having added that [value] to the twenty-first chord, one obtains the twenty-second chord;
then, having subtracted the value obtained from the first chord from the interval between the twenty-second and twenty-third chords, one obtains the twenty-third chordal interval.
Having added that [twenty-second] to the twenty-third chord, the twenty-third chord is obtained.
Then, having subtracted the first chord-obtained from the twenty-third chord-interval, the twenty-fourth chord-interval is obtained.
Having added that to the twenty-third chord, the twenty-fourth chord is obtained.
Then, having subtracted the first chord obtained from the twenty-fourth chord-interval, one obtains the twenty-fifth chord-interval.
By adding that to the twenty-fourth sine (jīvā), the twenty-fifth sine is produced.
And in the orbit where the diameter is one thousand two hundred [units], that same [interval] serves as the basis for successive placement.

When the intervals between the inverted sines (jyāntavyasta) are added together, they amount to twenty-four minutes of arc (śara). The square of the sequential sine (kramajyā) is determined by the sines of those minutes of arc for which the sine is being calculated; its designation as a "quarter" (pada) depends on its central point (kendrastha): if it is situated in the first quarter, it is additive; if it is situated in the fourth quarter, it is subtracted from the circle (cakra).
The minutes of the central point of the sine (jyākendra-liptā) are to be divided by the eighth part of the minutes of a zodiacal sign (rāśi-liptā).
Those with obtained whole-number parts should be set aside.
The remainder should then be multiplied by the interval of the sine (jyāntara) and divided by one-eighth of a degree in minutes (rāśiliptā).
Having added the quotient obtained for the established sine (*sthāpitajīvā*) to the desired sine, the calculation is complete.
From the moments of time converted into *liptās*, a sine must be computed.

From those *liptās*, subtract as many intervals between sines as can be subtracted; then multiply the remaining degrees and *liptās* by eight and divide by the unsubtracted interval between sines. Add the resulting product to the initial eight parts of the degrees and *liptās*.
In this manner, by means of the intervals between the arrows, the bow and arrow [are determined]; the maximum declination-chord (*paramāpakramajyā*) at twenty-four degrees is established.
A planet situated in Aries and so forth stands upon the equinoctial line (*viṣuvallekhā*), while one situated in Cancer and so forth stands within the interval of the maximum declination.

When situated in Libra and so forth, it is on the equinoctial line; when situated in Capricorn and so forth, it is to the south. One should divide [the sine of the argument] by the radius multiplied by the maximum declination. The result is the true latitude (vikṣepa) of the Moon. For Mercury and Venus, one should add the instantaneous true equation of center to the apogee. Then, one should divide [the sine of the argument] by the true hypotenuse multiplied by their respective maximum latitudes. The result is their true latitude.

One should multiply the sine of the sum of the true planet at that time and its true node by the mean latitude of Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn, and divide it by their true apsidal radius; the result is their true latitude.

The sum of the declination-arc and the true latitude, when they are of the same direction, is the declination of that [planet]; the subtraction of one from the other leaves the direction, and the planet is situated in that respective hemisphere.
In this manner, the motion of the planets toward the north or south is to be known.
Moving by way of the western direction, they cause the rising and setting [of the stars] through the power of the celestial sphere (bhacakravasa);

moving toward the east, they complete the revolutions of the zodiacal circle (bhagaṇaparivarta). And therein, simultaneously with the fall of the Sun’s horses, at the end of Phālguna, at the beginning of the Kalpa, at sunrise on the meridian line of Laṅkā, all [the planets] are situated at the junction of Pisces and Aries.

At the end of the eon, or at the sun's entry into Aries when the sun is situated in the middle of the sky, one should take the shadow on level ground using a gnomon twelve *aṅgulas* long. One should divide the square of that shadow by the product of the square of the radius (*vyāsārdha*) and the sum of the squares of the shadow and the gnomon; the result is the square of the latitude-sine (*akṣajyā*). The square root of that is the latitude-sine, and its arc is the latitude of one's own location. Subtracting that from three signs (90°) yields the colatitude (*avalambaka*) of one's own location.

The sine of that [latitude] is the multiplier-sine; it is the square root of the square of the radius (trijyā) diminished by the square of its own oblique ascension (krānti). Its direction is determined by its own oblique ascension. Multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by the gnomon (śaku), it is the [sine of] the horizon-point (kṣitijā). That, multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of its own day, is the sine of increase or decrease (kṣayavṛddhijyā).
The arc of that is the half-ascensional difference (carārdha), or the breaths (prāṇas); the ghatis of that, added to fifteen ghatis, constitute half the day.

When subtracted, they are the remaining portion of the night. Thus it is for those situated in the northern hemisphere; for the southern, the process is reversed, involving subtraction of their respective parts, while there is no understanding of the arcs on the left.

Purification (*śodhana*) consists of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) arising from the groups of two syllables, [applied] in direct order to Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, and in reverse order to Cancer, Leo, and Virgo.
The vital breaths of the *cara* [periods] for Aries, Taurus, and Gemini, beginning with Jupiter (*jīva*), should be calculated as before.

Their understanding and purification [are as follows]: by those [breaths] of one, two, and three syllables, Aries, Taurus, and Gemini are deprived of their breaths in direct order, while Cancer, Leo, and Virgo [are so deprived] in reverse order.

The movements of the planets are consistent with their own localities when they possess rising vitality; however, by the reverse process, for signs beginning with Libra and those beginning with Pisces, one must not perform a calculation of the longitudinal difference (deśāntara-karma) without first determining the east-west line—defined by the base of the midday shadow, the base of the southern and northern shadows, and the lines of the head and tail of the fish formed by the intersection of these lines—for either the Sun or the Moon at the time of an eclipse.
For example, if at the expected time of the eclipse the planet occurs within the meridian line, then one's own locality is known to lie upon that line.

If, however, the planet is first on the west line and subsequently on the east, then one should multiply the time interval between those two positions by sixty and divide by five thousand. This result gives the longitudinal correction in *ghaṭīs*.

Having determined the yojanas of the longitudinal difference, one should take two shadow measurements without overstepping the time of the sun: the first period from midnight until midday, and the second from midday until midnight.

Then Karṇa, having subtracted [the values] at the eastern and western ends of the gnomon from their respective positions, subsequently takes the equinoctial shadow on the desired day. This is added to the difference between the daily axial latitude and the equatorial axial latitude, provided they face the same direction; this result is the sun’s declination (*apakrama*). One should multiply the radius (*trijyā*) by that value and divide by the maximum sine of declination (*paramāpakramajyā*). The arc of the quotient is the sun: in the first quadrant, it is subtracted from the second sign;
in the third, it is added to the third; and in the fourth, it is subtracted from the circle (*cakra*).

The equinoctial shadow and the young (taruṇā) shadow—both decreasing and increasing—occur when the Sun is situated in the first quarter; it is decreasing-increasing when in the second quarter; increasing-decreasing when in the third quarter; and decreasing-increasing when in the fourth quarter. Thus, the difference between the Sun of the elapsed day and that [current] Sun is the true motion (*sphuṭabhukti*). Alternatively, having observed the Moon's rising from the sunrise or sunset of the Sun, the Sun is subtracted from that time to obtain the Moon; from the Moon, the knowledge of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is obtained. From the difference between the Moon and the Sun, the knowledge of the lunar day (*tithi*) is obtained; from that, the day-count (*ahargaṇa*).
The mean sun is derived from the true sun by means of the inverse operation.
A year is determined from the motion of the solar and Jupiterian [planets].
All planetary movements are like those of the moon; or, the knowledge of the time elapsed since the beginning of the Kalpa is derived from the planets. Thus is the determination of time.

The fixed values (dhruvakas) for Aśvinī and the other nakṣatras, beginning with their zodiacal signs, are as follows: zero and eight; zero, zero, zero, and five; zero, one, seven, and eight; one, nine, and one; one, two, and three; zero and two; mountains (seven), zero, and three; three, zero, and three; zero, three, and sixteen; zero, three, and twenty-four; four, nine, and zero; four, seven, and zero; five, twenty, and zero; six, twelve, and zero; six, nine, and one; zero, seven, and two; five, seven, and seven; and one, nine, and one. (Note: These figures represent the degrees, minutes, and seconds respectively for each nakṣatra starting from Aśvinī.)
Five, eight, and zero; eight, one, and zero; eight, two, and zero; zero, eight, four, and zero; nine, eight, and zero; twelve, seven, and zero.

Now, the portions of their dispersal (vikṣepāṃśāḥ) are: ten, twelve, fifteen, eleven, six, zero, seven, zero, twelve, thirteen, eleven, two, thirty-eight and a half, three and a half, four and a half, eight and a half, five parts, five, sixty-two, thirty; the division of degrees is twenty-four, twenty-six, and zero. [These correspond to] Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Maghā, Bhāgya, and Āryamāṇa.
The *yogatārās* (junction-stars) of all [the asterisms] are as follows: Svāti, Vaiśvadeva, Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Jāhirbudhnya, and Revatī belong to the east;

Uttarā-phalgunī, Rohiṇī, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Ārdrā, Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Hasta, Citrā, Viśākhā, Maitra (Anurādhā), Aindra (Jyeṣṭhā), Mūla, and Apvāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) belong to the south; and Yāmyā (Pūrva-bhadrapadā) belongs to the south. The rising of Revatī is toward the east. Each *yogatārā* consists of two *rāśis* and twenty-seven degrees. Agastya’s fixed point is at seven degrees [from the junction]; its southern declination (*vikṣepa*) is seven degrees.

Now, the retrograde central points (*vakra-kendra*) for Mars and the other planets, expressed in signs and so forth, are: five, nine, zero, four, six, two, zero, five, four, zero, five, fifteen, zero, four, thirteen, and zero.

Next, the non-retrograde central points (*anuvakra-kendra*) are: six, sixteen, zero, seven, four, zero, six, two, zero, six, twenty-five, zero, zero, fourteen, zero, six, and zero; seventeen, and zero.

Then, the central points for the rising of the eastern gate (*pūrvadvārodya-kendra*) are: zero, eight, two, zero, six, twenty-five, zero, zero, fourteen, zero, six, and zero; zero, zero, seventeen, and zero.

Now, the ascensional differences (kendra) for the western half-setting of [the planets] are: eleven, two, zero, five, five, zero, eleven, sixteen, zero, twenty-five, seven, and twenty-seven, zero, eleven, thirteen, and zero. Next, the ascensional differences for the eastern half-setting of Mercury and Venus are: ten, ten, zero, eleven, sixteen, zero, four, zeros, four, zeros, five, four, six, three, fire (three), Yama (two), wing (two), eight, arrow (five), and moon (one). These are the rising times of the asterisms in the order of their calculation; these same values, when subtracted from the solar revolutions, give the number of days.

The solar revolutions multiplied by twelve are the months; those multiplied by thirty are the days. The lunar revolutions multiplied by twenty-seven are the days of the asterisms (*nakṣatra*). The difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon is the lunar revolution; that multiplied by thirty is the lunar month. The intercalary months are the lunar months minus the solar months; the lunar day is the difference between the days. The *avama* (omitted lunar days) is the difference between the days.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Instruments," in the *Puṣkara-upākhyāna* addressed to Rāma, within the second section of the *Mānava-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Then, according to the time [elapsed],
the elapsed years should be multiplied by seventy-one and divided by the number of years in four yugas;
the measure of the Kṛta age should be added to those results.

That same [value] is then multiplied by the elapsed number of *manvantaras*; then the years of the current *caturyuga* are multiplied by the number of elapsed *caturyugas*, as well as the elapsed *yugas*. Furthermore, the years elapsed since the beginning of Caitra in the current *yuga* are added. In this way, the total number of years for the desired time is obtained.

That [total] is multiplied by twelve and increased by the months elapsed since the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra; then, divided by thirty, it is increased by the lunar days (*tithis*) elapsed from the first day.
Thus, the solar number of days is obtained.
Multiply that by the intercalary months of the separate kalpa and divide by the days of the kalpa;
the quotient is the elapsed intercalary months.
When the solar day-count (sūryāhargaṇa) is increased by thirty years multiplied by those [intercalary months], it becomes the lunar day-count (candrāhargaṇa).
One should divide that [intercalary remainder], diminished by the great aeon (*kalpa*), by the days of the moon in a kalpa.
The quotient obtained is the elapsed lunar nights; these [nights] are added to the lunar day-count (*candrāhargaṇa*) to become the calculated day-count (*sādhanāhargaṇa*).

When the intercalary remainder is divided by the intercalary months of a kalpa, and also divided by the future intercalary months, the time consisting of days and so forth for the elapsed intercalary month is obtained. Having subtracted the intercalary remainder from the solar days of a kalpa, when the remainder is divided by the intercalary months of a kalpa, the time for the future intercalary month is obtained.

When the remainder of the *avama* (omitted lunar days) is divided by the *kalpa*, the result is the time of the future *unārātra*. When the remainder of the *avama* is subtracted from the lunar days of the *kalpa*, and the remainder is divided by the *kalpa-unārātra*, the result is the time of the occurrence of the future *unārātra*. From the number of years multiplied by five, the remainder indicates the year starting from the current year: the Sun (*Āditya*), Moon (*Candra*), Mars (*Bhauma*), Mercury (*Budha*), Jupiter (*Jīva*), Venus (*Sita*), and Saturn (*Saura*) are the planets in order. From the number of years multiplied by seven, the remainder indicates the lord of the year (*Saṃvatsarādhipa*) according to the fourth sequence.

From the solar day-count (*sāvana-dinagaṇa*) divided by seven, the lord of the day is determined in due order. The lunar day-count (*cāndra-dinagaṇa*) multiplied by one hundred and ten, when divided [by seven], has its quotient multiplied by seven; the remainder thereof is the *parvan* (lunar phase). Brahmā, Candra, Indra, Vaiśravaṇa, Varuṇa, Agni, and Yama are the lords of the *parvas*. One should divide the day-count by the terrestrial days (*bhūdināni*) multiplied by the revolutions (*bhagaṇa*) of the desired planet. The result, beginning with revolutions, is the planet at sunrise on the line (*lekhārkodaya*). In this manner, the planetary motion is calculated from the day-count.
Having multiplied the daily motion of a planet by the time required for the sun to rise from the desired moment until sunrise, one should divide that product by sixty.
The resulting quotient is added to the planet's position at sunrise and subtracted at sunset.
In the same manner, in the northern hemisphere, one should multiply the yojanas of longitudinal difference by sixty and divide by five thousand; in the southern hemisphere, the process is reversed.

In the case of the initial longitude (lekhāprāgbhāva), that which has been obtained is to be subtracted; in the other case, it is to be added. Thus, in the desired place and at the desired time, the mean planet becomes the true planet.

The Sun and Moon at that time are made true by the slow-motion correction (mandakarma) alone. Mars must be made true by four corrections: its slow-motion, its fast-motion, its slow-motion again, and its fast-motion. These are the operations (karmāṇi).

For others, the operations for slow and fast [mean motions] are as follows: there, the correction for Mars (bhaumamarda) is to be applied, as is its fast epicycle; Venus has two epicycles. Therein, among Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, the Sun is the fast [mean]. For Mercury and Venus, the Sun itself is the mean. The [true] planet is the center (kendra) minus the [mean] planet, and the [true] planet is the [mean] planet minus the slow [mean]. The sine (jīva) of the smaller of the traversed or untraversed portions of the quadrant of Mars’s fast center is to be divided by four hundred and twelve using the sine of the [fast] planet minus the slow [mean]. This is what has been stated.

When the acquired [result] is in a quadrant beginning with Capricorn, it should be added to the slow anomaly of Mars; when it is in a quadrant beginning with Cancer, it should be subtracted—this is the anomaly of Venus. One should divide the sine of that anomaly by the radius (nyāsārdha) and multiply by five. That anomaly, diminished by the epicycle, becomes the true [anomaly]. One should likewise divide the sine of its own fast anomaly by the radius and by five.

When [the correction] is obtained, the sum with the epicycle of Venus's true velocity becomes the true [epicycle]. From the slow-motion anomaly (*mandakendra*), one should calculate the sine of the arm (*bhujajyā*) and the cosine of the complement (*koṭijyā*) by adding three signs to the sun; these two, the cosine and the arm-sine, should be multiplied by their respective semi-diameters and divided by sixty-three.
The result should be applied to the half-sum of the arm and the complement: if the anomaly begins with Capricorn (*makara*), it is added to the radius (*vyāsārtha*);
if it begins with Cancer (*kulīra*), it is subtracted, and thus the corrected cosine is obtained.

The *bhujāphala* (arcus correction) is the arc; the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the square root of the sum of the squares of the *bhujā* and the *koṭi*. One should divide the sine of the *bhujā* multiplied by the radius (*vyāsārdha*) by the true hypotenuse. The resulting arc is the *phalakalā* (minutes of correction). In the case of a planet whose apogee is Aries and so forth, these are to be subtracted; if the apogee is Libra and so forth, they are to be added. These values are specifically prescribed for Mars in its dark (*śyama*) slow-motion correction (*mandakarma*). Having thus derived the true moving planet (*spandasphuṭagraha*), one should subtract the apogee from it to obtain the anomaly (*kendra*), and perform this same operation using the true equation of the center (*śīghraparidhi*). That result is to be added to the slow-moving true planet if the anomaly is in Aries and so forth, and subtracted if it is in Libra and so forth.

In the first [half] of Mars's fast motion, the planet becomes true by subtracting that [correction]; Mercury, Venus, and the apogee are to be made true by the reverse annual correction; for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, the difference between the current true planet and that obtained by the direct method using the final fast-motion correction is the true motion, which is the solar correction. One should divide the solar correction multiplied by the true motion by the minutes of the zodiacal sign; the result, according to the nature of the Sun's anomaly, is to be added to or subtracted from the planet in the same manner.
One should divide the difference between the last true anomaly and the anomaly of the apogee (or the node for retrograde motion) by the true daily motion of the apogee (or the node).

The quotient is the time in days and so forth from the beginning of the retrograde motion (and so on); if the anomaly of the apogee is greater than the constant [mean] anomaly, it is yet to come (eṣya), and if the anomaly of the apogee is less, it has already passed (atīta).

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Motion of the Planets in the Science of Astrology," within the account of Puṣkara related to Rāma, in the second section of the Śrī Viṣṇu-māhātmya-vajrasaṃhitā. || 169 ||
One should convert the precise planet into minutes and divide by eight hundred.
The quotient represents the number of asterisms, beginning with Aśvinī, that have been traversed by the planet; the remainder should be divided by the true daily motion.

The quotient is the time in days and so forth for the planet's entry into the asterism. The remainder is subtracted from eight hundred, and the resulting time is prior to the subtraction of the omitted lunar days (*avama*). Whether the degrees in the zodiacal sign have been traversed or not, one should divide them by the true daily motion.

The time elapsed or yet to come since the solar transit (saṃkrānti), beginning with days and so forth, has been obtained. Now, one should divide all the values from the distance of the ear (yojanakarṇa) down to the end of the final specific ears (viśeṣakarṇa) by the radius (vyāsārdha) in reverse order. The result is the true semi-diameter of the ear in yojanas (sphuṭayojanakarṇārtha). The dimensions of the planets in yojanas (grahapramāṇaviṣkambhayojanāni) are multiplied by the radius (vyāsādha) and divided by the true semi-diameter of the ear in yojanas (sphuṭayojanakarṇārdha). The result is the true minutes of arc for the diameter of the planets' dimensions (sphuṭagrahapramāṇavyāsakalāḥ). The true semi-diameter of the Sun’s ear in yojanas is subtracted from the circumference of five thousand [yojanas] and then multiplied by that same [value]; it is then divided by the number representing the Sun’s diameter (ravinyāsa).

The shadow of the earth obtained from the circumference of five thousand [yojanas] diminished by half the karṇa of the true zodiacal sign should be multiplied by the karṇa and divided by the shadow of the earth. The result,
multiplied by the semi-diameter and divided by half the karṇa of the moon’s true yojana-measure, yields the minutes of arc representing the magnitude of Rāhu.
One should multiply the half-digit-measures of the planet by sixty and divide by its daily motion;
the quotient represents the auspicious period (puṇyakāla) prior to and following the moment of transit (saṃkrānti).
From the moon diminished by the sun, converted into minutes of arc, and divided by the elapsed [daily] motion, one obtains the lunar day (tithi) beginning with the first of the bright fortnight.

From the remainder multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in elapsed [mean] motion, the time in ghaṭīs and so forth is always Śakuni until the end of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight; in the first half of the new moon it is Catuṣpāt, in the second half Nāga; in the first half of the first lunar day it is Kiṃstughna. One should divide the minutes of arc of the moon diminished by the sun by thirty-three. From the remainder, the time is determined as in the case of the lunar date (tithi). From the quotient minus one and divided by seven, the remainder indicates the Karaṇa starting with Bava. When the sum of the longitudes of the moon and sun—or the product of their latitudes—is divisible by zero, there is an equality of the declinations of the moon and sun.

In that regard, *vyatīpāta* occurs when there is a difference in the *nayana* (longitude correction) and the spheres (*gola*) are identical; *vaidhṛta* occurs when the spheres are identical and the solstices (*ayana*) are the same. When the spheres are different, one should divide the difference between the fixed values (*dhruvaka*) of the sun and moon by the sum of the daily motions (*bhukti*) of the moon and sun.
Having obtained the result, if it is added to the fixed value of the sun, [it indicates] whether the sum of the moon and sun is greater [than the full circle].

Then, the declination at that time is subtracted from the moon’s own declination; when the moon’s declination is less than the declination of the sun situated at the end of the first or third quarter, then, while the moon is in the first or third quarter, the time of the equality of declination is yet to come (*eṣya*) if its declination is less than the sun’s declination, and otherwise it has already passed (*atīta*). In the second and fourth quarters, one should calculate the moon’s declination as exceeding [the sun’s] in the opposite case of the direction of the latitude (*vikṣepa*).
The sum of two [longitudes] situated in different directions, or the difference between those in the same direction, constitutes Vyatīpāta; conversely, it is called the first Vaidhṛti.

In this manner, using the Sun, Moon, and Node at the desired time, the second [Vaidhṛti] and subsequent ones are determined. Then, between the first and second times, if the Node is either yet to come (future) or has already passed, the interval between those two is taken; otherwise, their sum is calculated. The first product of the desired time is divided by that [interval]; having performed the calculation repeatedly with that time as the divisor, the precise time is established through the specific operation. That is the central time of the Vyatīpāta node.
The conjunction of the sun and the moon, multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference in their daily motions, is the quotient obtained as the duration [of the conjunction].

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Section on Lunar Days and Constellations," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the second section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.

For the remaining small portion of the day that has passed, when subtracted from the night in the northern hemisphere or added to it in the southern hemisphere, its sine (jīvā) multiplied by the day-and-night period (ahorātra) and divided by the radius (trijyā) yields another divisor (cheda), which is the radius plus or minus [the result] according to the reversal of the hemisphere. This divisor, multiplied by the gnomon-shadow (avalambaka) and divided by the radius, is the gnomon (śaṅku).

The square root of the square of the operation (kriyā) diminished by the square of the gnomon (śaṅku), multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon, is the midday shadow. The sum or difference of that with the axial [latitude] (akṣa) in the southern or northern hemisphere is undesirable; therefore, subtracting it from three signs (90°), one performs a division by the degrees of its sine (jyā). The quotient obtained from dividing the preserved sine (anaṣṭajīvā) multiplied by twelve is the midday shadow. The hypotenuse (karṇa) is the product of three and the day-measure (dyu) divided by the quotient of the midday shadow in degrees. One should divide the triad (tridyā) multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse by one's own desired shadow-hypotenuse.

The obtained [value] for the northern and southern hemispheres, increased or decreased by the terrestrial sine (kṣitijyā), should be multiplied by half the diameter and divided by half the equatorial day (svāhorātra).
The result is the arc; depending on the reversal of the hemisphere, this, when diminished or increased by half the diurnal arc (caradalā), becomes the elapsed or remaining portion of the day.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Section on Shadows," in the Science of Astrology (*Jyotiḥśāstra*) within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Then, one should take the minutes traversed by the true sun at the desired time; these should be multiplied by the *prāṇas* (seconds) of the rising of the sign of the [sun's] declination and divided by the minutes of the [sun's] longitude. The result is the time in *dinabhāga* (day-parts) for the sign of the sun’s declination. If the sun is in its waning phase (from the 15th to the 30th day), the untraversed minutes should be subtracted from the *prāṇas* of the desired time; if it is in its waxing phase, they should be added. To this, one should add the rising of the sign corresponding to the subsequent solar rising. From the remainder, the signs and so forth are determined by means of the rising times of the signs that have not yet been cleared.

Thus, the time of the rising of the zodiacal sign (rāśi-lagna) situated in the [ascendant] is as follows: the times beginning with the portion of the sun traversed by the sun added to six signs are the times; and the ascendants multiplied by the elapsed minutes—when that sum is joined with the interval between those [times], the time of the rising of the ascendant is obtained.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Section on Lagna," in the second part of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Mahāpurāṇa.

Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are slow; Mercury and Venus are fast; and [the Sun] is slow when retrograde. When a planet situated between the slow planet (the Sun) and the fast planet (Mercury or Venus) is within the degrees of visibility or invisibility according to its time, then at the eastern half of its rising it is heliacally risen according to the solar reckoning, and at the western half of its setting it is heliacally set. One should divide the latitude of the true planet at that time by the product of the radius and the sine of the maximum declination. The resulting value should be subtracted from the planet if it is heliacally risen, and added if it is heliacally set. One should divide [this result] by the maximum northern declination; the quotient should be subtracted from the oblique ascension if the latitude is north, and otherwise added.
In this manner, the ascendants at the rising and setting of the planet are determined.

Then, from the interval between the planets, one should calculate the time as for the ascendant by dividing the degrees of the interval between the minutes of arc of the planets by the difference in their longitudinal components (*bhuja*). If the planet is retrograde, the result in days and so forth is obtained by dividing by the sum of their motions; this is the time for the setting of the planet. For the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), their twelve visible and invisible degrees are treated similarly. Having performed the two corrections for Agastya’s fixed point (*dhruvaka*) and the *kṛdikka* correction, one should increase that by two *ghaṭikās* according to the local ascensional value of the sign (*rāśyudaya*).
In that portion, there is the rising of Agastya; his setting is retrograde, and his daily rising occurs until the end of the planet, according to the ascendant.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Section on Rising and Setting," in the second part of the second section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*. 173.

From the ascendants of the rising and setting [meridians] of the Moon and the Sun, the times of moonrise and sunset are to be calculated. One should multiply the declinations of the Moon and the Sun at the desired time by the radius (trijyā) and divide by their respective oblique ascensions (vilasvajyā). The results obtained in degrees should be added to the desired [ascensional] difference (iṣṭeśa). Then, the sines of the altitudes of the Sun and the Moon should be computed separately and divided by the product of the sine of latitude (akṣajyā) and the cosine of the zenith distance (avalambaka).

When the shadow of the gnomon (śaṅkutala) is obtained, those two [shadows] are in the north during the night and in the south during the day. The sum of the twelve [units] and the shadow of the gnomon is the single direction when they are in the same direction; their separation is the difference when they are in different directions. This is the separate arm (bāhu). The sum of the squares of those two arms, subtracting the square of the hypotenuse (dṛk), is the square root which is the sum of the segments (kapāla); when there is equality, it is the difference. The direction arising from the first part is the close conjunction; the second is the union when there is a difference in direction. The square root of the sum of the squares of the first and second [segments] is the perpendicular (koṭi). The hypotenuse (karṇa) is the square root of the sum of the squares of the perpendicular and the arm.

The half-circle is fifteen [digits]; from that, the arc-seconds of the apogee are the lunar-month seconds. From that, the arc-seconds of the apogee multiplied by the lunar measure and divided by ninety—this [value] is applied when the apogee is situated in the first or fourth quadrant; when it is in the second, it is black. When this is made into a quarter of the lunar measure, the sine, cosine, and hypotenuse lines of the solar measure reach the state of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). One should delineate the measured horn when the sun and moon are facing east or west, respectively, in the first quadrant.

In this manner, having imagined a black dot as the sun on the second and third [lines], then, just as the moon [is placed] from the sun, so should the arms be given; from their tip, the hypotenuse (koṭi) should be directed toward oneself. Then, by means of that which is joined at its end, the eastern limit is reached again and again until the true family (satkula) is obtained without distinction. This is the correction for parallax (lambana). At the end of the lunar day (tithyanta), when the middle of the eclipse occurs, the moon is to be calculated like the moon itself from the second or third part; its declination (svakrānti) is to be subtracted if north (saumyā) and added if south (yāmyā) from the latitude (akṣa). That sine (tajjyā) should be multiplied by the difference between the mean motions of the moon and the sun, and divided by the product of the arrow (śara) and the radius (trijyā) multiplied by the sun.

The obtained parallax (bhavanati) is northward when the latitude of the planet's own position is greater [than that of the moon]; otherwise, it is southward. When the directions of the instantaneous lunar latitude (vikṣepa) and the parallax are the same, they are added; when the directions differ, they are subtracted. This result is the true latitude (sphuṭavikṣepa). By means of this, the corrections for parallax (lambana) should be calculated for the planets at the times of contact, immersion, emergence, and release, using the true positions of the planets increased or decreased by the slow-motion correction (mandaphala). The difference or sum of the mean parallax and the desired parallax—depending on whether their signs are the same or different—is the result.

Therefore, by adding those two—the mean positions of the Sun and Moon at their respective times—to the fifteenth [term], which is the duration in ghaṭīs, the results become the true [positions] at that time; when the correction for parallax is subtracted from half the difference between the apogees, the remainder, increased by the sine of the latitude (pīralekhā), becomes as in the case of a lunar eclipse.
